items.text: משנת הפתיחה: פטור מבכורה בשותפות עם גוי
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists five cases where a Jew is involved with a non-Jew's animal (buying the fetus, selling, partnering, receiving, or giving on a receiving basis) and is exempt from the firstborn laws, citing the verse 'in Israel' to exclude others.
items.desc: המשנה מונה חמישה מקרים שבהם ולד חמור פטור מבכורה, כיוון שהגוי שותף בו, ומסיימת בפסוק 'בישראל' להוציא אחרים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists five cases of partnership with a non-Jew's animal that exempt from firstborn laws, citing the verse 'in Israel' to exclude others.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בחמישה מקרים שבהם ולד חמור פטור מבכורה בשל שותפות הגוי, ומסיימת בפסוק 'בישראל' להוציא אחרים.

items.text: צורך בכל המקרים במשנה
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the necessity of each case
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why all these cases are listed, explaining each is needed: buyer might be thought liable, seller might be penalized, partnership excludes Rabbi Yehuda's view, receiver is needed for the next clause, and giver on a receiving basis might be penalized due to confusion with other animals.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע הוצרכו כל המקרים, ומסבירה שכל אחד בא ללמד היבט אחר: לוקח – להיתר, מוכר – שלא לקנוס, שותף – נגד רבי יהודה, מקבל – כדי ללמד על נותן בקבלה, ונותן בקבלה – שלא לקנוס מחשש חילוף.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishna lists all these cases.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע המשנה מפרטת כל כך הרבה מקרים של שותפות עם גוי הפוטרים מבכורה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the case of a buyer is needed to avoid thinking he brings sanctity, and the case of a seller is needed to avoid penalizing him for abrogating sanctity.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שכל מקרה נצרך: לוקח – שלא נאמר שמביא לקדושה, מוכר – שלא נאמר לקנוס על הפקעת קדושה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the case of partnership is needed to exclude the opinion of רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda), who holds that a partnership with a gentile obligates firstborn status.
sub.desc: הגמרא ממשיכה לתרץ: מקרה השותפות בא להוציא מדעת רבי יהודה שחייב בבכורה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the case of one who receives a donkey is needed to introduce the next clause about giving on a receiving basis.
The Gemara explains that the case of giving on a receiving basis is needed to avoid penalizing the Jew, lest it be confused with another case where the offspring is a firstborn.

items.text: שאלה: דין עובר במכירה לגוי לפי רבי יהודה
items.text_en: Inquiry about Rabbi Yehuda's view on a fetus
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a related Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda permits a broken animal and Ben Betera permits a horse, then asks whether Rabbi Yehuda considers a fetus like a broken animal (since it is not whole) or not, because a fetus is naturally that way.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה משנה מעבודה זרה על היתר מכירת בהמה שבורה לגוי, ושואלת האם רבי יהודה מתיר גם מכירת עובר, משום שגם הוא 'שבור' ואינו ראוי למלאכה, או שאינו מתיר כי זה טבעו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a related Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a broken animal and Ben Betera permits selling a horse.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה משנה ממסכת עבודה זרה שבה רבי יהודה מתיר מכירת בהמה שבורה לגוי, ובן בתירא מתיר מכירת סוס.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does Rabbi Yehuda consider a fetus like a broken animal (permitted) or not, since a fetus is naturally in that state?
sub.desc: הגמרא מעלה ספק: האם רבי יהודה מתיר גם מכירת עובר לגוי, משום שגם הוא 'שבור' ואינו ראוי למלאכה, או שאינו מתיר כי זה טבעו ואינו נחשב שבור?

items.text: דחיית הראיה מהמשנה
items.text_en: Attempt to resolve from the Mishnah and counter-argument
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from the Mishnah's silence that Rabbi Yehuda does not dispute the exemption for selling a fetus, but the Gemara counters that the Mishnah also omits other cases where Rabbi Yehuda does dispute, so the silence is inconclusive.
items.desc: הגמרא דוחה ניסיון להוכיח מהמשנה שרבי יהודה אוסר מכירת עובר, משום שגם במקרים אחרים שבהם הוא חולק לא הוזכר במשנה, ולכן ייתכן שגם כאן הוא חולק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah's silence that Rabbi Yehuda does not dispute the exemption for selling a fetus.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ראיה מהמשנה שרבי יהודה לא חולק על איסור מכירת עובר, ולכן נראה שסובר שעובר אינו נחשב 'שבור'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara counters that the Mishnah also omits other cases where Rabbi Yehuda does dispute, so the silence is inconclusive.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את הראיה: גם במקרים אחרים במשנה שרבי יהודה חולק עליהם (כמו שותפות), לא הוזכרה מחלוקתו, ולכן אין ראיה מהעדר אזכור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yehuda does dispute the exemption for selling a fetus, but the Mishnah simply does not record his position.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסיקה שרבי יהודה חולק גם על מכירת עובר, והמשנה פשוט לא ציינה את דעתו.

items.text: ברייתא: שיטת רבי יהודה בקבלה ובנותן בקבלה
items.text_en: Baraita with Rabbi Yehuda's explicit ruling
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda rules that one who receives an animal from a non-Jew and it gives birth gives half the value to the priest, but one who gives on a receiving basis is penalized up to ten times the value and gives all to the priest.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שבה רבי יהודה מפרש: מקבל בהמה מגוי – נותן חצי דמים לכהן; נותן לגוי בקבלה – קונסים אותו עד עשרה בדמיו ונותן הכל לכהן.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda rules that one who receives an animal from a non-Jew and it gives birth gives half the value to the priest, but one who gives on a receiving basis is penalized up to ten times the value and gives all to the priest.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא בשם רבי יהודה המבחינה בין מקבל בהמה מגוי (נותן חצי דמים לכהן) לבין נותן לגוי בקבלה (קונסים אותו עד עשרה בדמיו ונותן הכל לכהן).

items.text: First attempt to prove penalty applies to fetus
items.text_en: First attempt to prove penalty applies to fetus
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes the penalty applies to the fetus, but then clarifies that the text should read 'her blood' (דָּמֶיהָ) and explains the case as a pregnant animal given for fattening, where the penalty on the animal extends to the fetus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the penalty applies to the fetus, then answers that it applies to the mother animal.
The Gemara objects that the mishna says 'its blood' (masculine), implying the fetus, and asks what a priest would do with a mother animal.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves a pregnant animal given for fattening, so the penalty on the mother extends to the fetus.

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof from Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof from Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi brings a proof from a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda permits a broken animal because it cannot heal, implying that a fetus, which can heal, is forbidden, thus supporting the penalty on the fetus.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that a broken animal is permitted because it cannot heal, implying that a fetus, which can heal, is forbidden, thus supporting the penalty on the fetus.

items.text: האם המשנה כרבי יהודה?
items.text_en: Alternative version: applying the proof to the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Some teach the proof regarding the Mishnah itself, suggesting it disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between a broken animal (not its natural state) and a fetus (natural), so the Mishnah can still align with him.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת האם המשנה, הפוטרת עובר מבכורה כשנמכר לגוי, סותרת את רבי יהודה האוסר מכירת בהמה שבורה. התשובה: אפשר לומר שהמשנה כרבי יהודה, כי עובר שונה משבורה – הוא במצבו הטבעי.

sub.desc_en: Some teach the proof regarding the Mishnah itself, suggesting it disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם המשנה הפוטרת עובר שנמכר לגוי אינה כרבי יהודה, שהרי הוא מתיר מכירת בהמה שבורה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between a broken animal (not its natural state) and a fetus (natural), so the Mishnah can still align with him.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: אפשר שהמשנה כרבי יהודה, כי שבורה אינה דרך טבעה, אך עובר הוא דרך טבעו ולכן אסור.

items.text: Second attempt to prove penalty applies to fetus
items.text_en: Second attempt to prove penalty applies to fetus
items.desc_en: The Gemara again tries to prove the penalty is on the fetus from a baraita, but again clarifies the text and explains the case as a pregnant animal given for fattening, with the penalty extending from the animal to the fetus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita of Rabbi Yehuda about a receiver of an animal from a gentile, to test whether the penalty applies to the fetus.
The Gemara asks whether the penalty in the baraita is imposed on the fetus.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the penalty is on the animal, not the fetus.
The Gemara objects that the baraita uses masculine 'דָּמָיו' (its blood), implying the fetus, and asks why a kohen would receive payment for an animal.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining the case as a pregnant animal given for fattening, so the penalty on the animal extends to the fetus.

items.text: Rav Ashi's repeated proof from Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's repeated proof from Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi again brings the proof from Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on a broken animal, concluding that a fetus, being able to heal, is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi brings a proof from Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that a broken animal is permitted because it cannot heal, implying that a fetus, which can heal, is forbidden.

items.text: בעיה: מכר בהמה לעובריה
items.text_en: Inquiry about selling an animal for its fetus
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new question: if one sells an animal for its fetus, what is the law? It considers the positions of Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, debating whether the leniency or stringency applies to a whole animal versus a broken one.
items.desc: הגמרא מעלה ספק: האם מותר למכור לגוי רק את זכויות העובר, תוך שמירת הבהמה? הספק נבחן הן לדעת רבי יהודה והן לדעת חכמים, תוך שקילת טעמי ההיתר והאיסור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: if one sells an animal for its fetus, what is the law? The question applies both to Rabbi Yehuda and to the Rabbis.
sub.desc: הגמרא מעלה ספק: האם מותר למכור לגוי רק את זכויות העובר תוך שמירת הבהמה, וספק זה נבחן הן לדעת רבי יהודה והן לדעת חכמים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara considers the possibility that Rabbi Yehuda only permits a broken animal because it will not be confused with a whole one, but a whole animal is forbidden.
sub.desc: הצד ראשון בספק: רבי יהודה מתיר רק שבורה שאינה באה להחליף, אבל שלמה הבאה להחליף – אסור, ולכן מכר לעובריה אסור.

sub.text_en: Gemara's alternative reasoning for Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: perhaps Rabbi Yehuda permits a broken animal because it is detached from him, and all the more so a whole animal which is not detached.
sub.desc: הצד שני: ומה שבורה שפסקה ממנו מותרת, כל שכן שלמה שלא פסקה ממנו – מותרת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara considers the possibility that the Rabbis only forbid a broken animal because it is detached from him, but a whole animal which is not detached is permitted.
sub.desc: הצד ראשון לדעת חכמים: חכמים אוסרים רק שבורה שפסקה ממנו, אבל שלמה שלא פסקה ממנו – מתירים.

sub.text_en: Gemara's alternative reasoning for the Rabbis
sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: perhaps the Rabbis forbid a broken animal even though it will not be confused, and all the more so a whole animal which will be confused.
sub.desc: הצד שני: ומה שבורה שאינה באה להחליף – אסרו, כל שכן שלמה הבאה להחליף – אסור.

items.text: בירור טעם חכמים
items.text_en: Clarifying the Rabbis' reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Rabbis' reason is indeed due to confusion, citing a baraita where they argue with Rabbi Yehuda that the animal can be impregnated and give birth, implying the issue is the fetus. Rabbi Yehuda responds that after birth, it will not accept a male.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת האם טעם חכמים באיסור מכירת בהמה שבורה הוא משום העובר או משום חשש החלפה. מהברייתא עולה שחכמים טוענים לרבי יהודה שהבהמה תרבה ותלד, אך רבי יהודה משיב שהיא אינה מקבלת זכר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Rabbis' reasoning is indeed due to confusion.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם טעם חכמים באיסור מכירת בהמה שבורה הוא משום העובר, כפי שנראה מהברייתא שאמרו לרבי יהודה 'והלא מרביעין עליה ויולדת'?

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: the Rabbis tell Rabbi Yehuda that the animal can be impregnated and give birth — implying the concern is the fetus themselves — and Rabbi Yehuda responds that a broken animal is like one sold for slaughter.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם טעם חכמים באיסור מכירת בהמה שבורה הוא משום העובר, כפי שנראה מהברייתא שאמרו לרבי יהודה 'והלא מרביעין עליה ויולדת'?

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis object that since the animal can be impregnated and give birth, one might delay slaughtering it.
sub.desc: חכמים משיבים לרבי יהודה: והלא מרביעין עליה ויולדת, ומאחר שכן ישהה אותה ולא ישחטה מיד.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda answers that after giving birth, the animal will not accept a male for impregnation.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה משיב לחכמים: לכשתלד, שהרי בהמה שבורה אינה מקבלת זכר ואינה יכולה ללדת.

items.text: דחיית הוכחה מהמשנה לקבלנות
items.text_en: Addressing the omission of 'even though not permitted' in the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita does not say 'even though not permitted' for the case of giving in kabbalah, but resolves that the Tanna taught sale and the same applies to partnership, and taught sale because it is the primary case.
items.desc: הגמרא דוחה את הראיה מהמשנה שקבלנות מותרת כי לא נאמר בה 'אף על פי שאינו רשאי', ומסבירה שהמשנה לא הזכירה איסור גם בשותפות, אף על פי שאסורה. לכן אין ראיה מהמשנה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: In the baraita, the case of giving in kabbalah (receiving an animal on commission) does not include the phrase 'even though not permitted', implying it might be permitted.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מהמשנה: בקבלנות לא נאמר 'אף על פי שאינו רשאי', משמע שקבלנות מותרת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: If the omission of 'even though not permitted' in kabbalah implies permission, then the omission in partnership would also imply permission, but Avuh de-Shmuel explicitly forbids partnership with a gentile due to the risk of a false oath.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה: גם בשותפות לא נאמר 'אף על פי שאינו רשאי', אף על פי שאסורה, כפי שאמר אבוה דשמואל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: The Tanna taught the case of sale, and the same law applies to partnership; similarly, the Tanna taught sale and the same applies to kabbalah, and sale was specified because it is the primary case.
sub.desc: הגמרא מיישבת: התנא נקט מכירה והוא הדין לקבלנות ולשותפות, והטעם שנקט מכירה משום שעיקר האיסור הוא במכירה.

items.text: ראיה אחרונה ממחלוקת רבי יהודה וחכמים
items.text_en: Final baraita with Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda rules on receiving an animal from a gentile, and the Rabbis say that as long as the gentile has a share, it is exempt from the firstborn.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שבה רבי יהודה וחכמים נחלקים בדין קבלנות, וחכמים פוטרים מבכורה כל זמן שיד הגוי באמצע. מכאן ניתן אולי ללמוד על דין מכירת עובר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda rules that one who receives an animal from a gentile and it gives birth gives half its value to the priest, and one who takes it on a receiving contract (even though forbidden) is penalized to give all its value to the priest.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שבה רבי יהודה וחכמים נחלקים בדין קבלנות, וחכמים פוטרים מבכורה כל זמן שיד הגוי באמצע, כדי ללמוד ממנה על דין מכירת עובר.

sub.desc_en: The baraita concludes with the Rabbis' position: as long as the gentile has a share in the animal, it is exempt from the law of the firstborn.

items.text: פירוש הברייתא: איסור נתינה בקבלה
items.text_en: Initial question and proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the fine of ten times the value applies to selling the animal itself or its fetus, and finds support from the phrasing 'up to ten times its value'.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה האם הברייתא אוסרת נתינת בהמה לגוי בקבלה, ומסיקה שהאיסור הוא על מכירת עובר קיים, ולא על זכויות לעובר עתידי. הדיוק מהמילה 'דמיו' תומך בכך.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the fine of ten times the value applies to selling the animal itself or its fetus, and answers that it applies to the fetus.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם הברייתא אוסרת את הבהמה עצמה בקבלה? ודוחה: לא, מדובר בעובר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports this by noting the precise wording of the Mishnah, which states 'they fine him up to ten times its value,' implying the fetus.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציינת שהלשון 'קונסין אותו עד עשרה בדמיו' מדויקת ומכריעה שהמדובר בעובר (דמיו לשון זכר).

items.text: Support for Resh Lakish's statement
items.text_en: Support for Resh Lakish's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this supports Resh Lakish's ruling that one who sells a large animal to a gentile is fined ten times its value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the mishnah's ruling supports Resh Lakish's statement that one who sells a large animal to a gentile is fined up to ten times its value.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling about a slave sold to a gentile being fined one hundred times its value challenges the previous conclusion, but is distinguished because a slave is constantly removed from mitzvot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the previous ruling is precise or not.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling that one who sells a slave to a gentile is fined up to one hundred times its value is brought as evidence.
The Gemara distinguishes a slave because every day the slave is removed from performing מצוות (commandments), justifying the higher fine.

items.text: Alternative version of Resh Lakish's statement
items.text_en: Alternative version of Resh Lakish's statement
items.desc_en: An alternative version states Resh Lakish fined one hundred times for selling an animal, but the Mishnah's case of a contractor (קבלנות) only fines ten times, distinguishing between sale and contract.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states Resh Lakish fined one hundred times for selling a large animal to a gentile.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah only fines ten times for a contractor (קבלנות), contradicting Resh Lakish's hundred-fold fine.
The Gemara resolves that a sale (מכירה) severs the animal from the Jew entirely, warranting a hundred-fold fine, while a contract (קבלנות) does not sever it, so only ten times applies.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding slave sale
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding slave sale
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling about a slave is cited again with a different fine, and the Gemara explains that a slave is not returned, while an animal is, but the fine is not increased because selling a slave is uncommon and the rabbis did not decree for uncommon cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the earlier statement about the fine is precise or not.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that one who sells his slave to a gentile is fined up to ten times the slave's value.
The Gemara explains that a slave is different because he is not returned to the seller.
The Gemara objects: since an animal is returned, why not fine the seller more heavily?
The Gemara resolves that selling a slave is uncommon, so the rabbis did not decree a higher fine for it.

items.text: מחלוקת רבי יהודה ורבנן בפירוש 'כל בכור'
items.text_en: Exegetical debate on 'כל בכור'
items.desc_en: The Sages and Rabbi Yehuda derive different laws from the phrase 'כל בכור': the Sages require the entire animal to be a firstborn, while Rabbi Yehuda exempts even a partial firstborn. An alternative explanation suggests they dispute whether 'כל' adds or subtracts.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה במחלוקת בין רבי יהודה לרבנן בעניין שותפות הגוי בבכור, ומסבירה שהם נחלקו בפירוש המילה 'בכור' והמילה 'כל'. מובאות שתי אפשרויות להבנת המחלוקת.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, stating that the Sages say a gentile's partnership exempts the animal from בכורה (firstborn sanctity) as long as the gentile has any involvement.
sub.desc: רבי יהושע מציין ששני הצדדים דורשים את אותו הפסוק 'כל בכור'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua states that both the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda derive their positions from the same verse, 'כל בכור' (every firstborn).
sub.desc: רבי יהושע מציין ששני הצדדים דורשים את אותו הפסוק 'כל בכור'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Sages interpret 'בכור' (firstborn) to mean a partial firstborn, so the Torah added 'כל' (all) to require the entire animal to be a firstborn.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסבירה שרבנן סוברים ש'בכור' משמעו מקצת בכור, ולכן 'כל' בא לדרוש שצריך את כל הבכור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda interprets 'בכור' to mean the entire firstborn, so the word 'כל' comes to include even a minimal amount of firstborn status.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסבירה שרבנן סוברים ש'בכור' משמעו מקצת בכור, ולכן 'כל' בא לדרוש שצריך את כל הבכור.

sub.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered: everyone agrees 'בכור' means the majority, but they dispute whether 'כל' adds to or subtracts from the meaning.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציעה הסבר חלופי: כולי עלמא מודים ש'בכור' משמעו רוב, והמחלוקת היא אם 'כל' בא למלא או לגרוע.

items.text: שיעור שותפות הגוי הפוטרת מהבכורה
items.text_en: Minimum gentile partnership to exempt from firstborn
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says even the ear of the animal suffices for partnership, but Rav Nachman objects. Rav Chisda and Rava debate whether the required part is something that makes it a neveilah or a treifah, based on whether a treifah can live.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בכמה שותפות של גוי פוטרת מהבכורה. רב הונא אומר שאפילו אוזן, ורב נחמן מקשה. רב חסדא ורבא נחלקו אם צריך דבר שעושה נבלה או טרפה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what minimum gentile partnership exempts an animal from firstborn status.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו השיעור המינימלי של שותפות הגוי הפוטרת מהבכורה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna answers that even the ear of the animal suffices for partnership.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו השיעור המינימלי של שותפות הגוי הפוטרת מהבכורה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects that the gentile could simply take his ear and leave, making the partnership meaningless.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו השיעור המינימלי של שותפות הגוי הפוטרת מהבכורה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda says the required part is one that makes the animal a נבלה (neveilah, a carcass that cannot be eaten).
sub.desc: הסתמא מביא מחלוקת בין רב חסדא לרבא: שותפות הגוי צריכה להיות בדבר שעושה את הבהמה נבלה, או די בדבר שעושה אותה טריפה.

sub.desc_en: Rava says the required part is one that makes the animal a טריפה (treifah, a fatal wound).
sub.desc: הסתמא מביא מחלוקת בין רב חסדא לרבא: שותפות הגוי צריכה להיות בדבר שעושה את הבהמה נבלה, או די בדבר שעושה אותה טריפה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute hinges on whether a טריפה (treifah) can live: Rava holds it cannot, so a wound that would make it a treifah suffices; Rav Chisda holds it can live, so only a wound that makes it a נבלה (neveilah) suffices.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבארת את מחלוקתם: האם טריפה חיה (ולכן דווקא דבר העושה נבלה פוסל) או אינה חיה (ודי בדבר העושה טריפה).

items.text: דיון בין רב פפא למר בר רב אשי
items.text_en: Reconciliation and objection by Mar bar Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rejects the suggestion that Rav Huna, Rav Chisda, and Rava disagree about the animal versus its mother, arguing both require 'all'. Mar bar Rav Ashi objects from the case of a stillborn, which is sanctified despite not being viable, but the Gemara distinguishes because a stillborn has no non-sacred mixture.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ניסיון ליישב בין דעת רב הונא לדעת רב חסדא ורבא, אך רב פפא דוחה את ההבחנה בין עובר לאם. מר בר רב אשי מקשה על עצם הפטור בשותפות בעובר, והגמרא מתרצת.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis before Rav Pappa propose that Rav Huna, Rav Chisda, and Rava do not disagree, but rather each refers to a different case: one to the animal itself, the other to its mother.
sub.desc: החכמים מציעים יישוב בין רב הונא לרב חסדא ורבא, בכך שאין מחלוקת: דברי רב הונא בעובר, ודברי רב חסדא ורבא באם.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects that both the animal and its mother require 'all' (כל), so the distinction is invalid.
sub.desc: רב פפא דוחה את היישוב, שכן גם באם נדרשת בעלות מלאה של היהודי, ולכן אין הבדל בין עובר לאם.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi objects from the case of a stillborn (נפלים), which is sanctified despite not being viable, citing the verse 'פֶּטֶר שֶׁגֶר בְּהֵמָה'.
sub.desc: מר בר רב אשי מקשה על עצם הפטור בשותפות בעובר, שהרי נפל שאינו בר קיימא קדוש, וכל שכן עובר עם שותפות גוי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes: a stillborn has no non-sacred mixture, so 'כל בכור' applies, but here non-sacred is mixed in, so it does not.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: בנפל אין תערובת חולין ולכן קרינן ביה 'כל בכור', אבל בעובר עם שותפות גוי יש תערובת חולין ולכן אינו קדוש.

items.text: שאלת רבי אלעזר לרבי אסי
items.text_en: Transition to next discussion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar finds Rabbi Asi and asks what the rabbis said in the study hall, setting up the next segment.
items.desc: רבי אלעזר שואל את רבי אסי מה אמרו חכמים בבית המדרש, וזה מתחיל לענות.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar, who did not attend the study hall, finds Rabbi Asi and asks what the rabbis said there.
sub.desc: רבי אלעזר, שלא נכנס לבית המדרש, שואל את רבי אסי מה אמרו החכמים שם.

items.text: Opening statement: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a minor blemish
items.text_en: Opening statement: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a minor blemish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that even a minor blemish (מום קל) exempts a firstborn animal. The Gemara notes that this is consistent with a mishnah about a sheep that gives birth to a goat-like offspring, which is exempt unless it has some signs of the other species, and then it has a permanent blemish (מום קבוע) for slaughter.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that even a minor blemish (מום קל) exempts a firstborn animal, citing a mishnah about a sheep that gives birth to a goat-like offspring which is exempt unless it has some signs of the other species, in which case it has a permanent blemish (מום קבוע) for slaughter.

items.text: Gemara's clarification: Minor blemish aligns with Rav Huna
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification: Minor blemish aligns with Rav Huna
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan's statement about a minor blemish teaches us the view of Rav Huna, and excludes the views of Rav Chisda and Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan's statement about a minor blemish (מום קל) teaches the view of Rav Huna and excludes the positions of Rav Chisda and Rava.

items.text: Question on permanent blemish: Is change alone sufficient?
items.text_en: Question on permanent blemish: Is change alone sufficient?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what Rabbi Yochanan's statement about a permanent blemish (מום קבוע) teaches, suggesting it might be that a change in appearance constitutes a blemish. It cites a mishnah about a mouth like a pig's as a blemish, and addresses a potential distinction between changes in species that are not sanctified in the firstborn versus those that are. It then cites another mishnah about one eye large and one small, and questions why a large eye like a calf's (a species sanctified in the firstborn) is considered a blemish, concluding that it must be because the change itself constitutes a blemish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yochanan's statement about a permanent blemish (מום קבוע) teaches, suggesting it might be that a change in appearance constitutes a blemish.
The Gemara cites a mishnah that a mouth resembling a pig's is a blemish, supporting the idea that change alone constitutes a blemish.
The Gemara raises a potential distinction that the pig is not a species sanctified in the firstborn, but then cites another mishnah about one eye large and one small to counter this.
The Gemara notes that a large eye like a calf's (a species sanctified in the firstborn) is still considered a blemish, concluding that change alone constitutes a blemish.

items.text: Rejection: It is due to the blemish 'Sarua'
items.text_en: Rejection: It is due to the blemish 'Sarua'
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous conclusion, arguing that the case of one large and one small eye is not due to change but because it is the blemish called 'שָׂרוּעַ' (sarua). It supports this by citing a mishnah listing blemishes that are disqualifying, and noting that for humans, both eyes large or both small are blemishes, but for animals they are not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous conclusion, arguing that the case of one large and one small eye is not due to change but because it is the blemish called 'שָׂרוּעַ' (sarua).
The Gemara supports this by citing a mishnah listing blemishes that are disqualifying, and noting that for humans, both eyes large or both small are blemishes.
The Gemara explains that for humans, the verse requires a priest to be 'אִישׁ' (a man) of equal appearance, but for animals, both eyes large or both small are not blemishes.

items.text: Further challenge: Why is one large and one small a blemish?
items.text_en: Further challenge: Why is one large and one small a blemish?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous answer: if the blemish is due to change, then both eyes large or both small should also be blemishes. It concludes that the reason must be the blemish 'שָׂרוּעַ' (sarua), not mere change.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if the blemish is due to change (שִׁינּוּי), then both eyes large or both small should also be blemishes.
The Gemara concludes that the reason must be the blemish 'שָׂרוּעַ' (sarua), not mere change.

items.text: Final resolution: Change is a blemish, but both large/small is natural
items.text_en: Final resolution: Change is a blemish, but both large/small is natural
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the issue: change does constitute a blemish, but both eyes large or both small are not considered a change because they are natural variations (due to excessive strength or weakness).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that change (שִׁינּוּי) constitutes a blemish, and both eyes large or both small are not a change because they result from natural excess or weakness.

items.text: Story of a female convert and Rav Mari bar Rachel's animal
items.text_en: Story of a female convert and Rav Mari bar Rachel's animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story of a female convert whose animals were entrusted to a gentile for fattening, and Rava ruled that Rabbi Yehuda's view (that partnership with a gentile obligates in the firstborn) is not followed. Then it discusses Rav Mari bar Rachel, who would transfer ownership of his animals' ears to a gentile to exempt them from the firstborn, while still treating them as sanctified. The Gemara questions why he did this, and explains it was to prevent a potential stumbling block, and that he knew how to make a complete transfer, unlike others who might mistakenly think it's a mere act.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story of a female convert whose animals were entrusted to a gentile for fattening, and Rava ruled that Rabbi Yehuda's view (that partnership with a gentile obligates in the firstborn) is not followed.

sub.text: Gemara's description of Rav Mari bar Rachel's practice
sub.text_en: Gemara's description of Rav Mari bar Rachel's practice
sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes Rav Mari bar Rachel's practice: he would transfer ownership of his animals' ears to a gentile to exempt them from the firstborn, while still treating them as sanctified.
The Gemara questions why Rav Mari bar Rachel transferred the ears to a gentile if he already treated the animals as sanctified, suggesting it was to prevent a potential stumbling block.

The Gemara answers that Rav Mari's transfer was necessary because it completely removes the animal from the priest's sanctity, unlike merely blemishing it before birth which only removes it from the altar's sanctity.
The Gemara offers an alternative answer: Rav Mari knew how to make a complete transfer, but others might mistakenly think it's a mere act and come to a stumbling block.

items.text: משנת כהנים ולויים פטורים מבכור חמור
items.text_en: Mishnah: Priests and Levites are exempt from the firstborn
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that priests and Levites are exempt from the firstborn offering, derived by a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if they exempted the firstborn of Israelites in the desert, they should certainly exempt their own.
items.desc: המשנה פוטרת כהנים ולויים מבכור חמור, ונובעת מקל וחומר: אם פטרו את של ישראל במדבר, דין הוא שיפטרו את של עצמם.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that priests and Levites are exempt from the firstborn offering, derived by a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if they exempted the firstborn of Israelites in the desert, they should certainly exempt their own.
sub.desc: המשנה פוטרת כהנים ולויים מבכור חמור, ונובעת מקל וחומר: אם פטרו את של ישראל במדבר, דין הוא שיפטרו את של עצמם.

items.text: Gemara's initial challenge to the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's initial challenge to the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's wording 'they exempt,' arguing that the verses explicitly state that Levites replace Israelites, not that they exempt their own animals. The objection is that the Mishnah seems to imply a direct exemption, which is not supported by the plain reading of the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's wording 'they exempt,' arguing that the verses explicitly state that Levites replace Israelites, not that they exempt their own animals.

Abaye explains that the Mishnah means that priests and Levites exempt their animals through a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if their animals exempted Israelite animals in the wilderness, they should certainly exempt their own.
Rava objects that the Mishnah explicitly says 'they exempt' (active), not 'they are exempt' (passive), contradicting Abaye's interpretation.

Rava further objects that if Abaye's reasoning were correct, priests and Levites would also be exempt from the firstborn of a kosher animal, yet the Mishnah states they are only exempt from פדיון הבן (redemption of the firstborn son) and פטר חמור (firstborn donkey).

Rava explains that the Mishnah means that priests and Levites exempted themselves (their own firstborn) through a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if their sanctity exempted Israelite firstborn in the wilderness, should it not exempt their own?

The Gemara asks: we have found the source for humans (firstborn son), but from where do we derive the exemption for a non-kosher animal? It answers by citing a verse linking the redemption of a firstborn son and a non-kosher animal, establishing that the same rules apply.

Rav Safra objects to Abaye: according to your view that the exemption depends on the Levite's animal having actually exempted an Israelite animal, a Levite who had a sheep that exempted would exempt his own, but one who did not have such a sheep would not exempt his own.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to both Abaye and Rava
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to both Abaye and Rava
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to both Abaye and Rava: according to either view, a one-month-old Levite who was counted in the census would exempt, but a Levite less than a month old who was not counted would not exempt — yet the Mishnah exempts all Levites uniformly.

The Gemara asks: would a female Levite not exempt her son? But Rav Adda bar Ahava said that a female Levite who gives birth has a son exempt from the five shekels of פדיון הבן (redemption of the firstborn).

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Yosef's resolution in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef's resolution in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava resolves that the exemption depends on the verse 'פטר רחם' (opening of the womb), which the Torah links to the womb, not to the father's status.

The Gemara asks: Aaron, who was not in that census (of Levites), would he not exempt his firstborn? But a baraita notes that the word 'Aaron' in the book of Numbers is dotted, indicating he was not included in the count.
The Gemara resolves that the verse says 'הלוים' (the Levites), implying that all Levites are compared to each other, so Aaron is included by analogy.

The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that priests are also exempt? It answers with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's statement that in twenty-four places priests are called 'Levites,' citing one example: 'והכהנים הלוים בני צדוק' (and the priests, the Levites, the sons of Zadok).

items.text: Abaye's explanation: kal vachomer from the wilderness
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation: kal vachomer from the wilderness
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Mishnah means that priests and Levites are exempt from the firstborn of their animals through a kal vachomer argument: if the Levites' animals exempted Israelites' animals in the wilderness, then certainly they should exempt their own animals.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Mishnah means priests and Levites are exempt from the firstborn of their animals through a kal vachomer argument: if the Levites' animals exempted Israelites' animals in the wilderness, then certainly they should exempt their own animals.

items.text: Rava's objection: Mishnah says 'they exempt' and excludes pure animals
items.text_en: Rava's objection: Mishnah says 'they exempt' and excludes pure animals
items.desc_en: Rava objects to Abaye's interpretation on two grounds: first, the Mishnah explicitly says 'they exempt' (active), not 'they are exempt'; second, if the kal vachomer were correct, it would also exempt them from the firstborn of pure animals, but the Mishnah states they are only exempt from redemption of the son and the firstborn of a donkey.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that the Mishnah uses the active form 'פָּטְרוּ' (they exempt), not the passive 'they are exempt', undermining Abaye's interpretation.

Rava further objects that if Abaye's kal vachomer were valid, it would exempt priests and Levites from the firstborn of pure animals too, but the Mishnah limits their exemption to redemption of the son and the firstborn of a donkey.

items.text: Rava's alternative kal vachomer: they exempt themselves
items.text_en: Rava's alternative kal vachomer: they exempt themselves
items.desc_en: Rava reinterprets the Mishnah: priests and Levites exempt themselves (their own firstborn sons and donkeys) through a kal vachomer. If the sanctity of the Levites exempted the sanctity of the Israelites in the wilderness, then certainly their own sanctity should exempt themselves.

sub.desc_en: Rava reinterprets the Mishnah: priests and Levites exempt themselves (their own firstborn sons and donkeys) through a kal vachomer, arguing that if the sanctity of the Levites exempted the sanctity of the Israelites in the wilderness, then certainly their own sanctity should exempt themselves.

items.text: Derivation for impure animals
items.text_en: Derivation for impure animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the exemption applies to impure animals as well. It answers with a verse: 'But you shall surely redeem the firstborn of man, and the firstborn of an impure animal you shall redeem,' teaching that whoever is subject to the redemption of a firstborn son is also subject to the redemption of an impure animal, and whoever is not (like priests and Levites) is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we derive that the exemption of priests and Levites applies to impure animals as well.

The Gemara answers by citing a verse that links the redemption of a firstborn son to the redemption of an impure animal, establishing that whoever is subject to the former is also subject to the latter.

items.text: Challenges to the kal vachomer: specific cases
items.text_en: Challenges to the kal vachomer: specific cases
items.desc_en: Rav Safra challenges Abaye and Rava: according to Abaye, a Levite who had a sheep that exempted others should exempt his own, but one who didn't should not; according to both, a one-month-old Levite who exempted should exempt, but a younger one who didn't should not. Additionally, a female Levite should not exempt, but Rav Adda bar Ahava says her son is exempt from the five shekels. The Gemara resolves this by citing Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava: the Torah linked the exemption to 'opening the womb,' so a female Levite's son is exempt because she has a womb.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra challenges Abaye's opinion: according to Abaye, a Levite who had a sheep that exempted others should exempt his own, but one who did not have a sheep should not exempt.

sub.text: Gemara's challenge to both Abaye and Rava
sub.text_en: Gemara's challenge to both Abaye and Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Safra challenges both Abaye and Rava: according to either, a one-month-old Levite who exempted others should exempt his own, but a younger one who did not exempt should not exempt.

sub.text: Gemara's challenge regarding a female Levite
sub.text_en: Gemara's challenge regarding a female Levite
sub.desc_en: Rav Safra challenges: a female Levite should not exempt her son, yet Rav Adda bar Ahava states that her son is exempt from the five shekels.

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava resolves the difficulty: the Torah explicitly linked the exemption to 'פֶּטֶר רֶחֶם' (opening the womb), so a female Levite's son is exempt because she has a womb.

items.text: Aaron's exemption and the inclusion of priests
items.text_en: Aaron's exemption and the inclusion of priests
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Aaron, who was not counted in the census of Levites, should be exempt. It answers that the verse says 'the Levites,' equating all Levites to each other. Then it asks how we know that priests are included, and cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: in twenty-four places priests are called 'Levites,' one of which is 'the priests the Levites, the sons of Zadok.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Aaron, who was not counted in the census of Levites, should be exempt from the redemption of the firstborn.
The Gemara answers that the verse says 'the Levites,' equating all Levites to each other, thereby including Aaron.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that in twenty-four places priests are called 'Levites,' one of which is 'the priests the Levites, the sons of Zadok,' to include priests in the exemption.

items.text: Derivation that redemption is with a sheep for all generations
items.text_en: Derivation that redemption is with a sheep for all generations
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the redemption of a firstborn donkey is with a sheep for all generations. Rav Chisda derives it from a verbal analogy between "silver" and "sheep" mentioned for generations. An objection is raised that silver is used for redeeming consecrated items and second tithe, so the analogy is rejected. Instead, a verse is cited comparing the redemption of a firstborn human (always with silver) to that of an unclean animal (always with a sheep).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the redemption of a firstborn donkey applies for all generations, and cites the verse 'וְהָיוּ לִי הַלְוִיִּם' to indicate that the Levites remain in their status.
Rav Chisda derives from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 'silver' and 'sheep' mentioned for generations that the redemption is with a sheep for all generations.
An objection is raised that silver is used for redeeming consecrated items and second tithe, so the analogy is rejected.
The Gemara resolves by citing a verse comparing the redemption of a firstborn human (always with silver) to that of an unclean animal (always with a sheep), establishing the rule for all generations.

items.text: One Levite's sheep exempts many firstborn donkeys
items.text_en: One Levite's sheep exempts many firstborn donkeys
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that one sheep of a Levite can exempt many firstborn donkeys of Israelites. Abaye supports this by noting that the Torah counted surpluses in humans but not in animals. A challenge is raised that perhaps there were not many animals, but it is dismissed by a verse about the abundance of cattle of Reuben and Gad. Another challenge suggests that the Levites' animals were matched one-to-one, but a verse shows one animal replaces many.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that one sheep of a Levite can exempt many firstborn donkeys of Israelites.
Abaye supports this by noting that the Torah counted surpluses in humans but not in animals.
A challenge is raised that perhaps there were not many animals, but it is dismissed.
The challenge is dismissed by a verse about the abundance of cattle of Reuben and Gad, and another verse shows one animal replaces many.

items.text: Rava's support from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rava's support from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rava cites a Mishnah that one can redeem with it many times, and explains that Rabbi Chanina is explaining the reason of the Mishnah: a single sheep of a Levite exempts many firstborn donkeys of Israelites.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by citing a Mishnah that one can redeem with it many times.
Rava explains that Rabbi Chanina is clarifying the Mishnah's reason: a single sheep of a Levite exempts many firstborn donkeys of Israelites.

items.text: Dispute: Were firstborn sanctified in the wilderness?
items.text_en: Dispute: Were firstborn sanctified in the wilderness?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish dispute whether firstborn animals were sanctified in the wilderness. Rabbi Yochanan argues they were, based on the verse "Sanctify to Me every firstborn." Reish Lakish argues they were not, citing the sequence of verses implying later sanctification. Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish with a baraita that before the Tabernacle was erected, service was performed by firstborns. Reish Lakish responds that those were the firstborns who left Egypt. The Gemara clarifies the logic of the challenge and the response.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says firstborn animals were sanctified in the wilderness, Reish Lakish says they were not.
Rabbi Yochanan argues that firstborns were sanctified because God commanded 'קַדֶּשׁ לִי כׇל בְּכוֹר' (Sanctify to Me every firstborn).
Reish Lakish argues that firstborns were not sanctified, citing the sequence of verses 'וְהָיָה כִּי יְבִיאֲךָ' and 'וְהַעֲבַרְתָּ' which imply that sanctification began only upon entering the land.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish with a baraita that before the Tabernacle was erected, service was performed by firstborns; Reish Lakish responds that those were the firstborns who left Egypt.
The Gemara supports Reish Lakish's answer: if the firstborns in the wilderness were sanctified, they would have been one-year-old animals unfit for service.
The Gemara asks: what exactly was Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Reish Lakish?
The Gemara explains: if you say their sanctification never ceased, the firstborns who left Egypt remained sanctified; but if you say it ceased, those firstborns would have lost their sanctity.
Reish Lakish resolves: those that were sanctified (in Egypt) remained sanctified; those that were not (in the wilderness) were not sanctified.

items.text: Further challenge and alternative version
items.text_en: Further challenge and alternative version
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that on the day the Tabernacle was established, firstborns were offered, implying they were not offered afterward. This challenges Reish Lakish's view. An alternative version has Reish Lakish challenging Rabbi Yochanan with the same baraita, concluding that obligations were not offered on a private altar, implying firstborns were not sanctified in the wilderness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that on the day the Tabernacle was established, firstborns were offered, implying that afterward they were not, challenging Reish Lakish's view that firstborns were not sanctified in the wilderness.

An alternative version is presented: Reish Lakish himself challenged Rabbi Yochanan with the same baraita, and Rabbi Yochanan reinterpreted it to mean 'from that day onward' rather than 'only on that day'.

The Gemara concludes that the baraita teaches only that obligations were not offered on a private altar before the Tabernacle was established, not that firstborns were not sanctified in the wilderness.

items.text: Baraita on three places and resolution
items.text_en: Baraita on three places and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that firstborns were sanctified in three places: Egypt, the wilderness, and entry into the land. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that they were commanded to sanctify but did not actually sanctify, except in Egypt. Rav Pappa challenges that the wilderness had a census of firstborns, implying sanctification. The Gemara concludes with a revised version of the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says they were sanctified and never ceased, Reish Lakish says they were sanctified but ceased.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that firstborns were sanctified in three places: Egypt, the wilderness, and entry into the land.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the baraita means they were commanded to sanctify in three places, but only in Egypt did they actually sanctify; some firstborns were sanctified and some were not.
Rav Pappa objects that the wilderness census of firstborns (במדבר ג, מ) implies they were sanctified there.

sub.text: Gemara's revised version of the dispute
sub.text_en: Gemara's revised version of the dispute
sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes with a revised version of the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says they were sanctified and never ceased, Reish Lakish says they were sanctified but ceased.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous dispute
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the earlier debate between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan regarding the sanctification of firstborns in the wilderness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the earlier dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan regarding the sanctification of firstborns in the wilderness.

items.text: Explaining Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.text_en: Explaining Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning, and Rabbi Elazar explains that Rabbi Yochanan derived from the verse 'li yihyu' that firstborns remain in their current state. The Gemara then addresses how Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'vehaya ki yevi'acha' used by the school of Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning, noting that Reish Lakish provided a reason but Rabbi Yochanan did not.
Rabbi Elazar explains that Rabbi Yochanan derived from the verse 'לִי יִהְיוּ' (they shall be Mine) that firstborns remain in their current state (בהתייתן יהיו).

The Gemara resolves how Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'וְהָיָה כִּי יְבִיאֲךָ... וְהַעֲבַרְתָּ' used by the school of Rabbi Yishmael, explaining that it teaches to perform this מצוה (commandment) in order to enter the land.

items.text: Alternative version of the dispute
items.text_en: Alternative version of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Mordechai informs Rav Ashi that their tradition reverses the opinions: Rabbi Yochanan says firstborns were not sanctified, Resh Lakish says they were. Rav Ashi questions whether they also reversed Rabbi Elazar's explanation, and Rav Mordechai clarifies that 'not sanctified' means they did not need to be sanctified. The Gemara notes that this teaches one should speak in the language of his teacher.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai informs Rav Ashi that their tradition reverses the opinions: Rabbi Yochanan says firstborns were not sanctified, Resh Lakish says they were.
Rav Ashi asks whether they also reversed Rabbi Elazar's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's position.
Rav Mordechai clarifies that 'not sanctified' means they did not need to be sanctified, not that they were never sanctified.
The Gemara notes that this alternative version is essentially the same as their own, and teaches that one should speak in the language of his teacher.

items.text: שאלת קונטרוקוס על מניין הלויים
items.text_en: Question of the Roman official about the Levite census
items.desc_en: The Roman official Quntruqus asks Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai about the discrepancy between the individual count of Levites (22,300) and the total count (22,000). Rabban Yochanan explains that the missing 300 were firstborns, and a firstborn does not exempt another firstborn. Abaye explains the reasoning.
items.desc: קונטרוקוס השר שואל את רבן יוחנן בן זכאי מדוע במניין הפרטי של הלויים מופיעים 22,300, אך במניין הכללי מופיעים רק 22,000. רבן יוחנן בן זכאי משיב ש-300 הלויים החסרים היו בכורות, ובכור אינו יכול לפדות בכור אחר, כפי שמסביר אביי.

sub.desc_en: Quntruqus asks Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai why the individual count of Levites (22,300) exceeds the total count (22,000) by 300.
sub.desc: קונטרוקוס השר שואל את רבן יוחנן בן זכאי: במניין הפרטי של הלויים מופיעים 22,300, אך במניין הכללי מופיעים רק 22,000; לאן נעלמו 300 הלויים?

sub.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan answers that the missing 300 were firstborns, and a firstborn does not exempt another firstborn.
sub.desc: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי משיב שאותן שלוש מאות היו בכורות, ואין בכור מפקיע בכור.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains the reasoning: a firstborn only exempts itself from the Levite count, not another firstborn.
sub.desc: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי משיב שאותן שלוש מאות היו בכורות, ואין בכור מפקיע בכור.

items.text: שאלת קונטרוקוס על חשבון כסף המשכן
items.text_en: Question about the silver collection and its use
items.desc_en: The official asks about the discrepancy between the collected silver (201 kikar and 11 maneh) and the silver used for the sockets (100 kikar), accusing Moses of theft or incompetence. Rabban Yochanan responds that Moses was trustworthy and that the sacred maneh was double the standard one.
items.desc: קונטרוקוס מקשה על חשבון כסף המשכן: לפי החישוב היה צריך להיות 201 כיכר ו-11 מנה, אך הכתוב מזכיר רק 100 כיכר. הוא שואל אם משה היה גנב או לא בקי בחשבון. רבן יוחנן בן זכאי משיב שמשה היה נאמן ובקי, ומנה של קודש היה כפול, ולכן 100 כיכר שווים ל-200 כיכר רגילים.

sub.desc_en: Quntruqus asks Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai about the discrepancy between the collected silver (201 kikar and 11 maneh) and the silver used for the sockets (100 kikar), accusing Moses of theft, incompetence, or poor accounting.
sub.desc: קונטרוקוס מקשה על חשבון כסף המשכן: בגיבוי נמצא 201 כיכר ו-11 מנה, אך בנתינה רק 100 כיכר; שואל אם משה היה גנב, קוביוסטוס, או אינו בקי בחשבון.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan responds that Moses was a trustworthy treasurer and knowledgeable in accounts, and explains that the sacred maneh (מנה של קודש) was double the standard one, resolving the discrepancy.
sub.desc: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי משיב שמנה של קודש היה כפול, ולכן מאה הכיכר שנתן שווים למאתיים.

items.text: Proof that the sacred maneh was double
items.text_en: Proof that the sacred maneh was double
items.desc_en: Rav Achai questions the official's difficulty, noting that the 100 kikar were for casting while the rest was for the treasury. The Gemara then seeks a scriptural proof for the doubled maneh, considering and rejecting proofs from the hooks (71 maneh) and the bronze (96 maneh), until Rav Chisda provides a proof from the verse defining the shekel.

sub.desc_en: Rav Achai questions the basis of the official's difficulty, noting that the 100 kikar were designated for casting while the rest was for the treasury, as another verse indicates.
The Gemara asks: From where does Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai derive that the sacred maneh was double?
The Gemara proposes a proof from the hooks: the verse lists 71 maneh in hooks, but if the maneh were standard, the total would be 101 kikar and 11 maneh, implying the maneh is double.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the verse counts only the total in kikar, not the fractional remainder, so no proof of doubling.
The Gemara proposes a proof from the bronze: the verse lists 96 maneh, but if the maneh were standard, the total would be different, implying the maneh is double.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the verse counts only a large remainder in kikar, not a small one, so no proof of doubling.

Rav Chisda provides the definitive proof from the verse defining the shekel, which explicitly states that the maneh is composed of 25 shekels, each of 20 gerah, totaling 100 gerah — double the standard maneh.

items.text: מנה כפול ומדות
items.text_en: Deduction about the sacred mina and additions to measures
items.desc_en: The Gemara deduces from the number 240 that the sacred mina was double (a mina kafu), that one may add to measures, but not more than a sixth, and that the sixth is measured from outside (milbar).
items.desc: הגמרא דנה במנה של קודש שהיה כפול, ומסיקה שמוסיפין על המדות עד שתות, ושותותא מחוץ. זה נלמד מהמקרה של מנה כפול.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the number 240 and deduces that the sacred mina was a double mina.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם מנה של קודש כפול, הרי מאתיים וארבעים הוו, ומסיקה שמוסיפין על המדות עד שתות, ושותותא מחוץ.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara further deduces that one may add to measures, not more than a sixth, and the sixth is measured from outside (מלבר).
sub.desc: הגמרא דנה במושג 'מנה של קודש' ומסיקה ממנו דינים: שמוסיפין על המדות, שאין מוסיפין יותר משתות, ושתות הוא מחוץ למידה.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's three questions to Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's three questions to Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina asks Rabbi Eliezer three questions: why donkey firstlings are different from horse and camel firstlings, the meaning of the name Refidim, and the meaning of the name Shittim. Rabbi Eliezer answers each, and the Gemara notes that the latter two are debated by Tannaim (Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua).

sub.text: Rabbi Chanina's first question to Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's first question to Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina asks Rabbi Eliezer why donkey firstlings differ from horse and camel firstlings.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer's answer to first question
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's answer to first question
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer answers that it is a divine decree and that the Israelites were aided by many donkeys during the Exodus.
Rabbi Chanina asks about the meaning of the name Refidim, and Rabbi Eliezer says it is the place's name.

sub.text: Stam cites Tannaic dispute about Refidim
sub.text_en: Stam cites Tannaic dispute about Refidim
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this is disputed by Tannaim: Rabbi Eliezer says it is the place name, Rabbi Yehoshua says it derives from relaxing from Torah study.
Rabbi Chanina asks about the meaning of the name Shittim, and Rabbi Eliezer says it is the place's name.

sub.text: Stam cites Tannaic dispute about Shittim
sub.text_en: Stam cites Tannaic dispute about Shittim
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes the Tannaic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says it is the place name, Rabbi Yehoshua says it derives from engaging in foolishness, with a supporting verse.

items.text: משנת פטר חמור ובהמה טהורה
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of a donkey that gives birth to a horse-like offspring
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a cow gives birth to a donkey-like offspring, or a donkey gives birth to a horse-like offspring, the offspring is exempt from the law of the firstborn, because the verse says 'petter chamor' twice, requiring both the mother and offspring to be donkeys. It then discusses the laws of eating such offspring: a kosher animal that gives birth to a non-kosher-like offspring is permitted to eat, while a non-kosher animal that gives birth to a kosher-like offspring is forbidden.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שפרה שילדה מין חמור וחמור שילדה מין סוס פטורים מהבכורה, שנאמר 'פטר חמור' פעמיים. כמו כן, דנה באכילת ולדות שאינם דומים לאמם.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a cow gives birth to a donkey-like offspring or a donkey gives birth to a horse-like offspring, the offspring is exempt from the law of the firstborn, because the verse says 'petter chamor' twice, requiring both mother and offspring to be donkeys.
sub.desc: המשנה פוסקת שפרה שילדה מין חמור או חמור שילדה מין סוס פטורים מהבכורה, שנאמר פטר חמור פעמיים עד שיהיה היולד חמור והנולד חמור.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah then discusses the laws of eating such offspring: a kosher animal that gives birth to a non-kosher-like offspring is permitted to eat, while a non-kosher animal that gives birth to a kosher-like offspring is forbidden.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה דין האכילה של ולדות אלו, ומשיבה שבהמה טהורה שילדה מין טמא מותר באכילה, וטמאה שילדה מין טהור אסור, שהיוצא מטמא טמא ומן הטהור טהור.

items.text: מקור לדין בכור שדומה לאם
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation from verses for the Mishnah's rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a parallel Mishnah about a sheep that gives birth to a goat-like offspring, and Rav Yehuda derives the rule from the verses 'ach bechor shor', 'bechor kesev', 'bechor ez', requiring the mother and offspring to be the same species. The word 'ach' excludes cases where the offspring has some signs of the mother's species, making it obligated.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה את דברי רב יהודה שמקור הדין שבכור חייב רק אם דומה לאם הוא מהפסוק 'אך בכור שור' וכו'. אם יש בו מקצת סימנים, הוא חייב, שנאמר 'אך' חלק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a parallel Mishnah about a sheep that gives birth to a goat-like offspring, stating that if it has some signs of the mother's species it is obligated in bechorah.
sub.desc: המשנה קובעת שרחל שילדה מין עז ועז שילדה מין רחל פטורים מהבכורה, ואם יש בהם מקצת סימנים חייבים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters derived?
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן למדים דין זה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda derives from the verses 'אך בכור שור', 'בכור כשב', 'בכור עז' that the mother and offspring must be the same species.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן למדים דין זה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that one might think even if it has some signs it is exempt, but the word 'אך' divides, making it obligated when it has some signs.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: יכול אפילו אם יש בו מקצת סימנים יהיה חייב?

items.text: Objection and resolution: The Tanna of our Mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: The Tanna of our Mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that our Tanna uses the repetition of 'petter chamor' for the donkey, not the verses from 'ach bechor'. It answers that our Tanna follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who derives the rule for kosher animals from 'ach bechor shor', 'bechor kesev', 'bechor ez', and the word 'ach' to exclude cases with some signs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that our Tanna derives the rule for the cow from the repetition of 'פֶּטֶר חֲמוֹר' (donkey firstborn), not from the verses of 'אַךְ בְּכוֹר' (but the firstborn).

The Gemara answers that our Tanna follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who derives the rule for kosher animals from the verses 'אַךְ בְּכוֹר שׁוֹר' (but the firstborn ox), 'בְּכוֹר כֶּשֶׂב' (firstborn sheep), and 'בְּכוֹר עֵז' (firstborn goat).

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
sub.desc_en: The baraita adds that one might think the rule applies even if the offspring has some signs of the mother's species, so the verse says 'אַךְ' (but) to exclude such cases.

items.text: Dispute between the Tanna of our Mishnah and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
items.text_en: Dispute between the Tanna of our Mishnah and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: our Tanna holds that the Torah revealed the rule in the case of sanctity of money (donkey firstlings), and the same applies to sanctity of the body (kosher firstlings). Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds that the Torah revealed the rule in the case of sanctity of the body, and the same applies to sanctity of money, learning the latter from the former.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: on what basis do the Tanna of our Mishnah and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili disagree?

The Gemara explains the dispute: our Tanna holds that the Torah revealed the rule in the case of sanctity of money (donkey firstlings), and the same applies to sanctity of the body (kosher firstlings); Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds that the Torah revealed the rule in the case of sanctity of the body, and the same applies to sanctity of money, learning the latter from the former.

items.text: Use of the repeated 'bechor' for Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's derivation
items.text_en: Use of the repeated 'bechor' for Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that our Tanna uses the repeated 'bechor' for the derivation of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina, who asks why the Torah specified 'bechor' for ox, sheep, and goat separately. The Gemara demonstrates that each is necessary because each has a unique aspect not shared by the others, and none can be derived from the others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what our Tanna does with the repeated 'בכור' (firstborn) in the verse, and answers that it is needed for the derivation of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina asks why the Torah separately mentions the sacrificial portions for a firstborn ox, lamb, and goat.
The Gemara explains that the mention for an ox is necessary because an ox has more wine libations (נסכים) than other animals.
The mention for a lamb is necessary because a lamb has an additional sacrificial portion — its tail (אליה).
The mention for a goat is necessary because a goat is used for the sin-offering of an individual who worships idols.
The Gemara objects that while one case cannot be derived from another, perhaps one case can be derived from the other two combined.
The Gemara rejects deriving the ox from the lamb and goat, because those two are notable for being used for the Paschal offering, unlike the ox.
The Gemara rejects deriving the lamb from the ox and goat, because those two are notable for being used for the community's idol-worship sin-offering, unlike the lamb.

The Gemara rejects deriving the goat from the ox and lamb, because those two have an element of increase regarding the altar (larger libations and the tail), and concludes that all three mentions are necessary.

The Gemara asks Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: if the verse only needed to teach the sacrificial portions, why repeat 'בכור' (firstborn) for each animal? It concludes that this repetition teaches that the firstborn must resemble its mother.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's use of the repeated 'bechor' and 'petter chamor'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's use of the repeated 'bechor' and 'petter chamor'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yosei HaGelili uses the repeated 'bechor' and 'petter chamor'. For 'bechor', he derives that the mother and offspring must be the same species. For 'petter chamor', he uses it to exclude horse and camel firstlings from the redemption requirement, and then questions whether donkey firstlings require a sheep for redemption while horse and camel firstlings can be redeemed with anything.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yosei HaGelili does with the repeated phrase 'פֶּטֶר חֲמוֹר' (firstborn of a donkey).
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yosei HaGelili requires the phrase to teach that only firstborn donkeys, not horses or camels, are subject to redemption.
The Gemara raises a further question: perhaps donkey firstlings require a sheep for redemption, while horse and camel firstlings can be redeemed with any item.

items.text: Derivation that only donkey firstlings are redeemed
items.text_en: Derivation that only donkey firstlings are redeemed
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the repetition of 'petter chamor' teaches that only donkey firstlings are redeemed with a lamb, excluding horses and camels. Rav Achai objects that one instance could have taught a general principle, so a second instance is needed to specify donkeys. The Gemara then questions why the Torah didn't write the phrase differently, and concludes that the repetition indeed limits the law to donkeys.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the repetition of 'פֶּטֶר חֲמוֹר' (firstling of a donkey) teaches that only donkey firstlings are redeemed, excluding horses and camels.

items.text: Question about the Tanna's source
items.text_en: Question about the Tanna's source
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where does our Tanna derive the exclusion of horses and camels?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how our Tanna derives the exclusion of horses and camels from the firstborn redemption law.
The Gemara asks: from where does our Tanna derive the exclusion of horses and camels from the law of firstborn redemption?

items.text: Rav Pappa's answer using a general and specific principle
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's answer using a general and specific principle
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that the verse 'kol miknecha tizakar' is a general statement, and 'shor veseh vachamor' is a specific list, so by the rule of general and specific, only ox, sheep, and donkey are included, excluding other animals.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that the verse 'כָּל מִקְנְךָ תִּזָּכָר' (all your livestock shall be remembered) is a general principle, and 'שׁוֹר וָשֶׂה וַחֲמוֹר' (ox, sheep, and donkey) is a specific list, so by the rule of 'כְּלָל וּפְרָט' (general and specific), only those listed are included.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yossi HaGelili and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yossi HaGelili and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yossi HaGelili holds that the word 'petter' interrupts the context, while the Rabbis hold that the 'vav' connects it. The Gemara then clarifies that according to Rabbi Yossi HaGelili, the Torah could have omitted both the 'vav' and 'petter', and according to the Rabbis, the distinction between קדושת דמים and קדושת הגוף causes the interruption and reconnection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yossi HaGelili interprets the verse, given that the word 'petter' interrupts the context.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yossi HaGelili holds that the word 'petter' interrupts the context, while the Rabbis hold that the 'vav' reconnects it.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yossi HaGelili does not simply omit both the 'vav' and 'petter' to avoid the interruption.
The Gemara explains that according to the Rabbis, the distinction between קדושת דמים (sanctity of monetary value) and קדושת הגוף (sanctity of the body) causes the interruption and reconnection.

items.text: Series of unresolved questions about cross-species births
items.text_en: Series of unresolved questions about cross-species births
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a series of questions: if a cow gives birth to a donkey-like offspring with some signs, what is the law? Then, if a goat gives birth to a sheep-like offspring, and vice versa, since both are pure, it is obligated in firstborn status. But here, one is impure and one is pure, so perhaps it is not obligated. The Gemara continues with hypotheticals about a donkey giving birth to a horse, and a cow giving birth to a horse, each time considering whether the offspring is obligated in firstborn status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about a cow that gives birth to a donkey-like offspring with some signs, asking what the law is regarding firstborn status.

The Gemara contrasts with a goat giving birth to a sheep-like offspring, where both are pure and obligated in firstborn status, and questions whether here, with one impure and one pure, the offspring is still sanctified.
The Gemara raises a further hypothetical: if a donkey gives birth to a horse, which is certainly not subject to firstborn redemption, is it still sanctified because it is a species of impure animal?

The Gemara raises a final hypothetical: if a cow gives birth to a horse, where one is pure and obligated in firstborn status and the other is not, is the offspring sanctified due to its signs, or not?

items.text: Attempted resolution from a baraita
items.text_en: Attempted resolution from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the questions from a baraita: a pure animal that gives birth to an impure species is exempt from firstborn status, but if it has some signs, it is obligated. The Gemara initially thinks this includes a cow giving birth to a horse, but then rejects that interpretation. Another baraita explicitly states that a cow giving birth to a donkey and a donkey giving birth to a horse are exempt unless there are signs, but the Gemara limits this to the cow-donkey case. The Gemara then explains why the donkey-horse case is necessary, lest one think that since both lack horns and have cloven hooves, it might be considered a red donkey.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: a pure animal that gives birth to an impure species is exempt from firstborn status, but if the offspring has some signs, it is obligated.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita includes even a cow that gives birth to a horse.
The Gemara rejects this interpretation, limiting the baraita to a cow giving birth to a donkey.
The Gemara cites another baraita: a cow that gives birth to a donkey and a donkey that gives birth to a horse are exempt unless there are signs.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita applies to both cases.
The Gemara rejects this, limiting the baraita to the cow-donkey case.
The Gemara questions why the donkey-horse case is stated, since it seems obvious that it is exempt.
The Gemara explains that the donkey-horse case is necessary, lest one think that since both lack horns and have cloven hooves, it might be considered a red donkey.

items.text: Discussion of signs for kosher animals
items.text_en: Discussion of signs for kosher animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state 'shehayotzei' (that which emerges) regarding signs of kosher animals. It explains that the signs are merely indicators, and one should follow the mother, not the offspring. The source is a verse that teaches that a kosher animal born from an impure mother is not to be eaten, and the Gemara considers whether the opposite case (impure born from pure) is also included.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to specify 'shehayotzei' (that which emerges) regarding the signs for kosher animals.
The Gemara explains that the signs are merely indicators (סִימָנָא בְּעָלְמָא) to prevent confusion, and one should follow the mother, not the offspring.

The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'אַךְ אֶת זֶה לֹא תֹאכְלוּ מִמַּעֲלֵי הַגֵּרָה וּמִמַּפְרִיסֵי הַפַּרְסָה' that a kosher animal born from an impure mother is forbidden, and considers whether the opposite case (impure born from pure) is also included.

items.text: Derivation of the prohibition of milk from non-kosher animals
items.text_en: Derivation of the prohibition of milk from non-kosher animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis regarding the source for the prohibition of milk from non-kosher animals. The Rabbis derive it from the repetition of 'gamal' in the Torah, while Rabbi Shimon derives it from the word 'et' before 'gamal'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Torah's phrase 'גָּמָל... טָמֵא הוּא' teaches that only a camel born from a camel is impure, but a camel born from a pure animal is pure.
Rabbi Shimon states that the double mention of 'גָּמָל' teaches about a camel born from a female camel and a camel born from a cow.
The Gemara asks what the Rabbis do with the double mention of 'גָּמָל', and answers that one prohibits the animal itself and one prohibits its milk.
The Gemara asks where Rabbi Shimon derives the prohibition of milk, and answers that he derives it from the word 'אֶת' before 'גָּמָל'.
The Gemara concludes that the Rabbis do not derive laws from the word 'אֶת'.

items.text: The story of Shimon HaAmsoni and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: The story of Shimon HaAmsoni and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about Shimon HaAmsoni who used to expound every 'et' in the Torah until he reached 'et Hashem Elokecha tira', which he could not expound. Rabbi Akiva later taught that this 'et' includes Torah scholars.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces Shimon HaAmsoni, who expounded every 'et' in the Torah until he reached 'et Hashem Elokecha tira' and withdrew.
His students ask what will become of all the 'et' words he already expounded.
Shimon HaAmsoni replies that he receives reward for the withdrawal just as for the exposition.
Rabbi Akiva later taught that the 'et' in 'et Hashem Elokecha tira' includes Torah scholars, resolving the difficulty.

items.text: קושיית רב אחא ותירוצי הגמרא
items.text_en: The necessity of a special verse for milk of non-kosher animals
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi why a special verse is needed to prohibit the milk of non-kosher animals, given that it could be derived from other sources. The Gemara explains that without the verse, one might have thought it is permitted due to the novelty of milk or because it is like a limb from a living animal.
items.desc: רב אחא מקשה: אם טעם רבנן הוא מ'גמל' 'גמל', אז בלא דרשה זו היה אפשר לחשוב שחלב בהמה טמאה מותר. הגמרא דוחה קושיה זו ומסבירה שהצורך בדרשה הוא כדי למנוע היתר אפשרי, שכן חלב בהמה טהורה הוא חידוש, ולכן יש סברה להתיר גם בטמאה.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi: if the Rabbis derive the prohibition of camel's milk from the repetition of 'camel' and Rabbi Shimon from 'et hagamal', would one otherwise think milk of a non-kosher animal is permitted?
Rav Acha bar Rava objects: what is different about milk from the baraita that prohibits the juice, gravy, and sediment of non-kosher animals?

Rav Ashi answers: a special verse was necessary because one might think milk of a non-kosher animal is permitted, since even kosher milk is a novelty (blood turns into milk), so the verse teaches it is forbidden.
The Gemara objects: this answer works for the view that blood turns into milk, but what about the view that the limbs become disjointed and the soul does not return for 24 months?

The Gemara answers: even according to that view, a verse was necessary because one might think milk is like a limb from a living animal (which is forbidden), yet the Torah permits it for kosher animals, so one might permit it for non-kosher animals too; the verse teaches it is forbidden.

items.text: Source for the permissibility of milk from kosher animals
items.text_en: Source for the permissibility of milk from kosher animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the permissibility of milk from kosher animals. It considers and rejects derivations from the prohibition of cooking meat in milk and from consecrated animals, ultimately finding proof from verses describing milk as a desirable food, such as 'a land flowing with milk and honey'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that the milk of a kosher animal is permitted?
The Gemara suggests a proof from the prohibition of cooking meat in milk, which implies that milk alone is permitted.
The Gemara objects: perhaps milk alone is forbidden for consumption but permitted for benefit, while meat cooked in milk is forbidden even for benefit.
