The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Shimon, who permits benefit from meat cooked in milk, the verse would still be needed to impose liability for cooking them together.
The Gemara proposes a proof from consecrated animals: the verse 'תִּזְבַּח' (you may slaughter) excludes shearing, and 'בָּשָׂר' (meat) excludes milk, implying that non-sacred milk is permitted.
The Gemara objects: perhaps non-sacred milk is forbidden for consumption but permitted for benefit, while consecrated milk is forbidden even for benefit.
The Gemara brings a proof from Proverbs 27:27, which describes goats' milk as food.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the verse refers to selling the milk as merchandise.
The Gemara brings a proof from I Samuel 17:18, where David sends cheeses to the captain.
The Gemara objects: perhaps this too refers to selling as merchandise.
The Gemara rejects the objection: is it the norm during war to engage in commerce?
The Gemara provides two alternative proofs: from the description of the land flowing with milk and honey, and from Isaiah 55:1 where milk is offered for consumption.

items.text: The repetition of other non-kosher animals
items.text_en: The repetition of other non-kosher animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the repetition of 'gamal' is not like the repetition of 'shafan', 'arnevet', and 'chazir', which come to teach about the shasuah and the ra'ah. It concludes that wherever there is room for exposition, we expound.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the repetition of 'gamal' is not treated like the repetition of 'shafan', 'arnevet', and 'chazir', which come to teach about the shasuah and the ra'ah.
The Gemara answers that the repetition of those animals is explained by a baraita: they are repeated because of the shasuah (in animals) and the ra'ah (in birds).
The Gemara resolves that the repetition of 'gamal' also comes for exposition, concluding that wherever there is room for exposition, we expound.

items.text: The law of a firstborn hybrid animal
items.text_en: The law of a firstborn hybrid animal
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a ewe that gives birth to a goat-like offspring, or a goat that gives birth to a sheep-like offspring, is exempt from the law of the firstborn unless it has some signs of its mother. Rabbi Shimon requires the head and most of the body to resemble the mother. The Gemara inquires whether this requirement applies only to the firstborn or also to the prohibition of eating non-kosher animals.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a ewe giving birth to a goat-like offspring, or vice versa, is exempt from the law of the firstborn unless it has some signs of its mother; Rabbi Shimon requires the head and most of the body to resemble the mother.
The Gemara inquires whether Rabbi Shimon's requirement of head and most of the body applies only to the law of the firstborn or also to the prohibition of eating non-kosher animals.

The Gemara resolves that for the firstborn, the verse requires the offspring to be the same species, but for eating, the Torah only forbids a camel, implying that a hybrid resembling its mother is permitted.

items.text: Initial question about a camel born from a cow
items.text_en: Initial question about a camel born from a cow
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a camel born from a cow is considered different from a regular camel and therefore permitted, or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a camel born from a cow is considered different from a regular camel and therefore permitted, or not.

items.text: Proof from a baraita about a kosher animal giving birth to a non-kosher offspring
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about a kosher animal giving birth to a non-kosher offspring
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita stating that if a kosher animal gives birth to a non-kosher offspring, it is forbidden for consumption, but if its head and most of its body resemble its mother, it is obligated in firstborn status. The Gemara initially infers that Rabbi Shimon requires head and most for consumption as well, but then concludes that the requirement is only for firstborn, not for consumption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a kosher animal that gave birth to a non-kosher offspring, and infers from it that רבי שמעון (Rabbi Shimon) requires head and majority resemblance for consumption as well.

The Gemara rejects the inference, saying the head-and-majority requirement applies specifically to בכורה (firstborn status), not to consumption, and notes the baraita's own shift in topic supports this.

The Gemara resolves that רבי שמעון (Rabbi Shimon) does require head and majority for consumption too, and the baraita needed to state it for בכורה (firstborn status) lest one think the verse 'אַךְ בְּכוֹר שׁוֹר' demands the whole animal resemble an ox.

items.text: Discussion of a single kosher sign and the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Discussion of a single kosher sign and the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse permitting an animal with a single kosher sign, identified as a non-kosher animal born from a kosher mother with kosher conception. Rabbi Yehoshua limits this to when both parents are kosher, while Rabbi Eliezer permits even when the father is non-kosher, based on the verse 'seh kesavim v'seh izim'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse from Leviticus to introduce the concept that an animal with a single kosher sign is permitted for consumption.
The Gemara asks which animal is permitted with a single sign, and answers that it is a non-kosher animal born from a kosher mother with kosher conception.
Rabbi Yehoshua limits the permission to when both parents are kosher, citing the verse 'seh kesavim v'seh izim' to require the father to be a lamb and the mother a ewe.
Rabbi Eliezer permits even when the father is non-kosher, arguing that the verse 'shor seh kesavim v'seh izim' teaches that the offspring is permitted in any case.

items.text: Reconciliation of the baraita with Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Reconciliation of the baraita with Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita calls the offspring 'tamei' like Rabbi Shimon, yet permits it with a single sign. It resolves that this tanna agrees with Rabbi Shimon on one point but disagrees on another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita calls the offspring 'tamei' like Rabbi Shimon, yet permits it with a single sign, creating a contradiction.
The Gemara resolves that this tanna agrees with Rabbi Shimon on one point (calling it tamei) but disagrees on another (permitting it with a single sign).

items.text: קושיית 'מי מעברא' ותירוץ רבי ירמיה
items.text_en: Challenge about conception from a non-kosher animal and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a non-kosher animal can impregnate a kosher one, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's rule that such cross-species conception is impossible except for Rabbi Eliezer's view. Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the case involves a קלוט בן פרה (a cloven-hoofed offspring of a cow) according to Rabbi Shimon, and the tanna agrees on one point but disagrees on another.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם טהורה יכולה להתעבר מטמא? רבי יהושע בן לוי אומר שלא, אלא רק רבי אליעזר וחבורתו סוברים שחיה מתעברת מבהמה. רבי ירמיה מתרץ שהמדובר בקלוט בן פרה, ולפי רבי שמעון, ובכל זאת התנא מתיר בסימן אחד, מה שמעורר דיון נוסף.

items.text: האם זה וזה גורם מותר או אסור? מחלוקת רבי אליעזר ורבי יהושע
items.text_en: Analysis of the principle 'zeh v'zeh gorem' and the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua hold that a product of two factors (one permitted, one forbidden) is permitted or forbidden. It brings a contradiction from a case of a fetus from a treifah, and resolves that Rabbi Eliezer generally holds 'zeh v'zeh gorem' is forbidden, but here the verse teaches otherwise, while Rabbi Yehoshua generally holds it is permitted, but here the verse requires both parents to be kosher.
items.desc: הגמרא בוחנת את שיטות רבי אליעזר ורבי יהושע בסוגיית 'זה וזה גורם'. מובאת מחלוקתם בולד טריפה, ומתורצת הסתירה: כאן דורשים את כפל 'שה' ו'שה' להיתר או איסור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the positions of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua imply that Rabbi Eliezer holds the principle 'zeh v'zeh gorem' (a product of two factors, one permitted and one forbidden) is permitted, while Rabbi Yehoshua holds it is forbidden.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם מהברייתא משמע שרבי אליעזר סובר 'זה וזה גורם' מותר ורבי יהושע סובר אסור?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the opposite is known from elsewhere: regarding a fetus from a טריפה (treifah), Rabbi Eliezer says it may not be offered on the altar, implying he holds 'zeh v'zeh gorem' is forbidden, while Rabbi Yehoshua permits it, implying he holds it is permitted.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי שמענו את ההפך במחלוקתם בולד טריפה, שרבי אליעזר אוסר ורבי יהושע מתיר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that in general Rabbi Eliezer holds 'zeh v'zeh gorem' is forbidden, but here the verse teaches otherwise through the extra word 'שֶׂה' (sheep), indicating that the offspring is permitted regardless of the father's status.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: בעלמא רבי אליעזר סובר 'זה וזה גורם' אסור, ושאני הכא משום דרשת 'שה' 'ושה' להיתר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that in general Rabbi Yehoshua holds 'zeh v'zeh gorem' is permitted, but here the verse requires both parents to be kosher, as indicated by the plural 'כְּשָׂבִים וְעִזִּים' (sheep and goats).
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: רבי יהושע בעלמא סובר 'זה וזה גורם' מותר, ושאני הכא משום דרשת 'כשבים ועזים' לאיסור.

items.text: הוכחה מברייתא של רבי שמעון על גמל הנולד מפרה
items.text_en: Final proof from Rabbi Shimon's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a direct statement from Rabbi Shimon that a camel born from a cow is permitted for consumption only if its head and most of its body resemble its mother, concluding that Rabbi Shimon indeed requires head and most for consumption.
items.desc: מובאת ברייתא שבה רבי שמעון דורש 'גמל' 'גמל' שני פעמים, ומתיר גמל הנולד מפרה אם ראשו ורובו דומים לאמו. מכאן מוכח שלרבי שמעון גם לאכילה צריך ראשו ורובו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Shimon explicitly states that a camel born from a cow is permitted for consumption only if its head and most of its body resemble its mother.
sub.desc: מובאת ברייתא שבה רבי שמעון דורש 'גמל' 'גמל' שני פעמים, ומתיר גמל הנולד מפרה אם ראשו ורובו דומים לאמו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes definitively that Rabbi Shimon requires head and most of the body for consumption, not just for firstborn status.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסיקה מכאן שלרבי שמעון גם לאכילה צריך ראשו ורובו.

items.text: בעיית מי רגליים של חמור
items.text_en: Question about donkey urine and the principle of 'yotzei min hatamei'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether donkey urine, which is thick and resembles milk, is forbidden because it is derived from a non-kosher animal, or permitted because it is merely water that passes through. Rav Sheishet answers by citing the Mishnah that 'what comes from a non-kosher animal is non-kosher', implying the urine is forbidden.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת על מי רגליים של חמור אם הם אסורים כחלב, ומבדילה בין חמור לשאר בהמות. רב ששת עונה מהמשנה ש'היוצא מן הטמא טמא', ודורש את הניסוח המדויק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rav Sheishet whether donkey urine, which is thick and resembles milk, is forbidden or permitted.
sub.desc: החכמים שואלים את רב ששת מה דין מי רגליים של חמור אם הם אסורים כחלב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the question is only about donkey urine because it is thick and resembles milk, unlike horse and camel urine which are thin and clearly just water.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבהירה מדוע לא נשאלה שאלה על סוסים וגמלים, ומפרטת את ספק הטומאה במי רגלי חמור.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheishet answers by citing the Mishnah that 'what comes from a non-kosher animal is non-kosher', implying the urine is forbidden.
sub.desc: רב ששת עונה מהמשנה שהיוצא מן הטמא טמא, ודורש את הניסוח המדויק להוכיח שגם מי רגליים אסורים.

items.text: Donkey's milk: the principle of 'offspring of a non-kosher species'
items.text_en: Donkey's milk: the principle of 'offspring of a non-kosher species'
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether donkey's milk is permitted, given that donkeys are non-kosher. Rav Sheishet cites the principle that whatever comes from a non-kosher species is non-kosher, so donkey's milk is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether donkey's milk is permitted, noting that some say the question only arises for donkey milk since people drink it as a remedy for jaundice.
Rav Sheishet answers that the principle 'what comes from a non-kosher species is non-kosher' applies, so donkey's milk is forbidden.

items.text: Objection from bee honey and Rabbi Yaakov's derivation
items.text_en: Objection from bee honey and Rabbi Yaakov's derivation
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: bee honey is permitted even though bees are non-kosher. The Gemara explains that this follows Rabbi Yaakov's view, who derives from a verse that honey produced by a non-kosher insect is permitted, unlike the honey of other insects.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised: bee honey is permitted even though bees are non-kosher, because bees store it in their bodies without it being secreted from them.
Rav Sheishet explains that he follows Rabbi Yaakov, who derives from a verse that bee honey is a special exception permitted by the Torah.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yaakov expounds the verse to permit bee honey but exclude wasp and hornet honey.

The baraita concludes that only bee honey is permitted, not the honey of hornets or wasps, because bee honey lacks a secondary name (i.e., it is simply called 'honey'), while the others have a qualifying name.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yaakov's view and a baraita on wasp honey
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yaakov's view and a baraita on wasp honey
items.desc_en: A baraita states that wasp and hornet honey is pure and permitted, which contradicts Rabbi Yaakov's view. The Gemara then notes that this honey requires intent to become susceptible to impurity, and a baraita confirms that honey in its comb is susceptible without intent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that a baraita permitting wasp and hornet honey follows the view opposing Rabbi Yaakov.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that honey requires intent to become susceptible to impurity, and cites a supporting baraita.

items.text: The case of 'chalei deyachmurta' (deer droppings)
items.text_en: The case of 'chalei deyachmurta' (deer droppings)
items.desc_en: The Rabbis thought that deer droppings (chalei deyachmurta) are eggs and forbidden, but Rav Safra explains they are deer semen, which is permitted because it comes from a kosher animal.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis initially thought that the testicles of a deer (יחמורתא) are eggs and therefore forbidden.
Rav Safra explains that these are actually deer semen, formed when the deer cannot mate with the doe and instead mates with a deer-like animal, causing them to fall off.

items.text: The skin that comes opposite a donkey's face
items.text_en: The skin that comes opposite a donkey's face
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that the skin that comes opposite a donkey's face is permitted, as it is merely a secretion. Rav Chisda brings a supporting baraita about human skin, and the Gemara clarifies the baraita's meaning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that the skin that comes opposite a donkey's face is permitted because it is mere secretion.
Rav Chisda cites a baraita that the skin opposite a human face is pure, and suggests it supports Rav Huna's ruling.
The Gemara rejects the interpretation, explaining the baraita differently, and notes that another baraita contradicts it but is accepted as is.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating that if the baraita is taught, it is taught, accepting the contradictory version without further reconciliation.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: a non-kosher fish that swallowed a kosher fish
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: a non-kosher fish that swallowed a kosher fish
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a non-kosher fish swallowed a kosher fish, the kosher fish is permitted, but if a kosher fish swallowed a non-kosher fish, it is forbidden. The Gemara discusses the reasoning, based on the principle that non-kosher fish spawn and kosher fish lay eggs, and various Amoraim explain how we know the fish was swallowed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: a non-kosher fish that swallowed a kosher fish is permitted, but a kosher fish that swallowed a non-kosher fish is forbidden, because the swallowed fish is not its own offspring.
The Gemara infers that the Mishnah's ruling applies only when we see the swallowing; otherwise, we assume the fish spawned (i.e., the swallowed fish is actually the offspring of the non-kosher fish).
The Gemara cites a baraita establishing that non-kosher fish spawn (give live birth) and kosher fish lay eggs, providing the biological basis for the assumption.

The Gemara objects: if non-kosher fish spawn, even when we see a kosher fish inside a non-kosher fish, we should say the kosher fish was eaten and the non-kosher fish spawned (i.e., the kosher fish is not the offspring but the prey).
Rav Sheishet answers that the Mishnah refers to a case where the kosher fish was found in the non-kosher fish's digestive tract (the rectum), proving it was swallowed, not spawned.
Rav Pappa answers that the case is where the kosher fish was found in the non-kosher fish's esophagus (the swallowing passage), indicating it was swallowed.
Rav Nachman answers that the case is where the kosher fish was found intact (whole), showing it was swallowed, not spawned.
Rav Ashi answers that since most fish spawn within their own species, finding a kosher fish inside a non-kosher fish is considered as if it was swallowed before us (i.e., it is the exception).

A baraita is cited, reiterating the biological rule that non-kosher fish spawn, kosher fish lay eggs, and generalizing to all animals: those that give birth nurse, those that lay eggs gather food, except the bat which lays eggs yet nurses.

items.text: Opening statement about dolphins
items.text_en: Opening statement about dolphins
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that dolphins reproduce like humans. Rav Yehuda explains that they are sea creatures.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that dolphins reproduce like humans.
The Gemara asks what 'dolphins' are.
Rav Yehuda answers that they are sea creatures.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution on reproductive classification
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution on reproductive classification
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially states that animals with external testicles give live birth, while those with internal testicles lay eggs. It raises an objection from Shmuel about geese and wild geese being interbred despite both laying eggs. Abaye resolves that the criterion is actually the location of the male organ: external gives live birth, internal lays eggs.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the rule: animals with external testicles give live birth, those with internal testicles lay eggs.
The Gemara objects from Shmuel's statement that domestic and wild geese are diverse kinds, yet both lay eggs, contradicting the rule.
The Gemara resolves that the criterion is the location of the male reproductive organ, not the testicles: external organ gives live birth, internal lays eggs.

items.text: Rule about mating time and birth time
items.text_en: Rule about mating time and birth time
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a principle: animals that mate during the day give birth during the day, those that mate at night give birth at night, and those that mate at any time give birth at any time. Examples are given: rooster (day), bat (night), and humans and similar (any time).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a general principle: the time of mating determines the time of birth — daytime mating leads to daytime birth, nighttime mating leads to nighttime birth, and flexible mating leads to flexible birth.
The Gemara provides specific examples: a rooster (day), a bat (night), and humans and similar creatures (any time).

items.text: Practical application of the rule
items.text_en: Practical application of the rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the practical relevance of the rule. Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana explains that if one checked a chicken coop on the eve of a festival and found no egg, but found one in the morning, it is permitted to eat on the festival, assuming the egg was laid after the check. The Gemara objects that the check was thorough, but resolves that the egg may have partially emerged and then retracted, citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that an egg that mostly emerged before the festival and retracted is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical halachic application emerges from the rule about animals that give birth by day or night.

Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana explains the application: if one checked a chicken coop on the eve of a festival and found no egg, but found one in the morning, it is permitted to eat on the festival, assuming the egg was laid after the check.
The Gemara objects that the check was thorough, so the egg should be forbidden.

The Gemara resolves that the egg may have partially emerged and then retracted, citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that an egg that mostly emerged before the festival and retracted is permitted to eat on the festival.

items.text: אופן ההזדווגות: פנים מול פנים
items.text_en: Mating positions and a baraita about the camel
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that animals with similar mating and gestation periods can interbreed. It lists three creatures that mate face-to-face: fish, humans, and snakes. The reason given is that the Divine Presence spoke with them. A baraita adds that the camel mates back-to-back.
items.desc: הברייתא קובעת שכל בעלי החיים מזדווגים פנים כנגד עורף, חוץ משלושה: דג, אדם ונחש, שמזדווגים פנים כנגד פנים. הסיבה: השכינה דיברה עמהם. כמו כן, גמל מזדווג אחור כנגד אחור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a general rule: creatures with matching mating and gestation periods can interbreed, and lists three that mate face-to-face: fish, humans, and snakes.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בכלל על הזדווגות וגידול צאצאים בין מינים, ומפרטת שכל בעלי החיים מזדווגים פנים כנגד עורף חוץ משלושה: דג, אדם ונחש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why these three are special, and Rav Dimi reports that in the West they say it is because the Divine Presence (שכינה) spoke with them.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה מיוחד בשלושה אלה שמזדווגים פנים כנגד פנים.

sub.desc_en: A baraita adds that the camel mates back-to-back, contrasting with the three that mate face-to-face.
sub.desc: תנא מוסיף שגמל מזדווג אחור כנגד אחור, כחריג נוסף.

items.text: תקופות היריון של בעלי חיים ואילנות מקבילים
items.text_en: Baraita of gestation periods and corresponding trees
items.desc_en: A baraita lists gestation periods for various animals and their corresponding trees: chicken (21 days, carob), dog (50 days, fig), cat (52 days, mulberry), pig (60 days, apple), fox and all creeping things (6 months, grain), small clean domesticated animal (5 months, grapevine), large unclean domesticated animal (12 months, palm), clean large animal (9 months, olive), wolf, lion, bear, leopard, bardelas, elephant, monkey, and kof (3 years, bnot shuach), viper (70 years, carob), snake (7 years). Some say the snake's gestation is like the moksasin.
items.desc: ברייתא מפרטת תקופות היריון של בעלי חיים שונים והאילנות המקבילים להם בזמן גידולם: תרנגולת (21 יום, לוז), כלב (50 יום, תאנה), חתול (52 יום, תות), חזיר (60 יום, תפוח), שועל ושרצים (6 חודשים, תבואה), בהמה דקה טהורה (5 חודשים, גפן), בהמה גסה טמאה (12 חודשים, דקל), בהמה גסה טהורה (9 חודשים, זית), חיות גדולות (3 שנים, בנות שוח), אפעה (70 שנה, חרוב), נחש (7 שנים, מוכססים).

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing gestation periods for chicken, dog, cat, pig, fox and creeping things, each paired with a corresponding tree.
sub.desc: ברייתא פותחת ברשימת תקופות היריון של בעלי חיים קטנים (תרנגולת, כלב, חתול, חזיר, שועל ושרצים) והאילנות המקבילים להם.

sub.desc_en: The baraita continues with gestation periods for small clean domesticated animal, large unclean animal, clean large animal, and wild beasts, each with a corresponding tree.
sub.desc: הברייתא ממשיכה ומפרטת תקופות היריון של בהמות וחיות גדולות (בהמה דקה טהורה, בהמה גסה טמאה וטהורה, חיות טורפות וקופים) והאילנות המקבילים.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists the viper's gestation of 70 years, paired with the carob tree, and notes the carob's growth cycle.
sub.desc: הברייתא מסיימת בתקופות היריון ארוכות במיוחד (אפעה, נחש) והאילנות המקבילים, ומוסיפה הערה על חרוב ועל מחלוקת בדבר האילן המקביל לנחש.

sub.desc_en: The baraita concludes with the snake's gestation of 7 years, noting no parallel tree, and records an alternative opinion that it is like the moksasin.
sub.desc: הברייתא מסיימת בתקופות היריון ארוכות במיוחד (אפעה, נחש) והאילנות המקבילים, ומוסיפה הערה על חרוב ועל מחלוקת בדבר האילן המקביל לנחש.

items.text: מקור תקופת היריון הנחש
items.text_en: Derivation of the snake's seven-year gestation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the snake's seven-year gestation. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya, derives it from the verse 'Cursed are you above all cattle and above all beasts of the field.' The logic: if cattle are cursed relative to beasts (one to seven, e.g., donkey from cat), then the snake is cursed relative to cattle (one to seven, yielding seven years). An alternative suggestion that the snake should be cursed relative to beasts (one to three years, yielding nine years) is rejected.
items.desc: הגמרא דורשת את הפסוק 'ארור אתה מכל הבהמה ומכל חית השדה' כדי לקבוע שנחש נידון ל-7 שנות היריון. הדרשה מבוססת על יחס של 1:7 בין בהמה לחיה (חמור לעומת חתול), ומכאן שנחש ארור פי 7 מבהמה, כלומר 7 שנים. נדחית אפשרות של 9 שנים על בסיס יחס 1:3.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the snake's seven-year gestation.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמדת תקופת ההיריון של הנחש, ומביאה את דברי רב יהודה בשם רב ורבי יהושע בן חנניה הדורשים את הפסוק 'ארור אתה מכל הבהמה ומכל חית השדה'.

sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya, derives the seven-year gestation from the verse 'Cursed are you above all cattle and above all beasts of the field,' arguing that just as cattle are cursed relative to beasts (one to seven, e.g., donkey from cat), so the snake is cursed relative to cattle (one to seven, yielding seven years).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמדת תקופת ההיריון של הנחש, ומביאה את דברי רב יהודה בשם רב ורבי יהושע בן חנניה הדורשים את הפסוק 'ארור אתה מכל הבהמה ומכל חית השדה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an alternative: perhaps the snake should be cursed relative to beasts (one to three years, e.g., lion from donkey), yielding nine years, but this is implicitly rejected.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אפשר לדרוש הפוך — שהחיה (אריה) ארורה פי שלוש מהבהמה (חמור), ואז הנחש ארור פי שלוש מהחיה, כלומר תשע שנים.

items.text: קללת הנחש ואורך תקופת העיבור
items.text_en: Debate on the serpent's gestation period
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the interpretation of a verse about the serpent's curse, suggesting it implies a gestation period of fifteen months. Two answers are offered: one based on the order of the verse, and another that the curse is a general malediction.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בפירוש הפסוק 'ארור אתה מכל הבהמה ומכל חית השדה' ומבררת האם הנחש ארוך יותר מבחינת תקופת העיבור מהבהמה. מוצעות שתי תשובות: האחת שהפסוק מתייחס לבהמה הארוכה ביותר (חמור), והשנייה שמדובר בקללה כללית.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the interpretation of the verse, noting that the actual wording is 'from among all animals and from among all beasts,' implying the serpent is cursed from the domesticated animals, which were already cursed from the undomesticated animals.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על הפירוש הפשוט של הפסוק, ומציעה שהנחש ארור יותר מהבהמה הארורה ביותר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the same proportion (one to three) would yield a fifteen-month gestation for the serpent, based on the goat's five months compared to the cat's fifty-two days.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שאם הקללה היא ביחס של אחד לשלוש, הרי שהנחש צריך להיות ארוך יותר במידה כזו, מה שמוביל לחמישה עשר חודשי עיבור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers two answers: either the verse is read as 'from among all animals' including the most accursed, or the curse is a general malediction without specific proportion.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציעה שני תירוצים: או שהפסוק מתייחס לבהמה הארוכה ביותר (חמור), או שמדובר בקללה כללית ללא חישוב יחסי.

items.text: ויכוח עם הקיסר על תקופת עיבור הנחש
items.text_en: Caesar's question about snake gestation
items.desc_en: Caesar asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya about the snake's gestation period. Rabbi Yehoshua answers seven years, but Caesar objects based on the experience of the sages of Athens. Rabbi Yehoshua explains that those snakes were already pregnant for four years, and they mate like humans.
items.desc: הקיסר שואל את רבי יהושע בן חנניה על תקופת העיבור של הנחש. רבי יהושע עונה שבע שנים, אך הקיסר מקשה מחכמי אתונה שטענו לשלוש שנים. רבי יהושע מתרץ שהנחשים היו מעוברים כבר ארבע שנים, ושנחשים מזדווגים גם שלא לשם רבייה.

sub.desc_en: Caesar asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya about the gestation period of a snake.
sub.desc: הקיסר שואל את רבי יהושע בן חנניה לכמה זמן מתעבר הנחש ויולד.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua answers that the gestation period is seven years.
sub.desc: הקיסר שואל את רבי יהושע בן חנניה לכמה זמן מתעבר הנחש ויולד.

sub.desc_en: Caesar objects, citing the sages of Athens who bred snakes and they gave birth after three years.
sub.desc: הקיסר שואל את רבי יהושע בן חנניה לכמה זמן מתעבר הנחש ויולד.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua explains that those snakes were already pregnant for four years beforehand.
sub.desc: הקיסר שואל את רבי יהושע בן חנניה לכמה זמן מתעבר הנחש ויולד.

sub.desc_en: Caesar objects that they engaged in intercourse, implying they were not already pregnant.
sub.desc: הקיסר שואל את רבי יהושע בן חנניה לכמה זמן מתעבר הנחש ויולד.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua answers that snakes also engage in intercourse like humans, not solely for reproduction.
sub.desc: הקיסר שואל את רבי יהושע בן חנניה לכמה זמן מתעבר הנחש ויולד.

items.text: האתגר לנצח את חכמי אתונה
items.text_en: Challenge to defeat the sages of Athens
items.desc_en: Caesar challenges Rabbi Yehoshua to defeat the sages of Athens, who are sixty in number. Rabbi Yehoshua agrees and requests a ship with sixty chambers, each with sixty cushions.
items.desc: הקיסר מאתגר את רבי יהושע להוכיח שחכמי ישראל חכמים יותר מחכמי אתונה, ומצווה עליו להביאם אליו. רבי יהושע שואל על מספרם (שישים) ומתכונן למסע.

sub.desc_en: Caesar challenges Rabbi Yehoshua, questioning the wisdom of the sages of Athens and demanding that he defeat them and bring them to him.
sub.desc: הקיסר מקשה על רבי יהושע: וכי חכמי אתונה אינם חכמים? אם אתה חכם מהם, לך נצח אותם והבא אותם אלי.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua asks how many sages there are, and Caesar responds that there are sixty men.
sub.desc: הקיסר מקשה על רבי יהושע: וכי חכמי אתונה אינם חכמים? אם אתה חכם מהם, לך נצח אותם והבא אותם אלי.

items.text: Journey to Athens and first encounter
items.text_en: Journey to Athens and first encounter
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua builds the ship and travels to Athens. He encounters a man skinning an animal and buys his head. He then finds the entrance to the academy, where he observes guards that kill those entering or leaving. He uses his sandal to trick the guards and enters, finding young and old sages.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya (רבי יהושע בן חנניה) requests a ship with sixty rooms and sixty mattresses each from the emperor, then travels to Athens and buys a butcher's head for half a dinar.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya (רבי יהושע בן חנניה) reveals he meant the butcher's head, then negotiates to be shown the entrance to the academy in exchange for sparing the butcher's life, instructing him to mark the spot with a bundle of reeds.
The narrator describes the guards stationed inside and outside the academy, who kill the outer guards for entering footsteps and the inner guards for exiting footsteps.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya (רבי יהושע בן חנניה) reverses his sandal to create misleading footprints, causing the guards to kill each other, and then enters the academy.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya (רבי יהושע בן חנניה) finds the younger sages seated above the elders and considers the social dynamics before greeting them.

items.text: Riddles and responses
items.text_en: Riddles and responses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua introduces himself and proposes a contest. The sages ask riddles about a man seeking a wife, a borrower, and a mule that gave birth. Rabbi Yehoshua answers each with clever parables, and when asked for nonsense, he tells a story about a mule with a note, which is absurd.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua greets the sages, introduces himself as a Jewish sage, and proposes a contest: if they win they may do as they wish, but if he wins they must eat with him on his ship.
The sages ask: why would a man rejected by one family go to a more distinguished family?
Rabbi Yehoshua answers with a parable: a peg that does not enter below may enter above; similarly, the man may find his destined match in the more distinguished family.
The sages ask: why would a man who lent and had to repossess lend again?
Rabbi Yehoshua answers with a parable: a man cutting reeds keeps adding until someone helps him carry the bundle; similarly, a lender keeps lending until he finds a reliable borrower.
The sages ask Rabbi Yehoshua to tell them something nonsensical.
Rabbi Yehoshua tells a story about a mule that gave birth with a note claiming a debt; the sages object that a mule cannot give birth.
Rabbi Yehoshua explains that the absurdity of the story is precisely why it qualifies as nonsense.

items.text: Further challenges and final victory
items.text_en: Further challenges and final victory
items.desc_en: The sages pose more challenges: salting spoiled salt, building a house in the air, bringing a well into the city, repairing a broken mill, killing a knife swarm, identifying eggs, and the exit of the soul. Rabbi Yehoshua answers each with clever wordplay or actions, ultimately defeating them.

sub.desc_en: The sages of Athens ask: When salt spoils, with what does one salt it?
Rabbi Yehoshua answers: With the placenta of a mule.
They object: But does a mule have a placenta?
Rabbi Yehoshua retorts: And does salt spoil?
They ask: Build us a house in the air of the world.
Rabbi Yehoshua utters a divine Name and hovers between sky and earth.
He tells them: Bring up bricks and mortar so I can build.
They ask: Where is the center of the world?
He raises his finger and says: Here.
They object: Who says so?
He says: Bring ropes and measure.
They say: We have a well in the field; bring it into the city.
He says: Braid ropes of bran for me and I will bring it.
They say: We have a broken mill; sew it together.
He says: Pull threads from it and I will sew it.
They ask: With what does one harvest a field of knives?
He answers: With the horn of a donkey.
They object: Does a donkey have a horn?
He retorts: Does a field of knives exist?
They bring two eggs and ask: Which is from a black hen and which from a white hen?
He brings two cheeses and asks: Which is from a black goat and which from a white goat?
They ask: From where does the spirit of a chick that dies in the egg exit?
He answers: From where it entered, it departs.
They ask: Show us a utensil that is not worth its damage.
He tells each to bring a mat and spread it out.
The mat does not fit through the gate.
He says: Bring axes and break the gate.
He concludes: This is a utensil not worth its damage.

items.text: Return and collection of dust
items.text_en: Return and collection of dust
items.desc_en: The sages realize they have been defeated and come to the ship. Rabbi Yehoshua takes dust from their land as a token of victory.

sub.desc_en: After defeating the sages of Athens, Rabbi Yehoshua brings them to the ship, each one seeing the sixty mattresses and assuming all his colleagues are coming, then orders the captain to sail and takes dust from their land as a token of victory.

items.text: סיפור רבי יהושע וחכמי אתונה
items.text_en: Opening story: the water from Beit Belyei
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's students, when brought before the Caesar, were saved by water from the House of Blinding. The Caesar tests them by making them drink the water, and they survive by cleverly spilling it.
items.desc: הסיפור מספר כיצד רבי יהושע בן חנניה, בליווי חכמי אתונה, מתמודד עם אתגר שהציב הקיסר. הוא ממלא כד מים מבית הבליעות, ולאחר שהחכמים מתנהגים בענווה, הוא משליך עליהם עפר מאתונה והם חוזרים להתנהגותם הרגילה. לבסוף הוא מביס אותם באמצעות המים מבית הבליעות, שגורמים להם למלא את הכלי שוב ושוב עד שכתפיהם נשמטות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's students were saved from the Caesar's test by spilling the water from Beit Belyei.
sub.desc: סיפור על רבי יהושע בן חנניה וחכמי אתונה, שבו הוא ממלא כד ממי בית הבליעות, משליך עפר מאתונה על החכמים כדי להחזירם להתנהגותם, ולבסוף מביסם באמצעות המים שגורמים להם למלא את הכלי עד שכתפיהם נשמטות.

items.text: משנת פטר חמור שילדה שני זכרים
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of firstborn donkeys
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details cases of a donkey that did not give birth to a firstborn and then gives birth to twins or mixed genders, specifying when a lamb must be given to the priest. It also states that the redemption lamb can be from sheep or goats, male or female, large or small, and can be used multiple times.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת דינים בפטר חמור שילדה שני זכרים: אם ילדה שני זכרים, נותן טלה אחד לכהן; אם זכר ונקבה, מפריש טלה לעצמו. במקרה של שתי חמורות, הדינים משתנים בהתאם למספר הזכרים והנקבות. כמו כן, המשנה דורשת את הפסוק 'ופטר חמור תפדה בשה' ומפרטת את דיני הפדיון, כולל אפשרות לפדות בשה גדול או קטן, תמים או בעל מום, ואם מת השה נהנים בו.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the laws of redeeming a firstborn donkey (פטר חמור) in various scenarios of multiple births, including cases of one or two donkeys, and the rules for the redemption lamb.
sub.desc: המשנה קובעת דינים בפטר חמור שילדה שני זכרים: אם ילדה שני זכרים, נותן טלה אחד לכהן; אם זכר ונקבה, מפריש טלה לעצמו. במקרה של שתי חמורות, הדינים משתנים בהתאם למספר הזכרים והנקבות. כמו כן, המשנה דורשת את הפסוק 'ופטר חמור תפדה בשה' ומפרטת את דיני הפדיון, כולל אפשרות לפדות בשה גדול או קטן, תמים או בעל מום, ואם מת השה נהנים בו.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah details cases involving two donkeys that did not give birth to a firstborn, specifying when the priest receives lambs and when he receives nothing.
The Mishnah addresses a case where one donkey had previously given birth and one had not, and they give birth to twins.
The Mishnah cites the verse for redeeming a firstborn donkey with a lamb, and states that the lamb can be from various types, used multiple times, and if it dies, one may benefit from it.

items.text: Gemara's question: Who is the Tanna?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Who is the Tanna?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya suggests the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who holds that it is possible for two animals to be born simultaneously (צמצום), which would affect the ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna authored the Mishnah's ruling that a single lamb suffices for two male firstborn donkeys.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who holds that it is possible to precisely designate which offspring belongs to which mother (צמצום).

items.text: Abaye's defense: The verse 'the males to God'
items.text_en: Abaye's defense: The verse 'the males to God'
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that even according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, the Mishnah is fine because the verse 'the males to God' excludes the case of simultaneous birth from the law of firstborn donkeys. The Gemara objects that this verse applies to sanctity of the body, not to redemption of a donkey.

sub.desc_en: Abaye argues that even according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, the Mishnah is fine because the verse 'the males to God' excludes the case of simultaneous birth from the law of firstborn donkeys.
The Gemara objects that this verse applies to sanctity of the body, not to redemption of a donkey.

items.text: Alternative version of the debate
items.text_en: Alternative version of the debate
items.desc_en: An alternative formulation of the same debate: some say the Mishnah is not like Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, and Abaye again responds with the same argument about the verse.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version presents the same debate: the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, and Abaye's objection is repeated.

Abaye responds that even if the Mishnah could be like Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, the case is different because the verse 'הַזְּכָרִים לַה׳' (the males to God) applies specifically to firstborn animals sanctified in body.

items.text: Refutation of Abaye: the baraita and the verse's context
items.text_en: Refutation of Abaye: the baraita and the verse's context
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye: if the Mishnah could accommodate Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, why does it not mention the case of two heads emerging together? A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yosei HaGelili explicitly rules that both donkeys go to the priest in such a case, based on 'the males to God'. The Gemara concludes that this verse applies to sanctity of the body, not to redemption, and thus Abaye's position is refuted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Abaye: if the Mishnah could accommodate Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, why does it not mention the case of two heads emerging together?
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yosei HaGelili explicitly rules that both donkeys go to the priest in such a case, based on 'the males to God'.
The Gemara concludes that the verse applies to sanctity of the body, not to redemption, and thus Abaye's position is refuted.

items.text: Gemara's question about the Rabbis' position on partial sanctification
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the Rabbis' position on partial sanctification
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Rabbis hold that partial sanctification of the womb is effective, and Rav answers that a substance of the same kind does not interpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Rabbis hold that partial sanctification of the womb (מקצת רחם מקדיש) is effective, given that if the entire womb sanctifies, there is an interposition issue.
Rav answers that a substance of the same kind (מין במינו) does not interpose, resolving the question.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's ruling on separating a lamb for oneself
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's ruling on separating a lamb for oneself
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why one must separate a lamb even for his own firstling donkey: to remove its prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one must separate a lamb for a male and female donkey, since the lamb is for the owner's own benefit.
The Gemara answers that the separation is to remove the prohibition (איסור) from the donkey.

items.text: Attribution of the Mishnah to Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Attribution of the Mishnah to Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara deduces that the Mishnah's view that an unredeemed פטר חמור is forbidden in benefit follows Rabbi Yehuda, as opposed to Rabbi Shimon who permits it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that since the separation does not remove the prohibition, the donkey is forbidden for benefit (אסור בהנאה).
The Gemara identifies the mishnah as following Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a firstborn donkey is forbidden for benefit, unlike Rabbi Shimon who permits it.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning and its defense
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning and its defense
items.desc_en: Ulla presents Rabbi Yehuda's argument that something requiring redemption cannot be permitted, but the Gemara challenges this with the case of a firstborn human. The Gemara refines the argument to focus on the Torah's insistence on a lamb, and then defends it by comparing to מעשר and citing Rabbi Elazar's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning, and Ulla answers that he holds: is there anything that requires redemption and is permitted?
The Gemara objects: but a firstborn human requires redemption and is permitted!
The Gemara refines Ulla's statement: is there anything that the Torah insisted on a lamb for its redemption and yet it is permitted?
The Gemara objects: did the Torah insist? Rav Nechemya bar Rav Yosef redeemed his פטר חמור (firstborn donkey) with vegetables of equal value!
The Gemara answers: we are not speaking about redemption with equal value; we are speaking about redeeming with a lamb to remove its prohibition.
The Gemara objects: but מעשר שני (second tithe) required silver coins, and yet Rabbi Yehuda ruled that if one intentionally redeemed it with something else, it is consecrated and permitted.

sub.text: Gemara's answer with Rabbi Elazar's principle
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer with Rabbi Elazar's principle
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: the same applies to פטר חמור (firstborn donkey) — it becomes consecrated, as per Rabbi Elazar's principle that a woman knows the prohibition and redeems it properly, consecrating the difference.

items.text: טעמו של רבי שמעון
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning and its defense
items.desc_en: Ulla presents Rabbi Shimon's argument that something whose redemption is permitted can itself be permitted. The Gemara challenges with שביעית, but answers that its redemption is actually forbidden.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה את טעמו של רבי שמעון: יש דבר שפדיונו מותר והוא אסור? כלומר, אם הפדיון מותר, גם החמור מותר. הגמרא דוחה את הקושיה משביעית, שפדיונה אסור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Shimon's reasoning, and Ulla answers that he argues: is there something whose redemption is permitted but the item itself is forbidden?
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו טעמו של רבי שמעון, ומנסחת: האם יש דבר שפדיונו מותר והוא עצמו אסור? כלומר, אם הפדיון מותר, גם החמור מותר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Sabbatical year produce (שביעית) is forbidden but its redemption is permitted, contradicting Ulla's principle.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה משביעית: פדיונה מותר, והפרי עצמו אסור לאחר זמן הביעור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the redemption of Sabbatical year produce is actually forbidden, as the Master said: the last [coin] is forbidden.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה: גם בשביעית פדיונה אסור, שכן האחרון אחרון אסור.

items.text: Alternative dispute based on biblical verses
items.text_en: Alternative dispute based on biblical verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative explanation that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon argue over the interpretation of the verses 'לא תעבד בבכור שורך' and 'לא תגוז בכור צאנך', with a detailed analysis of their respective positions and a difficulty for Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon argue over the interpretation of biblical verses.

The baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's position that the verses 'לֹא תַעֲבֹד בִּבְכוֹר שׁוֹרֶךָ' and 'לֹא תָגֹז בְּכוֹר צֹאנֶךָ' exclude only one's own animal, but permit working with or shearing another's.
Rabbi Shimon interprets the verses to exclude a human firstborn from the prohibition of work, and a donkey firstborn from the prohibition of shearing.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda's position: why are two verses needed to exclude one's own and another's animal, and why not also forbid a human firstborn?
The Gemara resolves that all agree 'שׁוֹרֶךָ' excludes a human firstborn; the dispute is over 'צֹאנֶךָ', where Rabbi Yehuda permits shearing and working with a partner's animal.
Rabbi Shimon holds that a partnership with a gentile is exempt from firstborn status, so the verse is needed only for the donkey firstborn.
The Gemara raises a difficulty: for Rabbi Shimon, why are both 'שׁוֹרֶךָ' and 'צֹאנֶךָ' needed, since he already excludes the human firstborn and the donkey?

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's concession after עריפה and the status of forbidden foods
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's concession after עריפה and the status of forbidden foods
items.desc_en: Rabbah states that Rabbi Shimon agrees that a פטר חמור is forbidden after עריפה, derived from a גזירה שוה. Rava cites a baraisa about items that contract food impurity, and Rabbi Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan explaining Rabbi Shimon's principle that only food which can be fed to others is called food.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states that Rabbi Shimon concedes that a פטר חמור (firstborn donkey) is forbidden after עריפה (neck-breaking).
The gemara explains that Rabbah derives the prohibition via a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) from the word 'עריפה' used in עגלה ערופה (the heifer whose neck is broken).

Rava cites a baraisa listing forbidden items that contract food impurity, including פטר חמור, and notes that Rabbi Shimon agrees only regarding בשר בחלב (meat in milk) because it had a brief period of permissibility.
Rabbi Asi reports Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of Rabbi Shimon's principle: only food that can be fed to others is called 'אוכל' (food) for impurity purposes, based on the verse 'מכל האוכל אשר יאכל'.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Why mention שעת הכושר for meat in milk?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Why mention שעת הכושר for meat in milk?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous argument: if the reason for impurity is that the animal had a moment of permissibility (שעת הכושר), then why mention this for meat in milk (בשר בחלב)? It should be considered 'food that can be fed to others' (אוכל שאתה יכול להאכילו לאחרים) and thus susceptible to impurity regardless.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if the animal had a moment of permissibility (שעת הכושר), why mention this for meat in milk (בשר בחלב)? It should already be considered 'food that can be fed to others' (אוכל שאתה יכול להאכילו לאחרים) and thus susceptible to impurity.

items.text: Supporting baraita: Rabbi Shimon on meat in milk
items.text_en: Supporting baraita: Rabbi Shimon on meat in milk
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Shimon that meat in milk is forbidden for eating but permitted for benefit, based on a scriptural analogy. This implies that meat in milk is not considered 'food that can be fed to others' because it is forbidden to eat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Shimon that meat in milk is forbidden for eating but permitted for benefit, based on a scriptural analogy.

items.text: Gemara's resolution: Two points in the statement
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: Two points in the statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the earlier statement had two points: first, that it is 'food that can be fed to others', and second, that for the owner himself, it had a moment of permissibility (שעת הכושר). This resolves the challenge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge by explaining that the earlier statement contained two points: the food is fit for others, and for the owner it had a moment of permissibility (שעת הכושר).

items.text: הוכחת רבא מפטר חמור
items.text_en: Challenge: Why not teach that Rabbi Shimon agrees about impurity?
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues: if Rabbi Shimon permits benefit from the carcass after decapitation (עריפה), then the Mishnah should have stated that Rabbi Shimon agrees that a firstborn donkey and meat in milk are susceptible to food impurity. The Gemara answers that this is only if he designated it for food; here we are dealing with a case where he did not designate it.
items.desc: רבא מוכיח שאם רבי שמעון היה מתיר בהנאה לאחר עריפה, היה צריך להורות שפטר חמור טמא טומאת אוכלין. מכיוון שלא הורה כן, מוכח שאסור בהנאה. הגמרא דוחה: מדובר במקרה שלא חישב עליו לאכילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if Rabbi Shimon permits benefit after decapitation (עריפה), then the Mishnah should have taught that Rabbi Shimon agrees that a firstborn donkey and meat in milk are susceptible to food impurity.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם רבי שמעון היה מתיר בהנאה לאחר עריפה, היה צריך לשנות במשנתנו שרבי שמעון מודה בפטר חמור ובשר בחלב שטמאים טומאת אוכלין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: if he designated it for food, indeed it would be susceptible; here we are dealing with a case where he did not designate it.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה: אם חישב עליו לאכילה, אכן כן; כאן מדובר שלא חישב עליו, ולכן אינו טמא.

items.text: Principle: 'Since its prohibition is its significance'
items.text_en: Principle: 'Since its prohibition is its significance'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Rabbis deem it susceptible to impurity. The students before Rav Sheishet answer: because its prohibition is its significance (הואיל ואיסורו חישובו) — the fact that it is forbidden makes it considered significant food.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Rabbis deem the carcass of a kosher bird susceptible to impurity.
The students before Rav Sheishet answer: because its prohibition is its significance (הואיל ואיסורו חישובו) — the fact that it is forbidden makes it considered significant food.

items.text: Objection: Does this principle contradict the Mishnah?
items.text_en: Objection: Does this principle contradict the Mishnah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Do the Rabbis really say 'since its prohibition is its significance'? But we learned in a Mishnah that a kosher bird carcass requires intent (מחשבה) to be susceptible to impurity. If prohibition alone suffices, why need intent? The Gemara answers: That Mishnah is Rabbi Shimon's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Do the Rabbis really say 'since its prohibition is its significance'? But the Mishnah teaches that a kosher bird carcass requires מחשבה (intent) to become susceptible to impurity — if prohibition alone suffices, why would intent be needed?
The Gemara answers: That Mishnah is the view of Rabbi Shimon, not the Rabbis.

items.text: הוכחות ממשניות טהרות
items.text_en: Further challenges from other Mishnayot
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings additional Mishnayot: a carcass of a non-kosher animal requires intent, and a kosher bird carcass in villages requires intent. If prohibition is significance, why need intent? The Gemara suggests these are Rabbi Shimon's view, but then notes that the latter clause explicitly attributes a statement to Rabbi Shimon, implying the first clause is not his. This creates a difficulty.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה שתי משניות: הראשונה (נבלת בהמה טמאה) דורשת מחשבה, מה שמתאים לרבי שמעון; השנייה (נבלת בהמה טהורה) מוכיחה שרבנן לא סוברים שאיסורו חשיבו, כי אחרת לא היה צריך מחשבה. הסיפא היא רבי שמעון, ולכן הרישא אינה כרבי שמעון.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah: a non-kosher animal carcass and a kosher bird carcass in villages require intent (מחשבה) but not preparation (הכשר), challenging the principle that prohibition itself constitutes significance.

The Gemara brings another Mishnah: a kosher animal carcass and kosher bird carcass in markets do not require intent, implying that a non-kosher carcass does require intent, again challenging the principle.
The Gemara objects that if one tries to attribute the first Mishnah to Rabbi Shimon, the later clause explicitly cites Rabbi Shimon, implying the first clause is not his view, creating a difficulty.

items.text: מסקנת רבא
items.text_en: Rava's conclusion: The principle is not accepted
items.desc_en: Rava concludes: Everyone agrees that we do not say 'since its prohibition is its significance'. If he had decapitated it, then yes, it would be considered food, but the principle itself is rejected.
items.desc: רבא מסיק שכולי עלמא לא אמרינן איסורו חשיבו, ואם ערף את הפטר חמור, גם רבנן מודים שאינו טמא טומאת אוכלין, כיון שלא חישב עליו לאכילה.

sub.desc_en: Rava concludes that everyone agrees the principle 'since its prohibition is its significance' (איסורו חישובו) is not accepted, but if one had decapitated the animal, then it would be considered food.

items.text: מחלוקת התנאים בדם שחיטה של עורב
items.text_en: The case of slaughtering a raven for study and the dispute between Nomos and Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the case involves slaughtering a raven for the purpose of learning, and explains the dispute between Nomos and Rabbi Eliezer. The Tanna Kamma holds that the blood renders food susceptible to impurity in general but requires intent for the raven itself, while Rabbi Eliezer holds that blood from slaughter always renders susceptible, even without intent for the raven itself.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה במקרה שבו שחט עורב כדי ללמוד ממנו, ונחלקו התנאים: נימוס אומר שדמו מכשיר רק במחשבה, ורבי אליעזר אומר שדם שחיטה לעולם מכשיר אף בלא מחשבה. הגמרא מביאה ברייתא ומנתחת את טעמו של רבי אליעזר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what case is being discussed, and answers that it involves slaughtering a raven for study, within the dispute between Nomos and Rabbi Eliezer.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבררת שהמקרה הוא בשחט עורב כדי ללמוד ממנו, ומביאה את מחלוקת נימוס ורבי אליעזר: נימוס מצריך מחשבה להכשר דם העורב, ורבי אליעזר פוטר ממחשבה גם לגופו.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yosei reports Nomos saying that the blood of a raven slaughtered for study renders food susceptible to impurity, while Rabbi Eliezer says blood from slaughter always renders susceptible.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Eliezer's statement seems identical to the Tanna Kamma, and concludes the difference lies in whether the prohibition of the raven itself constitutes intent (מחשבה).
The Tanna Kamma holds that the blood renders food susceptible in general, but for the raven itself, intent (מחשבה) is required.
Rabbi Eliezer comes to say that blood from slaughter always renders susceptible, and even for the raven itself, no intent (מחשבה) is required.

items.text: טעמו של רבי אליעזר וסימני טהרה
items.text_en: Rejection: Perhaps Rabbi Eliezer's reason is unique to the raven
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer's ruling is limited to the raven because it has signs of kashrut. It cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon explains that the raven is special due to its signs of purity. The Gemara then suggests that even for mere occupation, the blood would render susceptible, but the case is specifically about learning due to Nomos.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בטעמו של רבי אליעזר, ומעלה אפשרות שטעמו נובע מכך שבעורב יש סימני טהרה, ולכן דמו מכשיר אף בלא מחשבה. הגמרא מביאה את דברי רבי שמעון התומכים בכך, ומסיקה שאכן הטעם הוא סימני טהרה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer's ruling is limited to the raven because it has signs of purity (סִימָנֵי טׇהֳרָה).
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את ההבנה שטעמו של רבי אליעזר הוא שאין צריך מחשבה, ומעלה שטעמו נובע מכך שבעורב יש סימני טהרה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon explains that the raven is special because it has signs of purity.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה את דברי רבי שמעון בברייתא התומכים בכך שסימני טהרה הם טעם מספיק להכשר דם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that even for mere occupation (לְהִתְעַסֵּק) the blood would render susceptible, but the case is specifically about learning due to Nomos.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את ההבנה שסימני טהרה הם הטעם, ומסיקה שטעמו של רבי אליעזר הוא משום נמוס.

items.text: ברייתא על פדיון פטר חמור ועריפתו
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon regarding benefit from an unredeemed firstborn donkey
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda prohibits benefit from an unredeemed firstborn donkey after its neck is broken, while Rabbi Shimon permits it. The Gemara clarifies that the dispute applies both to the blood and the body, and explains why both cases are necessary to teach.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא הדנה בפטר חמור שלא נפדה, ועורפים את ראשו בקופיץ, ורבי יהודה אוסר ורבי שמעון מתיר. הגמרא דנה בפירוש הברייתא ומסבירה שהמחלוקת נוגעת להנאת דמים לעומת הנאת הגוף, ושתי הצדדים נצרכים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda prohibits benefit from an unredeemed firstborn donkey after its neck is broken, while Rabbi Shimon permits it.
The Gemara suggests that the dispute in the baraita actually concerns benefit from the living animal, not after death.
The Gemara objects that since the latter clause of the baraita explicitly deals with the living animal, the first clause must refer to a different state (after death).

The Gemara cites the latter clause of the baraita, which prohibits killing the animal in various ways and prohibits shearing and working it while alive, with Rabbi Yehuda prohibiting and Rabbi Shimon permitting.
The Gemara resolves that both clauses refer to the living animal: the first clause prohibits benefit from its blood, and the latter clause prohibits benefit from its body.

The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: without the first, one might think Rabbi Shimon only permits the blood but not the body; without the second, one might think Rabbi Yehuda only prohibits the body but not the blood.

items.text: מודה רבי שמעון לאחר עריפה
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's statement that Rabbi Shimon agrees the animal is forbidden after the neck-breaking
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports that Rabbi Shimon agrees the animal is forbidden after the neck-breaking. He derives this from a gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) on the word 'arifah'. Rav Sheishet challenges this, suggesting the source could be Rabbi Yehuda, but explains that the verse is needed to counter the assumption that the neck-breaking permits the animal like redemption does.
items.desc: רב נחמן בשם רבא בר אבוה אומר שרבי שמעון מודה שאסור להנות מהפטר חמור לאחר עריפתו. הגמרא מביאה מקור מגזירה שווה בין עריפת פטר חמור לעגלה ערופה, ודנה בזיהוי התנא בברייתא.

sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports in the name of Rabbah bar Avuh that Rabbi Shimon agrees the animal is forbidden after the neck-breaking.
sub.desc: רב נחמן בשם רבא בר אבוה אומר שרבי שמעון מודה שלאחר עריפה אסור.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman derives his ruling from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'עריפה' (neck-breaking): just as the neck-breaking of the עגלה ערופה (broken-necked heifer) renders it forbidden, so too here the animal is forbidden.
sub.desc: רב נחמן מביא מקור מגזירה שווה בין עריפת פטר חמור לעגלה ערופה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: whom does this גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) address? If it is Rabbi Yehuda, he already forbids the animal while alive, so the analogy is unnecessary; therefore it must be addressing Rabbi Shimon, who permits it while alive.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מי הוא התנא בברייתא, ודוחה שאינו רבי יהודה אלא רבי שמעון.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheishet objects: the source could still be Rabbi Yehuda, because one might have thought that neck-breaking (עריפה) permits the animal like redemption (פדייה) does, so the verse teaches that it does not.
sub.desc: רב ששת מתרץ שהברייתא היא רבי יהודה, והצורך הוא ללמד שעריפה במקום פדייה עומדת.

items.text: Rav Nachman's second proof from Levi's baraita
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's second proof from Levi's baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman brings another proof from a baraita of Levi, which states that the owner caused the priest to lose money, so his money should be lost. The Gemara questions whether this aligns with Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Shimon, and offers two resolutions: either it is Rabbi Yehuda referring to the intermediate value, or Rabbi Shimon referring to the minimal value before death.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman introduces a second proof from a baraita of Levi, which states that the owner caused the priest to lose money, so his money should be lost.
The Gemara questions whether the baraita aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, who already holds the animal is forbidden from life, or Rabbi Shimon, who permits it until death.

The Gemara offers two resolutions: either the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda and refers to the intermediate value between life and death, or it follows Rabbi Shimon and refers to the minimal value before death.

items.text: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan dispute whether the disagreement continues after the neck-breaking
items.text_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan dispute whether the disagreement continues after the neck-breaking
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish agrees with Rav Nachman that Rabbi Shimon concedes the animal is forbidden after the neck-breaking, while Rabbi Yochanan (or Rabbi Elazar) maintains that the dispute remains even after the neck-breaking.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that Rabbi Shimon concedes the animal is forbidden after the neck-breaking.
Rabbi Yochanan (or Rabbi Elazar) objects that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon continues even after the neck-breaking.

items.text: Application of the dispute to the case of consecrating a firstborn donkey
items.text_en: Application of the dispute to the case of consecrating a firstborn donkey
items.desc_en: The Gemara applies Rav Nachman's statement to a mishnah about consecrating a firstborn donkey. One version says that after the neck-breaking, all agree it is not consecrated. Another version questions whether the mishnah aligns with either Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Shimon. Rabbah bar Avuh resolves it by saying the donkey is worth only a shekel, and follows Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda who requires a minimum of a shekel for redemption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative version of Rav Nachman's statement, applying it to the mishnah about consecrating a firstborn donkey, and questions whether the mishnah contradicts Rabbi Shimon.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuh answers that the mishnah refers to after the neck-breaking, and all agree it is not consecrated.
Another version questions whose opinion the mishnah follows, arguing it fits neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Shimon.

Rabbah bar Avuh in the name of Rav resolves that the mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, but the donkey is worth only a shekel, and Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda who requires a minimum of a shekel for redemption.

items.text: Derivation of immediate and minimal redemption for a firstborn donkey
items.text_en: Derivation of immediate and minimal redemption for a firstborn donkey
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the derivation from the verse 'tifdeh' repeated, teaching that redemption can be immediate and for any amount. It then questions Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's requirement of a shekel, and Rava derives it from the verse about valuations, while the Rabbis reject that derivation.

sub.desc_en: Mar states the derivation from the repeated 'תִּפְדֶּה' that redemption can be immediate and for any amount.
The Gemara questions why this derivation is necessary, as it seems obvious.

The Gemara explains that the derivation is necessary because one might have thought to analogize the firstborn donkey to the firstborn human, requiring redemption after thirty days and for five shekels.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's requirement of a shekel, asking whether he analogizes to the firstborn human (requiring five shekels) or not (then where does he get a shekel?).
Rava derives the shekel requirement from the verse about valuations, stating that all valuations must be at least a shekel.
The Rabbis reject Rava's derivation, arguing that the verse about valuations applies only to human valuations, not to animal redemption.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on the valuation of a firstborn donkey
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on the valuation of a firstborn donkey
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules like the Sages that even a Patroza worth a danka suffices. Rava supports this from a mishna about 'great and small'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the verse that the valuation of a firstborn donkey is based on the owner's financial means (השג יד).
Rav Nachman rules like the Sages that even a Patroza worth a danka suffices, and Rava supports this from a mishna about 'great and small'.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's question to Rabbi Tarfon and Rava's ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's question to Rabbi Tarfon and Rava's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia asks Rabbi Tarfon how much to give a kohen for a firstborn donkey. Rabbi Tarfon cites the three standards: generous (sela), stingy (shekel), average (rigya). Rava rules the halakha is rigya, which is three zuz.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia sends his firstborn donkey to Rabbi Tarfon and asks how much to give the kohen; Rabbi Tarfon cites the three standards: generous (sela), stingy (shekel), average (rigya).

Rabbi Yehuda Nasi had a firstborn donkey and asked Rabbi Tarfon how much to give the kohen. Rabbi Tarfon cited the rule: a generous eye gives a sela, a stingy eye a shekel, an average eye a rigya (third of a shekel).
Rava rules the halakha is rigya, which is three zuz, and notes that the term rigya is used both here and elsewhere.

items.text: Resolution of the apparent contradiction between halakhot
items.text_en: Resolution of the apparent contradiction between halakhot
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between Rava's ruling and another halakha, and resolves it: one case is when the owner seeks advice, the other when he acts on his own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between Rava's ruling and another halakha.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when the owner seeks advice and when he acts on his own.

items.text: Redeeming a firstborn donkey with its value when no sheep is available
items.text_en: Redeeming a firstborn donkey with its value when no sheep is available
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak quoting Reish Lakish says one can redeem a firstborn donkey with its value if he has no sheep. The Gemara questions whether this follows Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Shimon, and concludes it can even be Rabbi Yehuda, as the Torah's requirement of a sheep is to be lenient, not strict. Rav Nachman bar Rav Yosef redeems with vegetables worth its value.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak quoting Reish Lakish rules that one who has a firstborn donkey but no sheep redeems it with its monetary value.
The Gemara asks whose opinion this follows, suggesting it cannot be Rabbi Yehuda who holds the Torah insisted on a sheep, so it must be Rabbi Shimon.
Ravina objects that the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda, not Rabbi Shimon, so the ruling cannot be according to Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara adds that the Mishnah is set anonymously according to Rabbi Yehuda, so how can the ruling follow Rabbi Shimon?

The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, the ruling stands because the Torah's requirement of a sheep was meant to be lenient, not strict, and the donkey is no more stringent than consecrated property.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Yosef's practice
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Yosef's practice
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Yosef actually redeems a firstborn donkey with vegetables worth its value, supporting the ruling.

items.text: The status of redemption by another person and the owner's rights
items.text_en: The status of redemption by another person and the owner's rights
items.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi quoting Rav Huna says if one redeems another's firstborn donkey, the redemption is valid. The Gemara debates whether the redemption money goes to the redeemer or the owner, especially under Rabbi Yehuda's view that the donkey is forbidden in benefit. Rav Nachman brings a proof from the law of theft: a thief pays double to the owner, implying the donkey is considered the owner's property, not consecrated.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi quotes Rav Huna stating that if one redeems another's firstborn donkey, the redemption is valid.
The Gemara asks whether the redemption money goes to the redeemer or to the original owner.
The Gemara clarifies that the question only arises under Rabbi Yehuda's view that the donkey is forbidden in benefit, not under Rabbi Shimon's view that it is permitted.
The Gemara poses the dilemma: is the donkey compared to consecrated property (הקדש), where the redeemer gains the money, or is it not, since the owner already acquired it in the interim?
Rav Nachman brings a proof from the law of theft: a thief pays double to the owners, implying the donkey is considered the owner's property, not consecrated.
The Gemara identifies that the baraita must be according to Rabbi Yehuda, not Rabbi Shimon, because under Rabbi Shimon the donkey would have current value.

The Gemara concludes that if the donkey were compared to consecrated property, the verse 'וְגֻנַּב מִבֵּית הָאִישׁ' (and it was stolen from the man's house) would exclude it, so the proof stands that the money goes to the owner.

items.text: Laws of uncertain firstborn donkeys and untithed produce in inheritance
items.text_en: Laws of uncertain firstborn donkeys and untithed produce in inheritance
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a baraita about how to handle ten uncertain firstborn donkeys: one separates ten sheep and tithes them, keeping them. This supports Rav Nachman's statement. Rav Nachman then cites three cases from Rabbah bar Avuha about uncertain firstborn donkeys and untithed produce inherited from a kohen who inherited from an Israelite, where the Israelite can tithe them and keep them. The Gemara explains why all three cases are necessary.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's clarification
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that produce purchased from a gentile after it has been separated (ממורחין) is tithed and belongs to the buyer. The Gemara questions who separated it: if the gentile, the Torah says 'your grain' not a gentile's grain; if an Israelite separated it from the gentile's property, it is tithed because a gentile has no acquisition in the Land of Israel to exempt from tithes, and it belongs to the buyer because he can claim he comes from the power of one who cannot litigate with him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that produce purchased from a gentile after it has been separated (ממורחין) is tithed and belongs to the buyer.
The Gemara questions who separated the produce: if a gentile, the Torah says 'your grain' not a gentile's grain.

The Gemara answers that an Israelite separated it from the gentile's property, so it is tithed because a gentile has no acquisition in the Land of Israel to exempt from tithes, and it belongs to the buyer because he can claim he comes from the power of one who cannot litigate with him.

items.text: Mishnah on depositing produce with a gentile
items.text_en: Mishnah on depositing produce with a gentile
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah from elsewhere: one who deposits his produce with a Cuthean or an am ha'aretz retains its presumption of being untithed, but with a gentile it is like his produce; Rabbi Shimon says it is doubtful (דמאי).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: one who deposits produce with a Cuthean or an am ha'aretz retains the presumption of being untithed and subject to Sabbatical year laws.
The Mishnah states: with a gentile, the produce is treated as the gentile's own (presumably exchanged); Rabbi Shimon says it is treated as דמאי (doubtfully tithed).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that all agree regarding separating terumah; the dispute is about giving it to a priest. The Tanna Kamma holds that the gentile definitely exchanged the produce, so it must be given to a priest; Rabbi Shimon holds it is doubtful (דמאי).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that all agree regarding the obligation to separate תרומה (priestly portion); the dispute is only about giving it to a priest.
The Tanna Kamma holds that the gentile certainly exchanged the produce, so the separated תרומה must be given to a priest.
Rabbi Shimon holds that the produce is treated as דמאי (doubtfully tithed), so the priest must bring proof to receive the תרומה.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi taught this halakha, and Abaye objected: if the dispute is only about doubt, then if it were certain that the gentile exchanged the produce, all would agree it must be given to a priest. But Rabbi Shmuel said Rabbi Chanina ruled that one who buys separated produce from a gentile tithes it and keeps it. The Gemara resolves that the two cases differ: one deals with terumah gedolah, the other with terumah ma'aser.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi sat and stated this halakha of Rabbi Elazar.
Abaye objected: the dispute is only about doubt; if it were certain that the gentile exchanged the produce, all would agree it must be given to a priest.
Abaye cited Rabbi Shmuel quoting Rabbi Chanina: one who buys separated produce from a gentile tithes it and keeps it.
The Gemara resolves that the two cases differ: one deals with תרומה גדולה (the priestly portion), the other with תרומת מעשר (the tithe of the tithe).

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's proof
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's proof
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites a verse to prove that one who buys separated produce from a gentile is exempt from terumah ma'aser, because the verse says 'when you take from the children of Israel' — only from Israelites must you separate terumah ma'aser and give it to a priest, not from a gentile.

sub.desc_en: Abaye recalls a statement of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that derives from a verse that one who buys separated produce from a gentile is exempt from separating תרומת מעשר (the tithe of the tithe) and giving it to a priest.

items.text: Clarification of 'if he died, one may benefit from it'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'if he died, one may benefit from it'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that if the owner dies, one may benefit from the produce. It asks: if the priest died, it is obvious; if the original owner died and the priest benefits, that is also obvious. The Gemara explains that one might have thought the priest does not acquire it until it reaches his hand, so it teaches that from the moment of separation it is in the priest's domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement about benefiting from the lamb if it dies, asking where it died and noting that both possibilities (in the priest's house or the owner's house) seem obvious.

The Gemara resolves that one might have thought the priest does not acquire the lamb until it reaches his hand, so the Mishnah teaches that from the moment of separation it is already in the priest's domain.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: בעלי חיים הפסולים לפדיון
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not redeem a firstborn donkey with a calf, a non-domesticated animal, a slaughtered animal, a terefah, a kil'ayim, or a koy. Rabbi Eliezer permits kil'ayim because it is a 'seh' and prohibits koy because it is a safek. If given to a priest, the priest must set aside a sheep in its place.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שאין פודין פטר חמור בעגל, חיה, שחוטה, טריפה, כלאיים או כוי. רבי אליעזר מתיר בכלאיים כי הוא 'שה', ואוסר בכוי כי הוא ספק. אם נתנו לכהן, אין הכהן רשאי לקיימו עד שיפריש שה תחתיו.
