Rav Chisda answers that Beit Shammai's leniency applies only to a firstborn (whose sanctity is from the womb), not to other disqualified consecrated animals.

items.text: Rejection of the attempt to align the mishnah with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Rejection of the attempt to align the mishnah with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the suggestion that the entire mishnah follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, arguing that he only permits selling blemished consecrated animals because their redemption value is significant, but a firstborn animal's redemption value is not significant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects aligning the mishnah with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, because his leniency applies only to consecrated animals with significant redemption value, not to a firstborn whose redemption value is insignificant.

items.text: Challenge from the baraita about selling blemished consecrated animals
items.text_en: Challenge from the baraita about selling blemished consecrated animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the distinction, citing a baraita where Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon permits selling blemished consecrated animals in the market, indicating that any profit for the Temple treasury is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous distinction by citing a baraita where Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon permits selling blemished consecrated animals in the market, implying that any profit for the Temple treasury is permitted.

items.text: Two alternative reasons for the prohibition
items.text_en: Two alternative reasons for the prohibition
items.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana and the Western scholars offer two reasons why one may not cause a blemish to a firstborn: either because the improvement to the hide comes at the expense of the meat, or because it appears as if one is performing labor with consecrated animals. Rabbi Yosei bar Avin adds a decree lest one raise entire herds from them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana gives the first reason: the improvement to the hide comes at the expense of the meat, so causing a blemish is forbidden.

sub.text: Western scholars in the name of Ravina
sub.text_en: Western scholars in the name of Ravina
sub.desc_en: The Western scholars in the name of Ravina give the second reason: it appears as if one is performing labor with consecrated animals.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin adds a decree lest one raise entire herds from them, as a third reason for the prohibition.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: דיני הקזת דם לבכור
items.text_en: Mishnah: Bloodletting a firstborn
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents a dispute about whether one may let blood from a firstborn animal that is suffering from an excess of blood. Rabbi Yehuda prohibits it even if the animal will die, while the Sages permit it as long as no blemish is caused, and Rabbi Shimon permits it even if it causes a blemish.
items.desc: המשנה פותחת במחלוקת בין רבי יהודה, חכמים ורבי שמעון לגבי היתר הקזת דם לבכור שנתקע בדמו, תוך דגש על איסור עשיית מום.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah presents a dispute about bloodletting a firstborn animal: Rabbi Yehuda prohibits it even if the animal will die, the Sages permit it as long as no blemish is caused, and Rabbi Shimon permits it even if it causes a blemish.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת במחלוקת בין רבי יהודה, חכמים ורבי שמעון לגבי היתר הקזת דם לבכור שנתקע בדמו, תוך דגש על איסור עשיית מום.

items.text: ברייתא המפרשת את המחלוקת
items.text_en: Baraita: Tannaitic dispute about bloodletting
items.desc_en: A baraita elaborates on the dispute: Rabbi Meir permits bloodletting only where no blemish is caused, the Sages permit it even where a blemish is caused but the animal may not be slaughtered for that blemish, Rabbi Shimon permits slaughtering for that blemish, and Rabbi Yehuda prohibits bloodletting even if the animal dies.
items.desc: הברייתא מרחיבה את מחלוקת התנאים: רבי מאיר אוסר הקזה במקום שעושה מום, חכמים מתירים בתנאי שלא ישחט על אותו מום, רבי שמעון מתיר לגמרי, ורבי יהודה אוסר בכל מקרה.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Meir's position: bloodletting is permitted only where no blemish is caused.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בדעת רבי מאיר: בבכור שאחזו דם, מזהים במקום שאין עושים בו מום, ואין מזהים במקום שעושים בו מום.

sub.desc_en: The Sages permit bloodletting even where a blemish is caused, but the animal may not be slaughtered for that blemish.
sub.desc: הברייתא מביאה את דעת חכמים: מתירים להקיז אף במקום שעושה מום, ובלבד שלא ישחט על אותו מום.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon permits slaughtering the animal for that blemish.
sub.desc: הברייתא מביאה את דעת חכמים: מתירים להקיז אף במקום שעושה מום, ובלבד שלא ישחט על אותו מום.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda prohibits bloodletting even if the animal would die.
sub.desc: הברייתא מביאה את דעת חכמים: מתירים להקיז אף במקום שעושה מום, ובלבד שלא ישחט על אותו מום.

items.text: השוואה למחלוקת בחבית של תרומה
items.text_en: Parallel dispute about a barrel of terumah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Chiyya taught their sons that the dispute about bloodletting parallels a dispute about a barrel of terumah that became doubtfully impure, where Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabban Gamliel disagree about whether to take action. The baraita then aligns Rabbi Meir with Rabbi Eliezer, the Sages with Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Yehuda with Rabban Gamliel.
items.desc: רבי אלעזר (או רבי חייא) מלמד את בנו שהמחלוקת בהקזת דם מקבילה למחלוקת בחבית תרומה שנטמאה בספק: רבי אליעזר, רבי יהושע ורבן גמליאל. הגמרא משווה את דעות התנאים: רבי מאיר כרבי אליעזר, חכמים כרבי יהושע, ורבי יהודה כרבן גמליאל.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar (or Rabbi Chiyya) taught his son that the dispute about bloodletting parallels a dispute about a barrel of terumah (תרומה) that became doubtfully impure, citing the positions of Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabban Gamliel.
sub.desc: רבי אלעזר (או רבי חייא) מלמד את בנו שהמחלוקת בהקזת דם מקבילה למחלוקת בחבית תרומה שנטמאה בספק, ומביא את דברי רבי אליעזר.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel rules that one should not initiate any new action with the barrel.
sub.desc: מביא את דעות רבי יהושע ורבן גמליאל בחבית תרומה, המקבילות לדעות חכמים ורבי יהודה בהקזת דם.

sub.desc_en: The baraita aligns Rabbi Meir with Rabbi Eliezer, the Sages with Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Yehuda with Rabban Gamliel.
sub.desc: הגמרא קובעת את ההקבלה: רבי מאיר כרבי אליעזר, חכמים כרבי יהושע, ורבי יהודה כרבן גמליאל.

items.text: דחיית ההשוואה הישירה
items.text_en: Challenge to the parallel: Different considerations
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the parallel, arguing that the cases differ: in the terumah case, one acts directly (בידים), while in the firstborn case, one only causes indirectly (גרמא); also, in the terumah case, there is hope that Elijah will purify it, while in the firstborn case, the animal will die if left untreated. These differences could lead to different rulings.
items.desc: הגמרא דוחה את ההקבלה הישירה בין המחלוקות, ומציעה סיבות שונות לכך שתנאים עשויים להחזיק בדעות שונות בכל מקרה: הבדל בין עשייה בידיים לגרמא, וחשש לבוא אליהו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the parallel regarding Rabbi Meir: perhaps he prohibits bloodletting only where he acts directly (בידים), but here where it is indirect (גרמא), he might agree with Rabbi Yehoshua.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על ההשוואה הישירה בין המחלוקות, ומציעה שרבי מאיר עשוי להחזיק כרבי יהושע בבכור משום שהדם הוא גרמא ולא מעשה בידיים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges regarding Rabbi Eliezer: perhaps he safeguards the barrel only because Elijah might purify it, but here where the animal will die, he might agree with the Rabbis.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שרבי אליעזר עשוי להתיר הקזת דם בבכור משום שאם ישאירו אותו ימות, בניגוד לחבית תרומה שבה יש תקווה לבוא אליהו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges regarding the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda: perhaps the Rabbis permit bloodletting only because the animal will die, but regarding teruma they might agree with Rabbi Eliezer; and Rabbi Yehuda prohibits bloodletting only because he acts directly, but regarding teruma he might agree with Rabbi Yehoshua.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שהרבנים עשויים להתיר הקזת דם בבכור משום שאם ישאירו אותו ימות, ואילו בחבית תרומה יחששו לבוא אליהו ויחזיקו כרבי אליעזר; וכן שרבי יהודה עשוי להחמיר בבכור משום מעשה בידיים, ובחבית תרומה יקל כרבי יהושע משום גרמא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges regarding Rabban Gamliel: perhaps he leaves the barrel untouched only because Elijah might purify it, but here where the animal will die, he might agree with the Rabbis.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שרבן גמליאל עשוי להתיר הקזת דם בבכור משום שאם ישאירו אותו ימות, בניגוד לחבית תרומה שבה יש חשש לבוא אליהו.

items.text: מחלוקת בפסוקים: מום בבעל מום
items.text_en: Alternative parallel: Dispute about causing a blemish to an already blemished animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests a different parallel: the dispute about bloodletting is actually about causing a blemish to an already blemished animal, which is derived from verses. Rabbi Meir and the Sages disagree about the interpretation of verses regarding blemishes, and the Gemara explains the scriptural basis for each opinion.
items.desc: הגמרא מסבירה שהמחלוקת האמיתית היא בפסוקים: האם איסור עשיית מום חל גם על בעל מום. רבי מאיר דורש 'כל מום לא יהיה בו' להרחיב, ורבנן דורשים 'תמים יהיה לרצון' לצמצם. הגמרא מביאה דרשות נוספות על הפסוקים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new parallel: the dispute about bloodletting is actually about the interpretation of verses, citing Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that all agree one is liable for leavening after leavening.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בטענה שהמחלוקות כאן ובמשנת תרומות מבוססות על דרשות פסוקים שונות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds that all agree one is liable for castrating after castration, derived from the verse 'וּמָעוּךְ וְכָתוּת וְנָתוּק וְכָרוּת' (crushed, bruised, detached, cut).
sub.desc: דוגמה נוספת: מסרס אחר מסרס חייב, מדין 'ומעוך וכתות ונתוק וכרות'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Sages only disagree about causing a blemish to an already blemished animal: Rabbi Meir derives from 'כל מום לא יהיה בו' (any blemish shall not be in it) and the Rabbis from 'תמים יהיה לרצון' (it shall be perfect to be accepted).
sub.desc: הגמרא מבהירה שהמחלוקת האמיתית היא במטיל מום בבעל מום: רבי מאיר דורש 'כל מום לא יהיה בו' להרחיב, ורבנן דורשים 'תמים יהיה לרצון' לצמצם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Meir does with the verse 'תמים יהיה לרצון' (it shall be perfect to be accepted), and answers that it serves to exclude an animal blemished from the outset.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מה עושה רבי מאיר בפסוק 'תמים יהיה לרצון'?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that an animal blemished from the outset is obvious like a palm tree, so no verse is needed to exclude it.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה: בעל מום מעיקרו פשיטא שאינו בכלל האיסור, שהרי הוא כדקל בעלמא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the verse excludes disqualified consecrated animals after their redemption, teaching that the prohibition against causing a blemish does not apply to them.
sub.desc: תירוץ אחר: הפסוק ממעט פסולי המוקדשין לאחר פדיונן, שאף על פי שאסורים בגיזה ועבודה, אין איסור להטיל בהם מום.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Rabbis interpret the verse 'כל מום לא יהיה בו' (any blemish shall not be in it), and answers that it comes to include a blemish caused by indirect action, citing a baraita.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: והרי גם לרבנן כתוב 'כל מום לא יהיה בו', שמרחיב את האיסור?

items.text: איסור גרימת מום עקיף בבכור
items.text_en: Derivation of indirect blemish prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that one may not place a fig-cake or dough on the ear of a firstborn to attract a dog to eat it, thereby causing a blemish. It answers that the verse 'any blemish' (כל מום) includes even indirect causation.
items.desc: הקטע דן במקור לאיסור להביא תאנים דבוקות או בצק על אוזן הבכור כדי שכלב יאכל ויגרום מום. הדרשה מהפסוק 'כל מום' מלמדת שהאיסור חל גם על גרימת מום עקיפה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that one may not place a fig-cake or dough on the ear of a firstborn to attract a dog to eat it, thereby causing a blemish.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'any blemish' (כל מום) includes even indirect causation of a blemish.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on guarding terumah
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on guarding terumah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel, Reish Lakish, and Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha cite the verse 'And I have given you the charge of My terumot' (ואני הנה נתתי לך את משמרת תרומתי). Rabbi Eliezer interprets this as referring to two terumot—pure and suspended—requiring guarding, while Rabbi Yehoshua argues that the singular 'terumati' indicates only one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the dispute is rooted in a verse, citing a tradition from Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel, Reish Lakish, and Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha, who all cite the verse 'And I have given you the charge of My terumot' (ואני הנה נתתי לך את משמרת תרומתי).
Rabbi Eliezer interprets the plural 'terumotai' as referring to two terumot—pure and suspended—both requiring guarding.
Rabbi Yehoshua counters that the verse writes 'terumati' in the singular, indicating only one terumah requires guarding.

items.text: Challenge from the principle of 'yesh em lamikra'
items.text_en: Challenge from the principle of 'yesh em lamikra'
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Eliezer's position by asking whether he holds that the verse has a 'mother' (i.e., a primary meaning), citing a baraita where Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer dispute the interpretation of 'בבגדו בה'. Rabbi Eliezer's view there seems inconsistent with his approach here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Eliezer holds that the vocalization of the Torah is authoritative, and raises a contradiction from the verse 'בבגדו בה' (Exodus 21:8).
Rabbi Akiva interprets 'בבגדו בה' as referring to the master spreading his garment over the maidservant, indicating that the vocalization is authoritative.
Rabbi Eliezer interprets 'בבגדו בה' based on the spelling, meaning 'since he dealt deceitfully with her,' showing he follows the written form, not the vocalization.

items.text: Resolution of the dispute: guarding only what is fit
items.text_en: Resolution of the dispute: guarding only what is fit
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the dispute is about whether one must guard only terumah that is currently fit for consumption (Rabbi Yehoshua) or also terumah that might become fit if Elijah comes and purifies it (Rabbi Eliezer).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute: Rabbi Yehoshua holds that only terumah fit for you must be guarded, while Rabbi Eliezer holds that even terumah of uncertain purity is fit because Elijah might come and purify it.

items.text: בירור דברי שמואל: הלכה כרבי שמעון דברייתא
items.text_en: Clarifying the halakhic ruling: Rabbi Shimon of the baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak questions which Rabbi Shimon is meant, noting that Shmuel had not previously permitted an unintended act. The Gemara cites conflicting traditions and concludes that it refers to Rabbi Shimon of a baraita, as taught explicitly by Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת לאיזה רבי שמעון התכוון שמואל באומרו 'הלכה כרבי שמעון'. לאחר דיון, מסיקים שמדובר ברבי שמעון דברייתא (לגבי היתר אכילת בכור בעל מום), ולא ברבי שמעון דמתניתין (לגבי דבר שאין מתכוין).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenges: which Rabbi Shimon is meant, since Shmuel had never before permitted an unintended act (דבר שאין מתכוין)?

The Gemara cites conflicting traditions: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi reports Rav ruling like Rabbi Yehuda, while Rav Chanin bar Ashi reports Shmuel ruling like Rabbi Shimon, and Rav Chiyya bar Avin teaches the same dispute without naming the tradents.
The Gemara resolves: it refers to Rabbi Shimon of a baraita (ברייתא), as Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi explicitly teaches that Shmuel's ruling follows that Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: משנה: צורם אוזן בבכור
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cutting the ear of a firstborn
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one cuts the ear of a firstborn, Rabbi Eliezer rules that it may never be slaughtered, while the Sages say that if another blemish develops, it may be slaughtered on account of that blemish.
items.desc: המשנה מביאה מחלוקת: רבי אליעזר אוסר לשחוט לעולם בכור שצרם את אוזנו, וחכמים מתירים לשחוט אם נולד בו מום אחר.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: cutting the ear of a firstborn animal renders it permanently unslaughterable according to Rabbi Eliezer, while the Sages permit slaughter if another blemish subsequently develops.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא: האם רבי אליעזר קונס לעולם?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Does Rabbi Eliezer penalize forever?
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to question whether Rabbi Eliezer indeed penalizes the person forever, citing a contradiction from a baraita about a person who had a bright spot (baheret).
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על שיטת רבי אליעזר במשנה, ושואלת האם הוא קונס לעולם, ומביאה ראיה ממשנה אחרת (נגעים) שסותר לכאורה את עמדתו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer penalizes forever, citing a contradiction from a baraita about a person who had a bright spot (baheret).

items.text: Opening Mishnah and dispute
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a nega was cut off intentionally: Rabbi Eliezer rules that when another nega appears, the person becomes tahor from it; the Sages require the nega to spread entirely or diminish to less than a gris.

items.text: Gemara's initial explanation: Rabbah and Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Gemara's initial explanation: Rabbah and Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef explain that Rabbi Eliezer penalizes only in monetary matters, not in bodily matters, because in monetary matters one might come to do it intentionally, but in bodily matters one would not.

items.text: תירוץ רבא לסתירה בדברי רבי אליעזר וחכמים
items.text_en: Rava's resolution of contradictions
items.desc_en: Rava resolves apparent contradictions within Rabbi Eliezer's and the Sages' positions: Rabbi Eliezer's view is consistent as previously explained, and the Sages penalize only in the specific act done, not in other cases.
items.desc: רבא מתרץ שגם בדברי חכמים אין סתירה, כי בשני המקומות קנסו אותו על מעשהו: בבכור קנסו שלא יופטר במום זה, ובצרעת קנסו שלא יטהר בקציצה זו.

items.text: בירור נוסח 'יִטְהַר' או 'וְיִטְהַר'
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's query: 'yit'har' or 'veyit'har'?
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether the Mishnah reads 'yit'har' (he becomes tahor) or 'veyit'har' (and he becomes tahor), affecting a groom with a nega: if 'yit'har', he is tahor from the first nega and waits seven days for the wedding; if 'veyit'har', he remains tamei from the first nega. The question remains unresolved (teiku).
items.desc: רב פפא שואל אם הנוסח הוא 'יִטְהַר' (מיד) או 'וְיִטְהַר' (לאחר שיטהר הנגע השני). ההבדל נוגע לחתן שנראה בו נגע בימי שמחתו: אם הנוסח 'יִטְהַר' הוא טהור מיד, ואם 'וְיִטְהַר' הוא נשאר טמא עד שיטהר הנגע השני.

items.text: שאלת רבי ירמיה: קנס לבן אחרי מות האב
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's query: penalizing the son after death
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether if one cuts the ear of a firstborn and dies, the son is penalized. The discussion compares to selling a slave to gentiles (where the son is penalized) and doing work on Chol Hamoed (where not). Rabbi Zeira answers with a baraita about a field improved in Shemittah: if the owner died, the son may sow, showing the penalty is on the person, not the property.
items.desc: רבי ירמיה שואל אם קנס על צורם אוזן בבכור עובר לבן לאחר מות האב. רבי זירא משיב ממשנה בשביעית: אם האב הטיב שדהו באיסור ומת, בנו זורעה – מכאן שקנסו רק את האב ולא את הבן.

items.text: סיום דברי אביי
items.text_en: Abaye's tradition
items.desc_en: Abaye states a received tradition (naktinan) on the matter, likely concluding the discussion.
items.desc: אביי אומר 'נקטינן' – יש בידינו מסורת, כנראה המשך או סיכום של הדיון הקודם.

items.text: Opening statement on the rule of one who defiles pure items and dies
items.text_en: Opening statement on the rule of one who defiles pure items and dies
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if a person defiles pure items and then dies, his son is not penalized after him, because the damage is not recognizable and the rabbinic penalty applies only to the offender himself.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of blemishes caused by a non-Jew and children
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of blemishes caused by a non-Jew and children
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: a non-Jew (castor) makes a blemish on a firstborn's ear, and the sages permit slaughter; later he does it again and they forbid it. Similarly, children playing tie tails of lambs, causing a blemish, and the sages permit it; when they repeat it, they forbid it. The rule: if done intentionally (with knowledge), it is forbidden; if unintentionally, it is permitted.

items.text: Gemara: Need for both cases in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Need for both cases in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both cases (non-Jew and child) are necessary: if only the non-Jew case was taught, one might think a child, who might learn to do it intentionally, is forbidden; if only the child case was taught, one might think a non-Jew, who might be confused with an adult, is forbidden. Therefore both are needed.

items.text: Rav Chisda and Rava on the wording of the statement
items.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rava on the wording of the statement
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says the Mishnah's leniency applies only when they said 'unless it has a blemish', but if they said 'if a blemish is made in it', it is like telling him to make a blemish. Rava objects that both phrases imply the same thing, so there is no difference.

items.text: Clarification of the rule: 'intentional' includes indirect causation
items.text_en: Clarification of the rule: 'intentional' includes indirect causation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'intentional' includes causing a blemish indirectly (גרמא), and 'unintentional' includes one who speaks casually without intending to cause a blemish.

items.text: Mishnah: Firstborn that kicks and causes a blemish
items.text_en: Mishnah: Firstborn that kicks and causes a blemish
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a firstborn was chasing someone and kicked, causing a blemish, it may be slaughtered on that blemish.

items.text: Rav Pappa's two versions on the timing of the kick
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's two versions on the timing of the kick
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa first says the Mishnah applies only when the kick occurs during the chase, not after, but then a second version says even after the chase it is permitted because the animal still remembers its pain.

items.text: Rav Yehuda and Rava on making a blemish before birth
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Rava on making a blemish before birth
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says it is permitted to make a blemish on a firstborn before it emerges into the world. Rava specifies the location: for a goat, on the ear; for a lamb, on the lip (or also on the ear, depending on the version).

items.text: Rava and Rav Pappa on blemishes that are visible when the animal opens its mouth
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Pappa on blemishes that are visible when the animal opens its mouth
items.desc_en: Rava states that a blemish on the inside of the mouth that is not visible when the animal eats but is visible when it bleats is a valid blemish. Rav Pappa explains that this is the reasoning behind the Mishnah's ruling on inner threads.

items.text: Mishnah: Trustworthiness of shepherds regarding blemishes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Trustworthiness of shepherds regarding blemishes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Israelite shepherds are believed about blemishes that can be caused by humans, but priestly shepherds are not. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says a shepherd is believed about his fellow's animal but not his own. Rabbi Meir says one who is suspect regarding a matter cannot judge or testify about it.

items.text: Gemara: Two interpretations of the Mishnah's ruling on shepherds
items.text_en: Gemara: Two interpretations of the Mishnah's ruling on shepherds
items.desc_en: One Amora explains that 'Israelite shepherds' who are priests are believed (no concern for favoritism), but priestly shepherds of Israelites are not believed (they might keep the animal for themselves). The same applies to a priest for another priest, due to reciprocity. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Meir add their own rulings. Another Amora says 'Israelite shepherds' who are priests are believed.

items.text: Opening statement: Distinction between Israelite and priest shepherds
items.text_en: Opening statement: Distinction between Israelite and priest shepherds
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Israelite shepherds are not trusted regarding priestly firstborns due to suspicion of favoritism, and priests are even less trusted for fellow priests. Rabban Shimon and Rabbi Meir add that one is trusted for another's animal but not one's own, and one suspected of a matter cannot judge or testify.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Israelite shepherds are not trusted regarding priestly firstborns due to suspicion of favoritism.
The Gemara adds that priests are even less trusted for fellow priests due to reciprocal behavior and favoritism.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that a priest is trusted for another's firstborn but not his own.
Rabbi Meir adds that one suspected of causing blemishes cannot judge or testify in such matters.

items.text: Gemara's question: What does Rabbi Meir add?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: What does Rabbi Meir add?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the necessity of Rabbi Meir's statement according to different interpretations of the earlier Mishnah. If the Mishnah refers to Israelite shepherds for priests, Rabbi Meir's ruling is novel; but if it refers to priest shepherds for Israelites, his ruling is redundant with the first Tanna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins its question: According to the opinion that the Mishnah's case of Israelite shepherds refers to priests employed by Israelites who are deemed credible, Rabbi Meir's statement is novel.

The Gemara continues: But according to the opinion that the Mishnah's case of priest-shepherds refers to Israelite shepherds for priests who are not deemed credible, Rabbi Meir's ruling is redundant with the first Tanna.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kapusai, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kapusai, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: A baraita presents three opinions: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kapusai requires two unrelated witnesses for a priest's firstborn; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel allows even his son or daughter; Rabbi Yosei says even ten family members are invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that distinguishes the opinions of the first tanna and Rabbi Meir regarding the testimony of a priest about a firstborn.
רבי יהושע בן קפוסאי (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kapusai) rules that a firstborn in a priest's house requires two unrelated witnesses from the marketplace to testify about its blemish.
רבן שמעון בן גמליאל (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel) permits even the priest's son or daughter to testify about the firstborn's blemish.
רבי יוסי (Rabbi Yosei) rules that even ten family members are invalid to testify about the firstborn's blemish.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling aligned with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kapusai
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling aligned with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kapusai
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Chisda's statement about a doubtful firstborn born to an Israelite requiring two unrelated witnesses follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kapusai's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In accordance with whose opinion does Rav Chisda's ruling about a doubtful firstborn born to an Israelite requiring two unrelated witnesses go?
The Gemara answers: It follows the opinion of רבי יהושע בן קפוסאי (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kapusai).

items.text: Rav Nachman: Owners are trusted for a doubtful firstborn
items.text_en: Rav Nachman: Owners are trusted for a doubtful firstborn
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman argues that owners can testify about their own doubtful firstborn, reasoning from Rabbi Meir's view on ma'aser. The Gemara supports this by noting that priests are suspected of blemishing, but Israelites are not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asserts that owners may testify about their doubtful firstborn, and challenges that otherwise, according to Rabbi Meir, no one could testify about ma'aser.
The Gemara objects that ma'aser is certainly trusted because the owner could blemish his whole flock, but asks who could testify for a doubtful firstborn according to Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that a doubtful firstborn has no remedy, citing a mishna where Rabbi Meir obligates gifts even when replacements are with a priest, showing he permits consumption.
The Gemara concludes that owners are trusted for a doubtful firstborn because only priests are suspected of blemishing, not Israelites.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Rava on halakha, and resolution
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Rava on halakha, and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, while Rava rules like Rabbi Yosei. The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction in Rava's views, concluding that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but only for son or daughter, not wife.

sub.desc_en: Stam reports that Rav Nachman rules the הלכה (binding law) follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel), while Rava rules it follows רבי יוסי (Rabbi Yosei).

The Gemara objects: Did Rava actually say that? But Rava himself said that if the owners were standing outside and the animal entered whole and emerged injured, the household members may testify — implying Rava does not follow Rabbi Yosei.
The Gemara answers: One can say that Rava refers to a case where all the owners are standing outside, so we are not concerned about false testimony.
The Gemara asks: If so, what is the point of Rava's statement? It seems obvious.
The Gemara answers: Rava's statement is necessary lest you think we should suspect the shepherd of causing the blemish; he teaches us that we do not suspect him.

Stam concludes that the הלכה (binding law) follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel), but specifically only his son and daughter may testify, not his wife, because a wife is considered like oneself.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question to Abaye about Rabbi Meir's principle
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question to Abaye about Rabbi Meir's principle
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if Rabbi Meir holds that one suspected of one thing is suspected of the entire Torah, how can priests judge cases as per the verse? This challenges the consistency of Rabbi Meir's view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if Rabbi Meir holds that one suspected of one transgression is suspected of the entire Torah, how can priests judge cases, given the verse that says all disputes shall be according to their word?

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Meir's position
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Meir's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Meir, who suspects a priest of lying about a blemish, would also apply that suspicion to establish the animal as a firstborn (chazakah).

items.text: עדות מפי עד בבכור
items.text_en: Testimony from a witness who heard from another witness
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates whether testimony from a witness who heard from another witness (עד מפי עד) is valid for firstborn animals. Rav Asi forbids it, citing a baraita that limits such testimony to matters of a woman's status, but Rav Ashi permits it. The halakha is decided in favor of permissibility.
items.desc: דיון בשאלה האם עדות מפי עד כשרה לעניין בכור בעל מום. רב אסי אוסר ורב אשי מתיר, וההלכה נפסקת כרב אשי שהדבר מותר.

items.text: The principle of 'the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted'
items.text_en: The principle of 'the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a teaches that if an animal was not established as a firstborn and one person says it is a firstborn with a blemish, he is believed. The Gemara explains this is based on the principle that the same mouth that created the prohibition (by declaring it a firstborn) also permits it (by stating the blemish was present). The Gemara distinguishes this from a case where the speaker had no choice but to mention the blemish, but concludes that the principle still applies because he could have thrown a recognizable blemish on it.

items.text: Mar bar Rav Ashi's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi challenges the application of the principle 'what reason does he have to lie' (מיגו), citing a case where Rava and Abaye debated its use in the presence of witnesses. The Gemara resolves that here, since it is a mere suspicion (חששא), the principle applies.

items.text: מעשה רבי צדוק ורבי יהושע ורבן גמליאל
items.text_en: The story of Rabbi Tzadok's firstborn and the dispute between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tzadok's firstborn animal split its lip while eating. He asks Rabbi Yehoshua if there is a distinction between a chaver and an am ha'aretz regarding credibility; Rabbi Yehoshua says yes. He then asks Rabban Gamliel, who says no. When confronted, Rabban Gamliel summons Rabbi Yehoshua to the study hall, where Rabbi Yehoshua retracts his statement. Rabban Gamliel forces him to stand while he lectures, until the people protest.
items.desc: סיפור על רבי צדוק שהיה לו בכור שנפצע, ושאל את רבי יהושע ורבן גמליאל האם יש הבדל בין כהן תלמיד חכם לעם הארץ. רבי יהושע אמר שכן, אך רבן גמליאל כעס והעמידו על רגליו עד שהעם רטן.

items.text: Mishnah: A priest is believed to say he showed a firstborn and it had a blemish
items.text_en: Mishnah: A priest is believed to say he showed a firstborn and it had a blemish
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a priest is believed to say 'I showed this firstborn and it is blemished.' Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that this is because people do not lie about a matter that will eventually become known (מילתא דעבידא לאגלויי). Rav Ashi supports this from the Mishnah itself.

items.text: Objection from the case of tithes and distinction
items.text_en: Objection from the case of tithes and distinction
items.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi raises an objection from a baraita about an untrustworthy person regarding tithes, where even though the matter will become known, he is not believed. The Gemara begins to distinguish the cases, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on trustworthiness
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on trustworthiness
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah's case of 'from a certain person' supports the view that the Israelite is believed: because the claimant is present, the Israelite fears being caught in a lie. This contrasts with the first clause where there is no claimant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that the agent has an easy way to extricate himself from the accusation.
The Gemara suggests that the latter clause of the mishna supports Rav's ruling, as it states that if the agent was told to buy from a specific person, he is deemed credible.
The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that in the mishna's case the agent has a claimant and therefore fears lying, unlike Rav's case.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba's tradition about Judah's ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba's tradition about Judah's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba reports that the ruling that an Israelite is believed to say 'I gave this firstborn to a priest while it was blemished' was established by Judah based on a tradition from Gidul. The Gemara clarifies that this applies even to a minor who grew up, lest one think he is not knowledgeable.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba questions the source of Yehuda's ruling and reports that he taught Gidul that an Israelite is believed to say 'I gave this firstborn to a priest while it was blemished'.
The Gemara asks: An Israelite? It is obvious that he is believed.
The Gemara answers that the ruling is necessary for a case where the animal was a minor and grew up, lest one think the Israelite is not knowledgeable.

items.text: Different versions of the Mishnah's text
items.text_en: Different versions of the Mishnah's text
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that in Sura they teach the later version of the Mishnah, while in Pumbedita they teach the earlier version, and the halakha follows even the earlier version.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that in Sura they teach the later version of the Mishnah, while in Pumbedita they teach the earlier version, and the halakha follows even the earlier version.

items.text: מעשה ברפרם והכהן הרמאי
items.text_en: Story of Rafram's firstborn and the dishonest priest
items.desc_en: Rafram gave his firstborn to a priest without a blemish. The priest later caused a blemish and claimed it was given to him blemished. Rafram exposed the priest's lie, but the Gemara notes that this case is exceptional because the priest was brazen, and others are not.
items.desc: מסופר על רפרם שנתן בכור תמים לכהן, והכהן הטיל בו מום והביאו לפני רפרם בטענה שקיבלו בעל מום. רפרם זיהה את הבכור, אך לא חשד בכהנים אחרים, וראה בכך מקרה של חוצפה יוצאת דופן.

sub.desc_en: Rafram gives his firstborn to a priest without a blemish; the priest later causes a blemish and brings it to Rafram claiming it was given blemished, but Rafram recognizes the animal and confronts the priest.
sub.desc: מסופר שרפרם נתן בכור תמים לכהן, הכהן הטיל בו מום והביאו לפני רפרם בטענה שקיבלו בעל מום, ורפרם זיהה את הבכור והעיר לו על כך.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that despite this incident, Rafram was not concerned about the matter because this priest was exceptionally brazen, and other priests are not suspected of such behavior.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסיקה שרפרם לא חשד בכהנים אחרים, וראה בכהן זה מקרה חריג של חוצפה.

items.text: בכור בעל מום מובהק והצורך בכהן
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's ruling on a blemished firstborn brought by a Sarua
items.desc_en: A sarua (a person with a skin condition) brought a firstborn with a blemish before Rav Ashi. Rav Ashi initially saw no concern, but Ravina questioned based on Rav Yehuda's rule that a firstborn of an Israelite is only examined with a priest present. Rav Ashi distinguishes: here the blemish is obvious, and the sarua would not violate the honor of the sages by lying.
items.desc: רב אשי פוסק שאין צורך בכהן לבדיקת בכור בעל מום מובהק, שכן ברור שאינו חשוד לאכול קדשים בחוץ. רבינא מקשה מדברי רב יהודה, ורב אשי משיב שבמום מובהק החשד אינו קיים, והבאת הבכור לחכם היא רק לשם כבוד.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that there is no concern about the blemished firstborn brought by a sarua, regardless of whether the owner is a priest or an Israelite, since the blemish is clearly present.
sub.desc: רב אשי פותח ואומר שאין לחשוש במום מובהק, בין אם המביא כהן או ישראל, שהרי הבכור והמום עמו.

sub.desc_en: Ravina questions Rav Ashi, citing Rav Yehuda's rule that a firstborn of an Israelite may only be examined with a priest present.
sub.desc: רבינא מקשה מדברי רב יהודה, שאין רואים בכור ישראל אלא אם כן כהן עמו.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi distinguishes the case: there, the blemish's status is uncertain and the Israelite is suspected regarding the priest's property; here, the blemish is obvious, and the sarua would not violate the honor of the sages by committing a transgression.
sub.desc: רב אשי משיב שאין להשוות: במום מובהק הישראל יודע שהמום ברור, והביאו רק לכבוד החכם, ולכן אינו חשוד לעבור איסור.

items.text: אמונת הכל על מומי מעשר
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on trustworthiness for ma'aser behemah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that everyone is believed regarding blemishes of the tithe animal. The Gemara explains the reason: since the owner could have inflicted a blemish on the entire herd, he is trusted. The Gemara addresses a potential objection about the verse 'lo yevaker bein tov lara'.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שהכל נאמנים על מומי מעשר, והגמרא מסבירה שהטעם הוא שהיה יכול להטיל מום בכל העדר לפני העישור, ולכן אין חשש שיטיל מום לאחר מכן.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that everyone is deemed credible to testify about blemishes of the animal tithe offering.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת וקובעת שהכל נאמנים על מומי מעשר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason and raises a difficulty: how could the owner have blemished the specific animal that would become the tithe, since he does not know which one will emerge?
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה הטעם שהכל נאמנים, ומקשה שהרי הבעלים לא יודע מראש איזו בהמה תצא לעשירי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the objection by citing the verse 'lo yevaker bein tov lara' and explains that the owner could have blemished his entire flock before tithing, so he is trusted.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את האפשרות שיוציא את הבהמה בראש העשרה, ומסבירה שהטעם הוא שהיה יכול להטיל מום בכל העדר לפני העישור.

items.text: התרת בכור על פי שלושה בני הכנסת ומומחה
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on permitting a firstborn with obvious blemishes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a firstborn with an obvious blemish (e.g., blinded eye) may be slaughtered based on three laymen. Rabbi Yosei requires an expert. The Gemara cites a tradition that this applies only outside the Land of Israel and only for obvious blemishes, clarifying that the Mishnah's examples are to show the extent of Rabbi Yosei's stringency.
items.desc: המשנה מתירה שחיטת בכור בעל מום מובהק על פי שלושה הדיוטות, ורבי יוסי מצריך מומחה. הגמרא מביאה את דברי רבי שמלאי ורבי יהודה נשיאה בשם רבי יהושע בן לוי, ורבא מחדש שההיתר בשלושה הדיוטות הוא דווקא בחוץ לארץ ובמומים מובהקים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a firstborn with an obvious blemish may be slaughtered based on three laymen, while Rabbi Yosei requires an expert even if twenty-three are present.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין בכור בעל מום מובהק הנשחט על פי שלושה בני הכנסת, ורבי יוסי חולק ומצריך מומחה.

sub.text: רבי שמלאי ורבי יהודה נשיאה בשם רבי יהושע בן לוי
sub.text_en: Rabbi Simlai and Rabbi Yehuda Nesia in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: A tradition is cited that permitting a firstborn outside the Land of Israel may be done by three laymen, and Rava adds that this applies only to clear-cut blemishes.
sub.desc: רבי שמלאי ורבי יהודה נשיאה אומרים בשם רבי יהושע בן לוי שהתרת בכור בחוץ לארץ היא על פי שלושה בני הכנסת, ורבא מוסיף שדווקא במומים מובהקים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rava's statement adds, since the Mishnah already teaches that a firstborn with obvious blemishes may be slaughtered based on three laymen.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מה חידש רבא, הרי כבר שנינו במשנה שבכור בעל מום מובהק נשחט על פי שלושה בני הכנסת?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that without Rava's statement, one might think the Mishnah permits non-obvious blemishes outside the Land of Israel, but Rava clarifies that only obvious blemishes are permitted, and the Mishnah's examples show the extent of Rabbi Yosei's stringency.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: אילו למדנו מהמשנה בלבד, היינו טועים שההיתר חל גם על מומים שאינם מובהקים בחוץ לארץ, ורבא בא לחדש שההיתר דווקא במומים מובהקים.

items.text: שלושה מתירים בכור במקום שאין מומחה
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav Chiyya bar Amram on three permit the firstborn
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav or Shmuel states that three laymen permit the firstborn where there is no expert. The Gemara clarifies this is only where there is no expert, not where one is available. Rav Chiyya bar Amram adds a parallel rule for permitting vows where there is no sage.
items.desc: רב יהודה בשם רבי ירמיה בר אבא (מספק בשם רב או שמואל) קובע ששלושה מתירים בכור במקום שאין מומחה. רב חייא בר עמרם מוסיף שדין זה דומה להתרת נדרים בשלושה במקום שאין חכם.

sub.text: רב יהודה בשם רבי ירמיה בר אבא
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports a halakha from Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba (uncertain whether from Rav or Shmuel) that three laymen may permit a firstborn animal in a place without an expert.
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם רבי ירמיה בר אבא (מספק בשם רב או שמואל) קובע ששלושה מתירים בכור במקום שאין מומחה.

sub.text: רב יהודה בשם רבי ירמיה בר אבא
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what novelty this statement teaches, since the mishna already says a firstborn with clear-cut blemishes may be slaughtered on the ruling of three regular Jews.
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם רבי ירמיה בר אבא (מספק בשם רב או שמואל) קובע ששלושה מתירים בכור במקום שאין מומחה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that without this statement, one might think three laymen can permit even where an expert is available; the teaching clarifies that this power applies only where there is no expert.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: אילו למדנו מהמשנה בלבד, היינו אומרים שההיתר תקף גם במקום שיש מומחה; רב יהודה בא ללמד שדווקא במקום שאין מומחה – כן, אבל במקום שיש מומחה – לא.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Amram adds a parallel ruling: three laymen permit a firstborn where there is no expert, and three laymen dissolve a vow where there is no sage.
sub.desc: רב חייא בר עמרם מוסיף ומחזק: שלושה מתירים בכור במקום שאין מומחה, ושלושה מתירים נדר במקום שאין חכם.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on the court for annulling vows
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on the court for annulling vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's requirement of three people for annulling vows excludes Rabbi Yosei's opinion that even twenty-three are needed, and also excludes Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that one of them must be a sage. Rav Nachman identifies himself as an example of a sage in a place without one, and Ravina explains that the other two must be capable of understanding the reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's requirement of three people for annulling vows excludes Rabbi Yosei's opinion that even twenty-three are needed, and also excludes Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that one of them must be a sage.
The Gemara asks for an example of a sage in a place without one.
Rav Nachman identifies himself as an example of a sage.
The Gemara asks whether the other two members can be anyone, even ignoramuses.
Ravina explains that the other two must be capable of understanding the reasoning.

items.text: Rav's ruling against Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Rav's ruling against Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Rav Chananel reports in Rav's name that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yosei, who requires twenty-three. The Gemara questions why this is necessary, since the majority opinion should prevail, and answers that one might think Rabbi Yosei's reasoning is compelling, so the ruling is taught to reject that.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chananel reports in Rav's name that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yosei.
The Gemara questions why this ruling is necessary, since the majority opinion should prevail.
The Gemara answers that the ruling is taught to reject the possibility that Rabbi Yosei's compelling reasoning might be followed.

items.text: Clarification of the source of the ruling
items.text_en: Clarification of the source of the ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the ruling about Rabbi Yosei might be inferred from an earlier statement attributed to Shmuel, because if it were from Rav, there would be two redundant statements. It concludes that one of the statements was derived from the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests resolving the earlier uncertainty by inferring that the first ruling was from Shmuel, because if it were from Rav there would be two redundant statements.
The Gemara concludes that one of the statements was derived from the other by inference, so there is no redundancy.

items.text: Mishnah: Sale of a firstborn or treifa animal
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sale of a firstborn or treifa animal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one slaughters a firstborn without showing it to an expert, or sells a treifa cow, the buyer keeps what was eaten and the seller refunds the money. For uneaten meat, the buyer returns the meat and the seller refunds the money. If sold to gentiles or fed to dogs, the buyer pays the value of treifa meat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for a firstborn slaughtered without being shown to an expert: the buyer keeps what was eaten and the seller refunds the money; uneaten meat is buried and the seller refunds the money.

The Mishnah adds the parallel rule for a treifa cow: the buyer keeps what was eaten, returns uneaten meat, and the seller refunds the money; if sold to gentiles or fed to dogs, the buyer pays the value of treifa meat.

items.text: Baraita on selling forbidden items
items.text_en: Baraita on selling forbidden items
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if one sells meat that turns out to be from a firstborn, or produce that is tevel, or wine that is yayin nesekh, the buyer keeps what was eaten and the seller refunds the money. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar distinguishes between items that are repulsive (neveilot, treifot, etc.) and those that are not (bekhorot, tevel, yayin nesekh), ruling that for repulsive items the seller refunds, while for non-repulsive items the seller deducts from the price.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states a general rule: one who sells meat of a firstborn, untithed produce, or wine used for idolatry must refund the buyers for what they ate.

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar distinguishes between repulsive items (neveilot, treifot, etc.) where the seller refunds fully, and non-repulsive items (bekhorot, tevel, yayin nesekh) where the seller deducts the value of the benefit.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the buyer cannot simply ask the seller what loss he caused. It explains that the case is where the seller sold from a place of blemish, and the buyer could have shown it to a sage to permit it, following Rabbi Yehuda. For tevel, the buyer could have tithed it, and for yayin nesekh, it could have been sold to gentiles via mixture, following Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the seller must deduct the value of the meat of a firstborn animal, since the buyer could claim he caused no loss.
The Gemara explains that the case is where the seller sold from a place of blemish, and the buyer could have shown it to a sage to permit it, following Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara adds that for tevel the seller could have tithed it, and for yayin nesekh it could have been sold to gentiles via mixture, following Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that wine used for libation that fell into a cistern may be sold to gentiles, except for the value of the libation wine.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the phrase 'Hadran alach kol pesulei hamukdashin' (We return to you, all invalidated consecrated animals).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard phrase 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you), marking the end of the chapter on invalidated consecrated animals.

items.text: Mishnah: Blemishes that permit slaughter of a firstborn
items.text_en: Mishnah: Blemishes that permit slaughter of a firstborn
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists blemishes that permit slaughter of a firstborn: a split ear from the cartilage (not the skin), a cracked ear even without a missing piece, a pierced ear the size of a carshina bean, or a dried ear. Rabbi Yosei ben Hameshulam defines a dried ear as one that crumbles when pierced.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the blemishes that permit slaughtering a firstborn: a damaged ear from the cartilage, a split ear, a pierced ear the size of a carshina bean, or a dried ear, defined as one that does not produce a drop of blood when pierced.
Rabbi Yosei ben Hameshulam offers an alternative definition: a dried ear is one that crumbles when touched.

items.text: Gemara's derivation of blemishes from the verse
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation of blemishes from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why these blemishes are valid, given that the Torah only mentions 'lame or blind'. It uses the hermeneutic principle of כלל ופרט וכלל (generalization, specification, and generalization) to derive that any visible, permanent blemish that impairs function is included. It then questions why the Mishnah includes ear blemishes that are not functionally impairing, and answers that the word 'רע' (bad) is an amplification. It further questions why internal blemishes are excluded, referencing the Mishnah about external and internal threads.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why these blemishes are valid, given that the Torah only mentions 'lame or blind'.
The Gemara initially suggests that 'any blemish' is a generalization, but then notes that with a generalization and a detail, only the detail is included, so only lame and blind would be valid.
The Gemara resolves that 'any ill blemish' is a second generalization, creating a כלל ופרט וכלל (generalization, specification, and generalization), which includes any visible, permanent blemish.
The Gemara objects that the detail also implies the blemish must cause the animal to desist from labor, and asks why the Mishnah includes ear blemishes that do not impair function.
The Gemara answers that the word 'רע' (bad) is an amplification, but then questions why internal blemishes are excluded, referencing the Mishnah about external and internal threads.

items.text: Distinguishing permanent from temporary blemishes for redemption
items.text_en: Distinguishing permanent from temporary blemishes for redemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists 'torn' ears but not 'cracked' or 'chipped' ears, and explains that a temporary blemish (מום עובר) cannot be used for redemption. A baraita derives from the verse 'אשר לא יקריבו ממנה' that only animals with permanent blemishes may be redeemed, excluding those with temporary blemishes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists 'torn' ears but not 'cracked' or 'chipped' ears, and asks why a temporary blemish is not included in the amplification of 'any ill blemish'.

The Gemara answers that a temporary blemish is excluded by logical reasoning: if we do not redeem an offering due to a temporary blemish, we certainly will not slaughter a firstborn due to it, and cites a baraita from Leviticus 27:11.
The baraita clarifies that the verse 'אשר לא יקריבו ממנה' refers to blemished animals that were redeemed, not actual impure animals.
The baraita concludes that the verse excludes temporary blemishes, as only animals that are never fit for sacrifice may be redeemed, not those temporarily unfit.

items.text: Alternative proof from the verse's redundancy
items.text_en: Alternative proof from the verse's redundancy
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative proof: if a temporary blemish sufficed for redemption, the verse's mention of 'blind or lame' would be superfluous, since those are permanent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative proof: if a temporary blemish sufficed for redemption, the verse's mention of 'blind or lame' would be superfluous, since those are permanent.

items.text: שיעור סדק ופגימה באוזן
items.text_en: Definitions of crack and chip in the ear
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a crack (סדק) is any size, while a chip (פגימה) can be caused by human or heaven. The Gemara clarifies that both crack and chip apply regardless of cause, and the minimum size for a chip is that a fingernail can fit into it.
items.desc: הברייתא קובעת שסדק באוזן פוסל בכל שהוא, ופגימה פוסלת בשיעור שתחגור בה ציפורן. הגמרא מבהירה שאין חילוק בין מום שנעשה בידי אדם למום שנעשה בידי שמיים.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that a crack (סדק) is any size, and a chip (פגימה) can be caused by human or heaven; the Gemara infers that a crack caused by heaven might not be a blemish.
The Gemara clarifies that both crack and chip apply regardless of cause, and the minimum size for a chip is that a fingernail can fit into it.

items.text: שיעור נקב באוזן ויובש
items.text_en: Dispute on the size of an ear perforation
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: the first Tanna says the perforation must be the size of a carshina (broad bean), while Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says the size of a lentil. Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshulam defines a dry perforation as one that crumbles. The Gemara notes that the opinions of the first Tanna and Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshulam are close.
items.desc: הברייתא מביאה מחלוקת: תנא קמא אומר שיעור הנקב כמלוא כרשינה, ורבי יוסי ברבי יהודה אומר כעדשה. נחלקו גם בפירוש 'יבשה': יש אומרים שאינה מוציאה דם, ורבי יוסי בן המשולם אומר שצריך שתיפררך. הגמרא מציינת שדברי התנא קמא ורבי יוסי ברבי יהודה קרובים להיות שווים.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the measure for a pierced ear is the size of a carshina (broad bean).
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda gives a different measure: the size of a lentil.
The baraita defines a dry ear as one that, when pierced, does not discharge a drop of blood.
Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshulam defines a dry ear as one that crumbles when touched.
The Gemara asks: whose statements are said to be close to identical?
The Gemara rejects the possibility that it refers to the first Tanna and Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshulam, since their opinions differ greatly.
The Gemara concludes that the statement refers to the first Tanna and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, whose measures (carshina and lentil) are close in size.

items.text: קושיה ממרצע ומחלוקת רב חנא בר קטינא
items.text_en: Digression: the awl for ear-piercing of a Hebrew slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's lentil-size requirement by citing a baraita where he allows any handheld tool for piercing a slave's ear. Rabbi requires metal. A later baraita says piercing is done only in the soft part (מילת), but Sages say a priest-slave cannot be pierced because it creates a blemish. Rav Hana bar Katina resolves: the dispute about the ear's location is for slaughter (where the blemish is defined) versus for disqualification (where the piercing is done).
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה מדברי רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה במסכת קידושין, שם נראה שנקב במחט פוסל בעבד אף שהוא קטן מעדשה. רב חנא בר קטינא מתרץ: שם מדובר בפסול לכהונה (או לעבדות), וכאן מדובר בשחיטת בכור, והשיעורים שונים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's lentil-size requirement by citing a baraita where he allows any handheld tool for piercing a slave's ear, implying even a tiny hole is a blemish.
The baraita presents two positions: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda allows any handheld tool, while Rabbi requires metal tools, both showing that a small piercing is a blemish.
The baraita further teaches that piercing is done only in the soft part of the ear (מילת).
The Sages object that a priest-slave cannot be pierced because it creates a blemish, implying piercing is done on the upper ear cartilage, not the soft part.

Rav Hana bar Katina resolves the contradiction: the lentil-size requirement applies to slaughter (where the blemish is defined), while the piercing discussion is for disqualification (where even a tiny hole is a blemish).

items.text: Identification of carshina
items.text_en: Identification of carshina
items.desc_en: Rav Sheravya explains that carshina (כרשינה) is a type of bean called הינדא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the identity of the plant called 'כרשינה' (karshina).
Rav Sheravya answers that it is the bean called 'הינדא' (hinda), i.e., a bitter vetch.

items.text: Digression: size of a carshina and a related discussion on skull perforation
items.text_en: Digression: size of a carshina and a related discussion on skull perforation
items.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya asks Rav Huna whether the carshina is inserted and removed or stationary. Rav Huna does not know but cites a similar case: the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on the minimum hole in a skull to transmit impurity. Rav Chisda asks the size of 'taken from a living person and he dies', and Rav Tachlifa bar Avudimi cites Shmuel: the size of a sela. The Gemara notes a contradiction with another baraita, and discusses the size of a hole made by human hands versus not.

sub.text: Rav Hoshaya's question to Rav Huna Rabba
sub.text_en: Rav Hoshaya's question to Rav Huna Rabba
sub.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya asks Rav Huna Rabba whether the measure of a carshina (bitter vetch) for the ear hole means the vetch can enter and exit or is stationary; Rav Huna says he has not heard this but heard a similar case.

sub.text: Supporting baraita on spine and skull deficiency
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita on spine and skull deficiency
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna cites a baraita about the spine and skull: Beit Shammai says two vertebrae or a drilled hole, Beit Hillel says one vertebra or an amount that if removed from a living person he would die.
Rav Chisda asks how much is 'an amount that if removed from a living person he would die'; Rav Tachlifa bar Avudimi answers that Shmuel said it is the size of a sela coin.

sub.text: Gemara's note on the source of the answer
sub.text_en: Gemara's note on the source of the answer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a dispute: Rav Safra says Rav Tachlifa cited a tradition from Shmuel, while Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda says he cited a baraita, with the mnemonic that Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda teaches.

Rav Chisda objects that if the measure is a sela, then Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel are the same, citing a baraita about a window not made by human hands having a measure of a large fist (like Ben Avatiaḥ's fist), which Rabbi Yosei says is like a large human head.

sub.text: Continuation of the baraita on a window made by human hands
sub.text_en: Continuation of the baraita on a window made by human hands
sub.desc_en: The baraita continues: a window made by human hands has a measure of a large drill of the chamber, which is like an Italian pundeyon and a sela of Nero, and its size is...

items.text: שיעור המקדח ומחלוקת בית שמאי ובית הלל
items.text_en: Dispute about the Mishnah's measure
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda suggests that the Mishnah's measure of 'the size of a drill hole' might include the drill and its rim. Rav Tachlifa insists it is definitely the drill and its rim, and cites a tradition from Chizkiyah father of Ikkesh to support this.
items.desc: רב תחליפא ורב חסדא דנים בשיעור הנקב בגולגולת: האם הכוונה למקדח בלבד או למקדח וחיסומו. רב תחליפא מכריע כי הכוונה למקדח וחיסומו, ומשווה זאת לעדותו המהימנה של חזקיה אבי עקש.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda suggests that the Mishnah's measure of 'the size of a drill hole' might include the drill and its rim.
Rav Tachlifa insists it is definitely the drill and its rim, and cites a tradition from Chizkiyah father of Ikkesh to support this.

items.text: עדות חזקיה אבי עקש על כלי חרס וכלי שטף
items.text_en: Chizkiyah's testimony about vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta where Chizkiyah testified before Rabban Gamliel in Yavneh that any earthenware vessel without an interior has no outer surface for the purpose of impurity. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin explains that this applies to a vessel that has no interior in earthenware, meaning its counterpart in a wooden vessel has no outer surface for impurity.
items.desc: מובאת עדותו של חזקיה אבי עקש בשם רבן גמליאל הזקן: בכלי חרס שאין לו תוך, אין חילוק בין תוכו לגבו; טומאת תוכו מטמאת את גבו. רבי יצחק בר אבין מסביר שהדין אמור בכלי שטף, ולא בכלי חרס.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Chizkiyah father of Ikkesh testified before Rabban Gamliel in Yavneh that any earthenware vessel without an interior has no outer surface for impurity; if its inside becomes impure, its outside also becomes impure, and vice versa.
The Gemara objects: For an earthenware vessel, the Merciful One made impurity dependent on having an interior; if it has no interior, it should not become impure at all.

Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin explains that the testimony refers to a vessel that has no interior in earthenware, meaning its counterpart in a vessel purified through rinsing has no outer surface for impurity; if its inside becomes impure, its outside becomes impure, and vice versa.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על הצורך בהשוואה לכלי חרס
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about the Tosefta
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Tosefta mentions earthenware vessels at all, suggesting it should simply state the rule for wooden vessels. It answers that the Tosefta teaches that a vessel with an interior is like an earthenware vessel: if its interior is impure, its exterior is impure, and vice versa.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע יש לתלות את הדין בכלי חרס? היה אפשר לומר ישירות שכלי שטף שאין לו תוך אין לו אחוריים לחליקה. התשובה: בא הדבר ללמד שכלי שטף שיש לו תוך דינו ככלי חרס לעניין טומאה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Tosefta needs to mention earthenware vessels at all, suggesting it should simply state the rule for wooden vessels.
The Gemara answers that the Tosefta teaches that a vessel with an interior is like an earthenware vessel: if its interior is impure, its exterior is impure, and vice versa.

items.text: בירור סוג הטומאה: דאורייתא או דרבנן
items.text_en: Distinction between Torah and rabbinic impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the rule applies to wooden vessels, since the Torah only mentions 'interior' for earthenware. It explains that the discussion is about rabbinic impurity of liquids, where the Sages decreed that the outer part of a vessel can become impure without the interior. They equated this to earthenware impurity but not to Torah impurity.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת: בכלי חרס התורה גילתה 'תוכו', אך בכלי שטף לא. התשובה: מדובר בטומאת משקין דרבנן, שגזרו משום משקה זב וזבה. לפיכך, החכמים השוו דין כלי שטף לדין כלי חרס, ולא לדין תורה של כלי שטף עצמו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the rule of 'interior' applies to wooden vessels (כלי שטף), since the Torah only explicitly mentions 'תּוֹכוֹ' (interior) for earthenware vessels.

The Gemara answers that the discussion is about rabbinic impurity of liquids (טומאת משקין דרבנן), citing a Mishnah that distinguishes between the outer and inner parts of a vessel when only the outside is contaminated by liquids.

The Gemara explains that by Torah law, food and liquid cannot render a vessel impure; the Sages decreed this impurity only because of the liquids of a זב (male with a discharge) and זבה (female with a discharge).
The Gemara concludes that the Sages equated this rabbinic impurity to the impurity of earthenware vessels (כלי חרס), but did not treat it as Torah-level impurity of the vessel itself.

items.text: The Sages' distinction for recognition
items.text_en: The Sages' distinction for recognition
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Sages made a distinction (heiker) to prevent burning terumah and sacrifices. It questions why they didn't make a similar distinction for vessels without an interior, and answers that since they made a distinction for those with an interior, it is known that vessels without an interior are rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Sages made a distinction (heiker) to prevent burning terumah and sacrifices.
The Gemara asks why the Sages did not also make a distinction for vessels without an interior.
The Gemara answers that since the Sages made a distinction for vessels with an interior, it is known that vessels without an interior are rabbinic.

items.text: Vessels without interior and Torah impurity
items.text_en: Vessels without interior and Torah impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a wooden vessel without an interior can receive Torah impurity, and explains that it must be similar to a sack, which is movable when full and empty. It then notes that these vessels are fit for sitting, but earthenware vessels are not subject to midras impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a wooden vessel without an interior can receive Torah impurity.
The Gemara answers that it must be similar to a sack, which is movable when full and empty.
The Gemara notes that these vessels are fit for sitting, but earthenware vessels are not subject to midras impurity.

items.text: שיעור המקדח: מחלוקת רב פפא ורב נחמן
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman's interpretations of the drill
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa says the Mishnah refers to a large drill, implying a standard drill is smaller than a sela coin. The Gemara questions this against the Mishnah's dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about the size of the drill. Rav Nachman says the Mishnah refers to a Neronian sela, which is like a large drill, while a standard sela is smaller than a standard drill.
items.desc: רב פפא אומר ששנינו 'מקדח גדול', ומכאן שמקדח סתם קטן מסלע. הגמרא מקשה על כך לפי שיטת רבי מאיר (מקדח קטן של רופאים) ולפי שיטת חכמים (מקדח גדול של לשכה). רב נחמן מיישב: סלע נירונית היא כגדול, אבל סלע סתם קטן ממקדח סתם, ולכן בית שמאי מחמירים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asserts that the Mishnah refers to a large drill (מקדח גדול), implying that a standard drill is smaller than a sela coin.

The Gemara questions Rav Pappa's interpretation: if the Mishnah specifies a large drill, then a standard drill is smaller than a sela, but this works for Rabbi Meir's view; what can be said for the Sages' view?
The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Meir says the drill is the small one of doctors, while the Sages say it is the large one of the chamber.

The Gemara objects: even for Rabbi Meir, is it satisfactory? The Mishnah's ruling would then be among the leniencies of Beit Shammai and stringencies of Beit Hillel, which is problematic; but the Gemara dismisses this by saying 'we have taught what we have taught, and what we have not taught we have not taught'.
Rav Nachman resolves the issue: the Mishnah refers to a Neronian sela (סלע נירונית), which is like a large drill, while a standard sela is smaller than a standard drill.

items.text: משנת מומי העין המתירים שחיטת בכור
items.text_en: Mishnah: Blemishes of the eye
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists blemishes of the eye that disqualify a firstborn: a perforated, cracked, or chipped eyelid; a thin membrane; a cataract; a snail; a snake; a nerve. It defines a cataract as a white line that crosses the iris and enters the black, while black entering the white is not a blemish.
items.desc: המשנה מונה מומי עין המתירים שחיטת בכור: הריס שניקב, נפגם, נסדק, תבלול, חלזון, נחש, עצב. ומבארת שתבלול הוא לבן הפוסק בסירא ונכנס בשחור, אבל שחור הנכנס בלבן אינו מום.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists blemishes of the eye that disqualify a firstborn and defines a cataract (תבלול) as a white line crossing the iris into the black, while black entering the white is not a blemish.

items.text: פירוש 'הריס' ודין תבלול שחור ולבן
items.text_en: Definition of הריס and resolution of contradiction about דק
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa defines הריס as the outer eyelid. A baraita states that a sunken דק is a blemish but a floating one is not; another baraita says the opposite. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between black and white דק, citing Rabba bar bar Chana's report from Yoshiya of Usha.
items.desc: הגמרא מפרשת ש'הריס' הוא העפעף, ודנה בדין תבלול: תבלול שקוע הוא מום, צף אינו מום. מובאת ברייתא הסותרת לכאורה, ומיושבת על ידי הבחנה בין תבלול שחור ללבן, תוך ציטוט רבה בר בר חנה בשם יאשיה מאושא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what הריס (the blemish of a split eyelid) means, and Rav Pappa answers that it is the outer eyelid.
A baraita is cited stating that a sunken דק (thin membrane) is a blemish but a floating one is not.
The Gemara objects that another baraita states the opposite, and resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between black and white דק.
The Gemara refines the resolution: the contradiction is between a white spot (דוק לבן) and a black spot (דוק שחור), since there are no blemishes in white.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Yoshiya of Usha
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Yoshiya of Usha
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports from Yoshiya of Usha that a black sunken דק is a blemish, a floating one is not; a white sunken דק is not a blemish, a floating one is, with the mnemonic ברקא (sparkle).

items.text: דין חלזון ונחש כמום קבוע
items.text_en: Clarification of חלזון and נחש as blemishes
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether חלזון is the same as נחש or a separate blemish. Rabba bar bar Chana recounts that Rabbi Yochanan ben Elazar told him that an elder named Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei Lakonya taught that חלזון is a permanent blemish for slaughter, and that is the נחש the Sages mentioned. The Gemara then addresses the apparent contradiction that one may not judge one's own blemishes but may teach the law to students.
items.desc: הגמרא מעלה ספק האם 'חלזון' ו'נחש' שבמשנה הם אותו מום או שניים. רבה בר בר חנה מביא מעשה מרבי יוחנן בן אלעזר ורבי שמעון בן יוסי לקוניא, המלמד שחלזון הוא מום קבוע והוא הוא הנחש. דנים באפשרות שהורה הלכה לעצמו, ומיישבים שאמר את ההלכה לפני המעשה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether חלזון is the same as נחש or a separate blemish.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan ben Elazar and Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei Lakonya
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan ben Elazar and Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei Lakonya
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana recounts that Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei Lakonya taught that חלזון is a permanent blemish for slaughter, and that is the נחש the Sages mentioned.
The Gemara objects that one may not judge one's own blemishes, yet Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei Lakonya taught about his own blemish.

sub.text: Gemara's objection citing Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection citing Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara further objects that a sage who teaches a halacha after the fact is not heeded, citing the rule of Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei Lakonya taught the halacha before the incident, so he was heeded.

items.text: פירוש 'תבלול' ומחלוקת רבי מאיר ורבי יוסי
items.text_en: Definition of תבלול and dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines תבלול as a white spot that crosses the iris. The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Yosei, who holds that white entering black is a blemish but black entering white is not, since there are no blemishes in the white. Rav explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning from a verse, while Rabbi Meir derives from the word תבלול that it is anything that confuses the eyes.
items.desc: הגמרא מגדירה 'תבלול' כלבן הפוסק את הסירה, ומבררת שהמשנה כרבי יוסי. מובאת מחלוקת בין רבי מאיר לרבי יוסי: לרבי יוסי רק לבן הנכנס בשחור הוא מום, ואילו לרבי מאיר גם שחור הנכנס בלבן הוא מום. רב מסביר את טעמו של רבי יוסי מהפסוק, ורבי מאיר דורש את לשון 'תבלול' מלשון בלבול.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines תבלול (a blemish) as a white spot that crosses the iris.
The Gemara asks which Tanna's opinion the Mishnah follows.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei.

A baraita cites the dispute: Rabbi Meir says both white entering black and black entering white are blemishes, while Rabbi Yosei says only white entering black is a blemish, since there are no blemishes in the white.
Rav explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning from the verse 'יצא מחלב עינימו' (their eyes bulge from fat), showing that only the white part is called 'חלב' (fat), not the entire eye.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Meir's reasoning: the word תבלול implies anything that confuses (מבלבל) the eyes.

items.text: Definition of חוורור קבוע and מים קבועים, and attribution to Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Definition of חוורור קבוע and מים קבועים, and attribution to Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines a permanent חוורור as one lasting eighty days, with Rabbi Chananya ben Antigonus requiring three checks within that period. The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Yehuda, who argues with Rabbi Meir about the duration: Rabbi Meir says חוורור is forty days and מים קבועים eighty, while Rabbi Yehuda says both are eighty days. The baraita also specifies the order of eating wet and dry fodder for מים קבועים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines a permanent חוורור (white cataract) as one lasting eighty days, with Rabbi Chananya ben Antigonus requiring three checks within that period.
The Mishnah specifies the conditions for מים קבועים (permanent watery eyes): eating wet then dry fodder, not the reverse.
The Gemara asks whose opinion the Mishnah follows, and answers that it follows Rabbi Yehuda.
A baraita records the dispute: Rabbi Meir says חוורור lasts forty days and מים קבועים eighty, while Rabbi Yehuda says both are eighty days.
The baraita further specifies the order of eating wet and dry fodder for מים קבועים, adding a duration of three months.

items.text: Resolution of contradiction between Mishnah and baraita about מים קבועים
items.text_en: Resolution of contradiction between Mishnah and baraita about מים קבועים
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah lists both rain and irrigation water as causing a blemish, while the baraita distinguishes them. It resolves by saying the Mishnah is missing a clause: rain water is a blemish, irrigation water is not, and even for rain, the order must be wet then dry. The Gemara then questions the duration of three months, citing Rav Idi bar Avin's statement about wet and dry seasons, and adjusts it to Adar and half Nisan for wet, Elul and half Tishrei for dry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction: the Mishnah lists both rain and irrigation water as causing a blemish, while the baraita distinguishes them.
The Gemara resolves by saying the Mishnah is missing a clause: rain water is a blemish, irrigation water is not, and even for rain, the order must be wet then dry.
The Gemara questions the duration of three months, citing Rav Idi bar Avin's statement about wet and dry seasons.
The Gemara adjusts the seasons to Adar and half Nisan for wet, Elul and half Tishrei for dry.

items.text: בירור זמני הלח והיבש וכמות ההאכלה
items.text_en: Inquiry about feeding wet and dry fodder and the measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the animal must eat wet fodder during the wet season and dry during the dry season, or both during the wet season. It cites Rav Idi bar Avin's statement but suggests it might mean feeding dry fruits from Elul and Tishrei during Adar and Nisan. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Pinchas ben Arova states the amount is a fig-bulk, and Rava reports that in the West they asked whether this is in one meal.
items.desc: הגמרא מעלה ספק האם מאכילים לח בזמן לח ויבש בזמן יבש, או שמא שניהם בזמן לח. מובאת ראיה מדברי רב אידי בר אבין, אך נדחית. לבסוף, מבואר שצריך להאכיל בכמות של גרוגרת, ורבא מעלה שאלה מהמערב האם הכוונה לגרוגרת בסעודה ראשונה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the animal must eat wet fodder during the wet season and dry during the dry season, or both during the wet season.

sub.text: Supporting baraita (Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan)
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita (Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Idi bar Avin's statement that Adar and Nisan are wet, Elul and Tishrei are dry, to resolve the question.
