items.desc: המשנה מגדירה גיבן כמי שאין לו גבינים או שיש לו גבין אחד. רבי דוסא מגדירו כמי שגביניו שוכבים, ורבי חנינא בן אנטיגנוס מגדירו כבעל שני גבין ושתי שדראות. הגמרא דנה באפשרות החיים של בעל שתי שדראות, ומתרצת שמדובר בשדרה עקומה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines gibben as lacking eyebrows or having only one eyebrow, with Rabbi Dosa and Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus offering alternative definitions.
The Gemara questions whether gibben means lacking eyebrows, citing a baraita that includes both having many eyebrows and lacking eyebrows.
Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita is a midrashic exposition of the word 'או' (or) in the verse.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus's creature with two spines cannot be viable, citing Rav's ruling that such a creature is not a valid offspring.
Rav Shimi bar Chiyya resolves the objection by explaining that the Mishnah refers to a curved spine, not two separate spines.

items.text: דין החירום ומומי עיניים
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on charum
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists disqualifications for charum (one with a sunken nose) and other eye-related conditions. The Gemara cites a baraita defining charum as a sunken, protruding, or blocked nose, with Rabbi Yosei limiting it to one who paints both eyes at once, to which the Sages object.
items.desc: המשנה מגדירה חירום כמי שכוחל שתי עיניו כאחת (חוטם שקוע), ומפרטת מומי עיניים נוספים הפוסלים משום מראית העין. הגמרא מביאה ברייתא המרחיבה את הגדרת חירום למומי חוטם נוספים, ורבי יוסי מצמצם את ההגדרה רק לכוחל שתי עיניו כאחת.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the disqualifications of a charum (one with a sunken nose) and other eye-related conditions, including those who paint both eyes at once, have eyes misaligned, or have missing eyelashes, all invalid due to מראית העין (appearance).
A baraita defines 'charum' as having a sunken, protruding, or blocked nose, deriving this from the extra word 'אוֹ חָרוּם' (or a charum) in the verse.
Rabbi Yosei limits the definition of 'charum' to one who paints both eyes at once.
The Sages object to Rabbi Yosei, saying he has exaggerated (הפלגתָּ) by narrowing the definition too much.

items.text: Clarification of eye positions in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Clarification of eye positions in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's terms 'two eyes above' and 'two eyes below', initially interpreting them as directional vision, but then reinterprets them as the physical placement of the eyes, leading to the condition of seeing a room and an attic simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's terms 'two eyes above' and 'two eyes below', initially interpreting them as directional vision and showing that this would be identical to the condition of seeing a room and an attic simultaneously.

The Gemara reinterprets the terms as referring to the physical placement of the eyes, so that the condition is one where the eyes are positioned at different heights while still aligned normally, enabling simultaneous vision of a room and an attic.

items.text: Source for eye defects from a baraita
items.text_en: Source for eye defects from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the laws of eye blemishes from the verse 'in his eye', including conditions where eyes are positioned abnormally or where one sees a room and attic simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited as the source for the Mishnah's conditions, listing the same eye-position defects and adding that a person who sees a room and an attic simultaneously, or who speaks with one person while another claims to see him, is considered blemished.
The baraita derives from the verse 'in his eye' that all eye defects, including abnormal positioning and double vision, are disqualifying blemishes.

items.text: דרשת הפסוקים: 'איש', 'עיוור', 'דק', 'תבלול', 'בעינו'
items.text_en: Rava's derivation of blemishes from the Torah
items.desc_en: Rava explains why the Torah wrote multiple terms ('ish', 'iver', 'dak', 'tevalul', 'be'eino') for blindness and eye blemishes, each teaching a different category: total blindness, white spots, missing parts, cataracts, and discoloration. He then summarizes the halakhic principle.
items.desc: הברייתא מלמדת ש'עיוור' כולל סומא בשתי עיניים או באחת, וממנה שחצוורור ומים הקבועים נלמדים מ'איש'. רבא דורש את חמשת המונחים שבפסוק (איש, עיוור, דק, תבלול, בעינו) כדי לכלול סוגי מומים שונים: עיוורון מוחלט, חוסר ראייה חלקי, ערבוב של חלקי העין, וסטייה ממראה רגיל.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that 'עִוֵּר' includes blindness in one or both eyes, and derives white spots and fixed water from the extra term 'אִישׁ עִוֵּר'.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בלימוד ש'עיוור' כולל סומא בשתי עיניים או באחת, ושואלת מהיכן נלמדים חצוורור ומים הקבועים, ומשיבה מ'איש עיוור'.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks why the Torah wrote five separate terms for eye blemishes, and begins explaining that each term is needed to include a category not covered by the others.
sub.desc: רבא שואל מדוע הוצרך הכתוב לחמשת המונחים, ומסביר שאם היה כתוב רק 'עיוור' היינו חושבים שפסול רק כשאין עיניים כלל, לכן הוסיף 'איש' לכלול חצוורור ומים הקבועים.

sub.desc_en: Rava continues: 'אִישׁ' covers total blindness but not missing parts, so 'דַּק' is needed; 'דַּק' covers missing parts but not cataracts, so 'תְּבַלּוּל' is needed.
sub.desc: רבא ממשיך ומסביר שאם היה כתוב רק 'איש' היינו חושבים שפסול רק כשאינו רואה כלל, לכן הוסיף 'דק' לכלול מחוסרי ראייה; ואם היה כתוב רק 'דק' היינו חושבים שפסול רק משום חיסרון, לכן הוסיף 'תבלול' לכלול ערבוב של חלקי העין.

sub.desc_en: Rava concludes: 'תְּבַלּוּל' covers cataracts but not discoloration, so 'בְּעֵינוֹ' is needed to include any change in the eye.
sub.desc: רבא מסביר שאם היה כתוב רק 'תבלול' היינו חושבים שפסול רק משום ערבוב, לכן הוסיף 'בעינו' לכלול סטייה ממראה רגיל.

sub.desc_en: Rava summarizes the halakhic principle: total blindness from 'אִישׁ', missing parts from 'דַּק', cataracts from 'תְּבַלּוּל', and discoloration from 'בְּעֵינוֹ'.
sub.desc: רבא מסכם: כל מומי עין נלמדים מארבעת המונחים: כהות מ'איש', חיסרון מ'דק', ערבוב מ'תבלול', וסטייה מ'בעינו'.

items.text: פירוש מומים נוספים: סכי שמש, זגדום, צירן, זידיר ולופיין
items.text_en: Definitions of other eye blemishes
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines terms like 'sanei shemesh' (sun-hater), 'zagdayan' (cross-eyed), 'shakhbana' (drooping eyelids), 'zagdom' (different colored eyes), 'hatzayran' (teary eyes), and other conditions, concluding with a distinction between remaining stubs and complete loss of eyelashes.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה פירושים למומים נוספים: 'סכי שמש' – מי ששונא את השמש (רב יוסף); 'זגדום' – עין אחת שחורה ואחת לבנה, או כל זוג לא שווה; 'צירן' – עיניים תרוטות, צירניות, דומעות, דולפות, טורדות; 'זידיר' – שמזוור עיניו, 'לופיין' – שנפישין זיפיה, 'תימין' – שתמו זיפיו. הגמרא מבחינה בין מקרה שנשרו הריסים לגמרי לבין שנשארו גדמים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef's baraita defines 'sanei shemesh' (sun-hater) and 'zagdayan' (cross-eyed), and Rav Huna demonstrates the latter with one eye from each side, with Rav Yehuda objecting.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה את פירושו של רב יוסף ל'סכי שמש' – מי ששונא את השמש, ומעשה שבו רב הונא ממחיש את 'זגדיין' תוך שהוא מצביע על רב יהודה, שנפגע.

sub.desc_en: A baraita defines 'shakhbana' (drooping eyelids) and 'zagdom' (one black eye and one white eye), and the Tanna states that any mismatched pair is called 'zagdom'.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא המפרשת 'זגדום' כגבות שונות בצבע, ומתרצת שהברייתא קוראת 'זגדום' לכל זוג לא שווה.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna lists 'hatzayran' (teary eyes) with various descriptions: drooping, weeping, dripping, and troubled eyes.
sub.desc: ברייתא מפרשת את המום 'צירן' – עיניים תרוטות, צירניות, דומעות, דולפות, טורדות.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna defines 'zideir' (squinting), 'lufyan' (thick eyebrows), and 'timyan' (eyebrows that have fallen out).
sub.desc: ברייתא מונה מומים נוספים: זידיר (מזוור עיניו), לופיין (ריסים מרובים), תימין (ריסים שתמו).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why these conditions are listed among blemishes, citing the Mishnah that loss of eyelashes disqualifies due to appearance.
sub.desc: ברייתא מונה מומים נוספים: זידיר (מזוור עיניו), לופיין (ריסים מרובים), תימין (ריסים שתמו).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one case is where stubs of eyelashes remain, the other is where no stubs remain.
sub.desc: ברייתא מונה מומים נוספים: זידיר (מזוור עיניו), לופיין (ריסים מרובים), תימין (ריסים שתמו).

items.text: Mishnah: Other physical blemishes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Other physical blemishes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists additional blemishes: eyes too large or small, body disproportionate to limbs, nose disproportionate, ears that are small or spongy, lips overlapping, and missing teeth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists additional blemishes: eyes too large or too small, body disproportionate to limbs, nose disproportionate, 'צִומֵּם' and 'צִומֵּעַ' (ears small or spongy), lips uneven, and missing teeth.

items.text: Gemara: Moses' stature and the definition of disproportionate body
items.text_en: Gemara: Moses' stature and the definition of disproportionate body
items.desc_en: Rav states that Moses was ten cubits tall, based on the verse about the Tabernacle. Rav Shimi bar Chiya objects that this would make Moses a ba'al mum (blemished) because his body would be larger than his limbs. Rav responds that he was referring to the sacred cubit.

sub.desc_en: Rav asserts that Moses was ten cubits tall, deriving this from the verse about the Tabernacle boards.
Rav Shimi bar Chiya objects that if Moses were ten cubits tall, his body would be disproportionately large relative to his limbs, making him a בעל מום (blemished priest).
Rav resolves the objection by clarifying that he was referring to the sacred cubit (אמה של קודש), which is smaller than the standard cubit, so Moses' proportions were normal.

items.text: Definitions of nose size and ear blemishes
items.text_en: Definitions of nose size and ear blemishes
items.desc_en: A baraita defines a large nose as the size of a small finger. Another baraita adds 'tzime'ach' to the list of ear blemishes, and the rabbis learn its meaning from an Arab who used the term for a kid goat with split ears.

sub.desc_en: A baraita defines a large nose as the size of a small finger.
Another baraita adds 'tzime'ach' to the list of ear blemishes.
The rabbis did not know the meaning of 'tzime'ach' until they heard an Arab use the term for a kid goat with split ears.

items.text: Discussion of animal blemishes: horns and hooves
items.text_en: Discussion of animal blemishes: horns and hooves
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a goat without horns and a ewe with horns are fit for the altar. A baraita lists these as 'like blemishes' but not actual blemishes. Rav Chisda cites Amemar regarding removed horns or hooves with their sockets, and the Gemara resolves contradictions by distinguishing between uprooting and filing.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a goat without horns and a ewe with horns are fit for the altar.
A baraita lists these cases as 'like blemishes' but not actual blemishes, permitting slaughter in the Temple but not in the provinces.
Rav Chisda cites Amemar regarding removed horns or hooves with their sockets, distinguishing between disqualification with no redemption and disqualification with redemption.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states removed horns and hooves with their sockets are disqualified but redeemable, contradicting Amemar's distinction.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between uprooting (אִיתְעֲקוּר) and filing (אִיגּוּם) of the horns or hooves.
The Gemara objects that even filing should not disqualify, citing a baraita about a red heifer with black horns or hooves that are simply cut off.
Ze'iri resolves the objection by explaining that the baraita refers to cutting above the socket (זַכְרוּת), not filing the horn itself.

items.text: משנת המומים הפוסלים
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: List of blemishes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates physical defects that disqualify: breasts like a woman's, a swollen belly, protruding navel, epilepsy, shortness of breath, and two types of genital defects (מאושבן and בעל גבר).
items.desc: המשנה מונה מומים גופניים הפוסלים כהן לעבודה: דדין שוכבין, כרסו צבה, טבורו יוצא, נכפה, רוח קצרה, מאושבן ובעל גבר.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists disqualifying blemishes: breasts like a woman's, swollen belly, protruding navel, epilepsy, shortness of breath, and two genital defects (מאושבן and בעל גבר).

items.text: דיני השתנה בציבור וסכנת עיכוב שתן
items.text_en: Gemara: Urination and the case of swollen belly
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba rules that one may urinate in public but not drink. A story illustrates that suppressing urination causes a swollen belly. Samuel and Mar bar Rav Ashi's actions are discussed, with a tangent about a worm (עלקא) in the urethra.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה דיונים על היתר השתנה בציבור מחשש סכנה, סיפורים על אמוראים שנצרכו לכך, והבהרה שהבטן הנפוחה נגרמה מעיכוב שתן ולא מעלוקה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba rules that one may urinate in public but not drink in public, and a supporting baraita is cited.
A story is told of a man who suppressed urination and developed a swollen belly, illustrating the danger.
Samuel needed to urinate on the festival Shabbat; his father advised him to pay 400 zuz to undo the act, distinguishing between one who can and cannot suppress.
Mar bar Rav Ashi urinated behind a camel's saddle, and when warned about his bladder, he replied that it was in the camel's ear.
The gemara questions whether Mar bar Rav Ashi's action risks a worm (עלקא) entering the urethra.
The gemara answers that the risk applies only to one who drinks (שותת), not to one who urinates.

items.text: Baraita: Two orifices and infertility
items.text_en: Baraita: Two orifices and infertility
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a man has two orifices—one for urine and one for semen—separated by a garlic-skin thickness. If they perforate into each other, the man becomes sterile.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that a man has two orifices separated by a garlic-skin thickness, and if they perforate into each other, he becomes sterile.

items.text: Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on sterility
items.text_en: Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on sterility
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the verse 'no barren one among you' as conditional on one's animal being barren. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi applies it to students and prayer, linking it to humility like a beast.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the verse 'no barren one among you' as conditional on one's animal being barren.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi applies the verse to students and prayer, linking it to humility like a beast.

items.text: Rav Papa and Abaye: Urination practices
items.text_en: Rav Papa and Abaye: Urination practices
items.desc_en: Rav Papa forbids urinating on clay vessels or hard ground, citing Rav that Babylonian waters return to the Eye of Etam. Abaye adds that a woman should not stand before her child while nursing.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa rules that a person should not urinate on clay vessels or on hard ground.
Rav provides the reason: Babylonian waters return to the Eye of Etam, so urinating on hard surfaces may cause harm.
Abaye adds that a woman should not stand directly before her nursing child, and notes that regarding a basin (אגיסה) we have no concern.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Resh Lakish: Bodily fluids and diseases
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Resh Lakish: Bodily fluids and diseases
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that a returning column (of urine) causes dropsy, and a returning tube causes jaundice. Resh Lakish links excess blood to boils, excess semen to leprosy, excess feces to dropsy, and excess urine to jaundice.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement that a returning column of urine causes dropsy (הִדְרוֹקָן) and a returning tube causes jaundice (יֵרָקוֹן).

sub.text: Resh Lakish via Rabba bar Rav Huna and Rav Katina
sub.text_en: Resh Lakish via Rabba bar Rav Huna and Rav Katina
sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish, transmitted through Rabba bar Rav Huna and Rav Katina, expands the principle: excess blood causes boils, excess semen causes leprosy, excess feces causes dropsy, and excess urine causes jaundice.

items.text: פירוש 'רוח קצרה'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'shortness of breath'
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's 'shortness of breath' (רוח קצרית) as the spirit of a fallen child (רוח בן נפלים) coming upon him.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת ש'רוח קצרה' האמורה במשנה היא רוח של שד (בן נפלים) שבאה על האדם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's 'shortness of breath' (רוח קצרית) refers to.
The Tanna answers that it means the spirit of a fallen child (רוח בן נפלים) comes upon him.

items.text: פירוש 'מאושבן' ו'בעל גבר' ושיעור הפסול
items.text_en: Definitions of מאושבן and בעל גבר, and measurement
items.desc_en: A baraita defines מאושבן as a defect in the testicles and בעל גבר as a defect in the penis. Another baraita gives synonyms. Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov debate the measurement of the defect (up to the ridge or above).
items.desc: ברייתות מפרשות: מאושבן הוא בעל אשכים גדולים, בעל גבר הוא בעל גיד ארוך. נחלקו התנאים אם הפסול הוא עד הרכובה או למטה ממנה.

sub.desc_en: A baraita defines מאושבן as a defect in the testicles and בעל גבר as a defect in the penis, and another baraita provides synonyms for these terms.
The gemara asks what is the measurement for the defect to disqualify the animal.
Rav Yehuda demonstrates that the defect is measured up to the ridge (רכובה).

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov who rules that up to the ridge is invalid, but above the ridge is valid.
An alternative version reverses the ruling: up to the ridge is valid, but below the ridge is invalid.

items.text: Mishnah: Missing testicle and related conditions
items.text_en: Mishnah: Missing testicle and related conditions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses the condition of 'מרוח אשך' (crushed testicle) and its variants: no testicles, one testicle, or crushed testicles. Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus offer different definitions.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the basic condition of missing testicles or having only one testicle, which defines the blemish 'מרוח אשך' (crushed testicle).
The Mishnah identifies this condition as the 'מרוח אשך' (crushed testicle) mentioned in the Torah.
Rabbi Yishmael defines the blemish as one whose testicles have dissolved (נימוחו אשכיו).
Rabbi Akiva defines the blemish as one whose testicles contain wind (רוח באשכיו).
Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus defines the blemish as one whose testicles appear dark (מראיו חשוכין).

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural derivation of the Mishnah's definitions
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural derivation of the Mishnah's definitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges each rabbi's reading of the verse: Rabbi Yishmael should say 'חסר אשך', Rabbi Akiva 'ממרוח אשך', and Rabbi Chanina 'רוח אשך'. The Gemara resolves by emending the text and noting that Rabbi Chanina does not include 'כושי' (dark-skinned).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yishmael's phrase 'נימוחו אשכיו' (his testicles were crushed) does not match the verse's term 'חסר אשך' (missing a testicle).
The Gemara emends the Mishnah text to read 'שנמרחו אשכיו' (his testicles were flattened), aligning with the verse's 'חסר אשך'.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Akiva's phrase 'רוח באשכיו' (wind in his testicles) does not match the verse's term 'ממרוח אשך' (flattened testicle).
The Gemara emends the Mishnah text to read 'שהרוח באשכיו' (that the wind is in his testicles), aligning with the verse's 'ממרוח אשך'.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonos's phrase 'מראיו חשוכין' (his appearance is dark) does not match the verse's term 'רוח אשך' (wind of the testicle).

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Chanina holds the hermeneutical principle of 'גורעין ומוסיפין ודורשין' (subtracting, adding, and interpreting), allowing him to derive his definition from the verse despite the textual discrepancy.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Chanina's definition of 'מראיו חשוכין' (dark appearance) is identical to the Mishnah's term 'כושי' (dark-skinned person), which is a separate disqualification.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonos does not include the term 'כושי' (dark-skinned) in his version of the Mishnah, so his definition is distinct.

items.text: תחילת משנה נוספת: מומי רגליים
items.text_en: Beginning of next Mishnah: Ankles and knees
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins listing blemishes of the ankles and knees, but the segment is cut off.
items.desc: המשנה מתחילה למנות מומים נוספים: המקיש בקרסוליו ובארכובותיו.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins listing blemishes of the ankles and knees.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: מומי רגל ויד הפוסלים כהן
items.text_en: Mishnah: Blemishes of the foot and hand
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines the blemishes of 'ba'al hapikim' and 'ikeil', then lists other disqualifying conditions of the foot and hand, including an extra digit (yeteret) and the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding extra fingers.
items.desc: המשנה מפרטת מומים שונים הפוסלים כהן לעבודה: בעל הפיקים, העיקל, פיקה יוצאת מגודלו, עקיבו יוצא לאחוריו, פרסות רחבות כשל אווז, אצבעות מורכבות או קלוטות, ויתרת אצבע. נדונים גם מקרים של אצבעות מורכבות מעל ומתחת לפרק, ויתרת שיש בה עצם או אין בה. לבסוף, מובאת מחלוקת בין רבי יהודה לחכמים לגבי יתר בידיים וברגליים, ובין רבי לחכמים לגבי השולט בשתי ידיו.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by defining the blemishes of 'ba'al hapikim' (one with many calluses) and 'ikeil' (one with crooked legs).
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בפירוט מומי רגל הפוסלים כהן: בעל הפיקים, העיקל, פיקה יוצאת מגודלו, עקיבו יוצא לאחוריו, ופרסות רחבות כשל אווז.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists additional conditions of the fingers and toes, including overlapping or fused digits, and the rule for an extra digit (yeteret) with a bone.
sub.desc: המשנה ממשיכה בדיני אצבעות מורכבות או קלוטות, ומבחינה בין מעל ומתחת לפרק, וכן דנה ביתרת שיש בה עצם או אין בה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah records the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding extra fingers, and between Rabbi and the Sages regarding one who controls both hands.
sub.desc: המשנה מסיימת במחלוקות: רבי יהודה מכשיר וחכמים פוסלים ביתר בידיים וברגליים; רבי פוסל וחכמים מכשירים בשולט בשתי ידיו.

items.text: גמרא: בירור המומים 'בעל הפיקים' ו'שופנר'
items.text_en: Gemara: Elaboration on the blemishes
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives these blemishes from the verse 'or broken foot', and Rabbi Yochanan explains the terms 'ba'al hapikim' and 'shufnar'. Rabbi Elazar and Rav Pappa add further anatomical clarifications.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא הדורשת את הפסוק 'או שבר רגל' לרבות מומים נוספים: קישָׁן, עיקל, קילבן. רבי יוחנן מפרש 'בעל הפיקים' כמי שיש לו כסתות הרבה, ו'שופנר' כמי שאין לו כסתות כלל. רבי אלעזר מפרש 'עקיבו יוצא לאחוריו' ששוקו יוצא באמצע רגלו. רב פפא מוסיף לגבי 'פרסות רחבות כשל אווז' שאין הכוונה דווקא טריפה וסדוקה, אלא כל שטריפה אף על פי שסדוקה.

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse 'or broken foot' that the blemishes of the קישָׁן (hock-joint), the עִיקֵּל (clubfoot), and the קִילְבָּן (hollow-foot) are included.
sub.desc: ברייתא דורשת את הפסוק 'או שבר רגל' לרבות מומי רגל נוספים: קישָׁן, עיקל, קילבן.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna lists two additional blemishes: בעל הקיפין (one with many calluses) and שופנר (one with no calluses at all).
sub.desc: ברייתא דורשת את הפסוק 'או שבר רגל' לרבות מומי רגל נוספים: קישָׁן, עיקל, קילבן.

sub.text: רבי יוחנן משם רבי חייא בר אבא
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that בעל הפיקין means one who has many calluses (כסתות), and שופנר means one who has no calluses at all.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מבאר: 'בעל הפיקים' הוא מי שיש לו כסתות רבות, ו'שופנר' הוא מי שאין לו כסתות כלל.

sub.text: רבי יוחנן משם רבי חייא בר אבא
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar clarifies that the phrase 'עקיבו יוצא לאחוריו' means his shin protrudes in the middle of his foot.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מבאר: 'בעל הפיקים' הוא מי שיש לו כסתות רבות, ו'שופנר' הוא מי שאין לו כסתות כלל.

sub.text: רבי יוחנן משם רבי חייא בר אבא
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa qualifies the description of wide hooves like a goose: it is not that the hoof is split but not cracked, but rather once it is split, even if it is also cracked, it is a blemish.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מבאר: 'בעל הפיקים' הוא מי שיש לו כסתות רבות, ו'שופנר' הוא מי שאין לו כסתות כלל.

items.text: גמרא: דרשת 'שבר יד' לרבות אצבעות מורכבות או קלוטות
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation for 'broken hand'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the disqualification of fused or clubbed fingers from the verse 'or broken hand', and resolves an apparent contradiction regarding the status of such fingers above the joint.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא הדורשת את הפסוק 'שבר יד' לרבות אצבעות מורכבות או קלוטות מעל הפרק. הגמרא מקשה: והא אמרת כשר? ומתרצת: הברייתא עוסקת במקרה שלא חתכן, והפסוק 'או שבר יד' מלמד שהן פסולות.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'or broken hand' to limit the disqualification to a broken hand alone.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בדרשת הפסוק 'שבר יד' ומצמצמת אותו לפסול של יד שבורה בלבד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita earlier deemed fused or clubbed fingers above the joint as kosher, contradicting the new derivation.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: והרי במשנה נאמר שאצבעות מורכבות או קלוטות מעל הפרק כשרות לאחר חיתוך, ואילו הברייתא משתמעת כפוסלת?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the verse applies only when the fingers were not cut off, teaching that such a condition disqualifies the animal.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: והרי במשנה נאמר שאצבעות מורכבות או קלוטות מעל הפרק כשרות לאחר חיתוך, ואילו הברייתא משתמעת כפוסלת?

items.text: Gemara: Condition for an extra digit
items.text_en: Gemara: Condition for an extra digit
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the disqualification of an extra digit with a bone applies only if it is aligned with the hand (nisparet al gabei hayad).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an extra digit with a bone disqualifies the animal, but without a bone it is kosher.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the disqualification applies only when the extra digit is aligned with the hand (nisparet al gabei hayad).

items.text: Gemara: Laws of impurity for an extra digit
items.text_en: Gemara: Laws of impurity for an extra digit
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the impurity status of an extra digit with a bone but no nail, and Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes between one that is aligned (nisparet) and one that is not. Rav Chisda and Rav Pappa debate the rationale, concluding that the Sages made a distinction to avoid burning terumah and kodashim.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that an extra digit with a bone but no nail conveys impurity through contact, carrying, and tent (אוהל), and counts toward the 248-limb total.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan qualifies the baraita: this applies only when the extra digit is aligned (נספרת) with the hand.
Rav Chisda reports a version of the baraita that says the extra digit conveys impurity through contact and carrying but not through tent (אוהל).

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan qualifies this version: it applies when the extra digit is not aligned (אינה נספרת) with the hand.
Rabbi Yochanan objects: the Sages' ruling seems inconsistent — if it is a limb, it should convey impurity through tent; if not, it should not convey impurity through contact and carrying either.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Manoach citing Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach citing Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha explains that the impurity through contact and carrying is due to a bone the size of a barley grain (עצם כשעורה), not because it is a full limb.
Rav Pappa suggests it is a decree (גזירה) lest one confuse a non-aligned digit with an aligned one, but then objects that this would also require tent impurity for the non-aligned case.
The gemara resolves that the Sages made a distinguishing mark (היכירא) so that people would not mistakenly burn תרומה (priestly portion) and קדשים (sacred offerings) due to uncertainty.

items.text: Gemara: Tangent on the number of bones
items.text_en: Gemara: Tangent on the number of bones
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah in Oholot about the majority of a person's bone structure, citing a baraita about 125 bones. Ravina questions Rava, and a story is told about Rabbi Yishmael's students who found 252 bones in a woman, leading to a dispute about the extra bones (tzirim and delatot). The section concludes with Rav's statement that these extra bones do not transmit impurity in a tent, and Abaye's objection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah in Oholot about the majority of a corpse's structure and count, and the baraita defining the majority of count as 125 bones.
Ravina asks Rava whether the baraita merely teaches a number or rather the principle that the 125 count follows the majority of people, and Rava answers that it follows the majority.

Rabbi Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name a story about Rabbi Yishmael's students who found 252 bones in a woman, and Rabbi Yishmael explained that a woman has extra bones called צירִים (hinges) and דְּלָתוֹת (doors).

sub.text: Baraita with Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Baraita with Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yehoshua, each deriving from a verse that a woman has extra bones analogous to a house's hinges and doors.
Rabbi Akiva adds that a woman has a 'key' bone, and the Gemara notes that this contradicts the story of Rabbi Yishmael's students, but resolves that the key bone is small and may have been lost.
Rav rules that all these extra bones do not transmit impurity in a tent, because the verse requires a structure common to all people.

Abaye objects that men also have 'tzirim' (pangs), but the Gemara distinguishes between 'tzirei basar' (muscle pains) and the actual bones, concluding that without this distinction one could not find the standard 248 bones in either men or women.

items.text: Extra fingers and the biblical source
items.text_en: Extra fingers and the biblical source
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the dispute about whether extra fingers are a blemish stems from a single verse about a giant with six fingers on each hand and foot. Rabbah elaborates on the verse's wording to clarify the count.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the dispute about extra fingers derives from a single verse about a giant with six fingers on each hand and foot, with one sage interpreting it as a defect and the other as a virtue.
Rabbah elaborates on the verse's wording 'שש ושש עשרים וארבע מספר' to clarify that the count refers to the total number of fingers on the hand.

items.text: A story about Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: A story about Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts a man with 24 fingers who came before Rabbi Tarfon, who blessed him. Rabbi Yosei objects, saying the blessing was actually a curse that such mamzerim and netinim should diminish.

sub.desc_en: A baraita introduces a story about a man with 24 fingers who came before Rabbi Tarfon.
Rabbi Tarfon blesses the man, saying 'May those like you increase in Israel.'
Rabbi Yosei objects, arguing that the blessing was actually a curse that mamzerim and netinim should diminish.

items.text: מחלוקת רבי וחכמים בשולט בשתי ידיו
items.text_en: Ambidexterity dispute
items.desc_en: A baraita states that an ambidextrous person is disqualified by Rabbi but validated by the Sages, based on whether left-handedness indicates weakness or strength.
items.desc: הברייתא קובעת שאיטר פסול לעבודה, ומובאת מחלוקת בין רבי הפוסל שולט בשתי ידיו לבין חכמים המכשירים. טעם המחלוקת: רבי סובר שהשליטה בשמאל מעידה על חולשה בימין, וחכמים סוברים שמדובר בחיזוק טבעי בשמאל.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that a left-handed person (איטר), whether in hand or foot, is disqualified.
The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi disqualifies an ambidextrous person, while the Sages validate him.

The gemara explains the dispute: one authority holds that weakness begins in the right hand, so ambidexterity shows strength; the other holds that strength begins in the left, so ambidexterity shows weakness.

items.text: Mishnah: Disqualifications for humans but not animals
items.text_en: Mishnah: Disqualifications for humans but not animals
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists conditions like albinism, dwarfism, and deafness that disqualify a kohen but are valid for animal offerings, with additional opinions from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by listing conditions (albinism, dwarfism, deafness, etc.) that disqualify a human kohen but are valid for animal offerings.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that a mentally incompetent animal is not considered choice.
Rabbi Elazar adds that those with dangling growths are also disqualified in humans but valid in animals.

items.text: Gemara: Definitions and additional disqualifications
items.text_en: Gemara: Definitions and additional disqualifications
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the terms for skin colors, defines קִפֵּחַ as tall, and cites Resh Lakish's warnings against certain marriages to avoid blemished offspring.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially defines the Mishnah's terms: כּוּשִׁי (dark-skinned) means black, גִּיחוֹר (red-skinned) means white, לַבְקָן (albino) means red.
The Gemara objects: but there is a story where someone asked 'who wants white (לוּקְיָאנֵי)?' and a white person was found, contradicting the identification of גִּיחוֹר as white.
The Gemara corrects: rather, כּוּשִׁי is black, גִּיחוֹר is red (as people say 'reddish גִּיחְיָא'), and לַבְקָן is white, consistent with the story about finding a white person.
The Gemara asks about קִפֵּחַ, and cites Rav Zevid who taught that it means tall.
The Gemara objects: but Rabbi Avahu taught that God praises tall people, citing the verse 'whose height was like the height of cedars', implying tallness is a virtue, not a disqualification.
Rav Pappa answers: the disqualification is for an abnormally tall person who is 'a hated long one' (a freakish height), not for ordinary tallness.

Resh Lakish warns against certain marriages to avoid blemished offspring: a tall man should not marry a tall woman (lest they produce a mast-like child), a dwarf not a dwarf (lest they produce a finger-sized child), a white man not a white woman (lest they produce a leprous child), a black man not a black woman (lest they produce a spotted child).

items.text: Drunkenness and disqualification
items.text_en: Drunkenness and disqualification
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why drunkenness is listed alongside permanent blemishes, and explains it refers to other intoxicants, disagreeing with Rabbi Yehuda who holds dates or milk also disqualify.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a drunk person (שיכור) is listed among permanent blemishes, since drunkenness is a temporary state that disqualifies service, not a permanent blemish.
The Gemara answers that the mishna refers to other intoxicating substances, not wine, which cause a permanent disqualification.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of Rabbi Yehuda's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of Rabbi Yehuda's view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this interpretation disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that eating dried figs, drinking milk or honey also disqualifies one from entering the Temple.

items.text: Mishnah: Disqualifications for animals but not humans
items.text_en: Mishnah: Disqualifications for animals but not humans
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists cases like 'it and its son' and treifah that disqualify animals but not human kohanim, and adds that a kohen who marries forbidden women or becomes impure for the dead is disqualified until he vows or accepts not to do so.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah lists disqualifications that apply to animals but not to human kohanim: 'it and its son', treifah, yotzei dofen, animals used for transgression, and those that killed a person.
The mishnah adds that a kohen who marries forbidden women or becomes impure for the dead is disqualified until he vows or accepts not to do so.

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of 'it and its son' and the vow requirement
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of 'it and its son' and the vow requirement
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that 'it and its son' refers to a female animal and its offspring, not Aaron and his sons, and discusses the mechanism of the vow for a kohen who married forbidden women, addressing concerns about dissolution by a sage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'אותו ואת בנו' (it and its son) means in the context of humans, since the Mishnah lists it as a disqualification for animals but here it appears as a human disqualification.
The Gemara objects: if it refers to Aaron and his sons, then the parallel case of a he-goat and its son does not apply, as the law of 'אותו ואת בנו' (it and its son) does not apply to males.
A baraita is cited: the law of 'אותו ואת בנו' (it and its son) applies to females and not to males.
The Gemara objects further: if it refers to a she-goat and its daughter, the parallel here would be a priestess and her son, but a priestess is not fit for service (עבודה).
The Gemara answers: it indeed refers to Aaron and his sons, and the parallel is a he-goat and its son.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin in the name of Chananyah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin in the name of Chananyah
sub.desc_en: In the West they said in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Avin: this is the opinion of Chananyah, who holds that the law of 'אותו ואת בנו' (it and its son) applies to both males and females, resolving the objection.
A Tanna taught: regarding one who marries women in transgression, he vows (to withhold benefit) and serves (as a priest), and if he later divorces, he descends from the priesthood.
The Gemara objects: we should be concerned that he might go to a sage who will dissolve the vow, thus circumventing the requirement.
The Gemara answers: the Tanna holds that one must specify the details of the vow (to the sage), which prevents easy dissolution.
The Gemara objects: this works for the one who says one must specify the vow, but for the one who says one need not specify, what can be said?
The Gemara answers: we administer the vow to him in the presence of many (ברבים), which makes it harder to dissolve.
The Gemara objects: this works for the one who says a vow made in the presence of many has no annulment, but for the one who says it does have annulment, what can be said?
The Gemara answers: we administer the vow (in a way that prevents annulment), though the text is cut off here.

items.text: Gemara on vows made with public consent
items.text_en: Gemara on vows made with public consent
items.desc_en: Amemar rules that a vow made with public consent cannot be annulled, even for those who hold that a public vow can be annulled. However, for a mitzvah matter, it can be annulled, as illustrated by the case of Rav Acha who excommunicated a teacher and Ravina who revoked it.

sub.desc_en: Amemar rules that a vow made with public consent (על דעת רבים) cannot be annulled, even according to the view that a public vow can be annulled.
Amemar qualifies that this applies only to a discretionary matter, but for a mitzvah matter the vow can be annulled.
The gemara cites the case of Rav Acha who excommunicated a teacher who neglected children, and Ravina who revoked the excommunication because no one else was as precise.
Amemar cites the case of a children's teacher whom Rav Acha banned for negligence, and Ravina later annulled the ban because no one else was as meticulous.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why in the Mishnah's case of one who becomes impure for the dead, acceptance of the vow suffices, while elsewhere we force a vow. It answers that there, his evil inclination overpowered him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why in the Mishnah's case of one who becomes impure for the dead, acceptance of the vow suffices, while elsewhere we force a vow.
The Gemara answers that there, his evil inclination overpowered him, so a vow is necessary.

items.text: סיום הפרק הקודם
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous chapter with the phrase 'We have returned to you, these blemishes.'
items.desc: קטע מעבר קצר המסכם את הפרק הקודם ('הדרן עלך מומין אלו').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous chapter with the standard formula 'We have returned to you, these blemishes.'

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Categories of firstborn
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Categories of firstborn
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that there are four categories of firstborn: one for inheritance but not for the priest, one for the priest but not for inheritance, one for both, and one for neither.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that there are four categories of firstborn: one for inheritance but not for the priest, one for the priest but not for inheritance, one for both, and one for neither.

items.text: First category: Firstborn for inheritance but not for the priest
items.text_en: First category: Firstborn for inheritance but not for the priest
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir defines this as a child born after a non-viable fetus, even if the head emerged alive, or after a nine-month fetus whose head emerged dead, or after a miscarriage resembling an animal. The Sages require human form. Also included are cases of a sandal, afterbirth, or formed embryo.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks which child is a firstborn for inheritance but not for the priest, and Rabbi Meir lists cases: a child born after a non-viable fetus (even if the head emerged alive), after a nine-month fetus whose head emerged dead, or after a miscarriage resembling an animal, bird, or beast.

The Sages require human form for the preceding birth to disqualify the firstborn from the priest, and list additional cases: a sandal, afterbirth, or formed embryo, after which the subsequent child is a firstborn for inheritance but not for the priest.

items.text: Second case: Man with no children marries a woman who already gave birth
items.text_en: Second case: Man with no children marries a woman who already gave birth
items.desc_en: If a man with no children marries a woman who already gave birth while a slave or gentile, and she gives birth after conversion or emancipation, the child is a firstborn for inheritance but not for the priest. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili argues it is a firstborn for both, citing the verse 'petter rechem beYisrael'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a child born to a man with no children who married a woman who already gave birth while a slave or gentile is a firstborn for inheritance but not for the priest.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili argues that the child is a firstborn for both inheritance and the priest, citing the verse 'פֶּטֶר רֶחֶם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל' (the first who opens the womb among Israel).

items.text: Third category: Firstborn for the priest but not for inheritance
items.text_en: Third category: Firstborn for the priest but not for inheritance
items.desc_en: This includes a man with children who marries a woman who never gave birth, a pregnant convert or freed slave who gives birth, a woman who gave birth before, a woman who remarries within three months and gives birth with uncertain paternity, and a Kohenet or Leviyah who gives birth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the first category: a man who already has children marries a woman who never gave birth, or a pregnant convert or freed slave gives birth.

The Mishnah adds further cases: a Kohenet or Leviyah who gives birth, a woman who already gave birth, and a woman who remarries within three months and gives birth with uncertain paternity — all produce a firstborn for the priest but not for inheritance.

items.text: דין שמואל: ראש נפל אינו פוטר
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on the head of a nefel
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that the head does not exempt subsequent births in the case of a nefel (non-viable fetus). The Gemara explains the reason: only where the breath of life is in the nostrils is the head considered significant; otherwise it is not.
items.desc: שמואל קובע שיציאת ראשו של נפל אינה נחשבת ללידה ואינה פוטרת את הבא אחריו מבכורה, משום שהפסוק 'כל אשר נשמת רוח חיים באפיו' מלמד שרק בעובר חי נחשב ראשו.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that the head does not exempt subsequent births in the case of a nefel (non-viable fetus).
The Gemara explains the reason: only where the breath of life is in the nostrils is the head considered significant; otherwise it is not.

items.text: קושיא ממשנתנו: ראש נפל פוטר
items.text_en: Gemara questions the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'its head' regarding a live birth after a nefel, but argues that the real criterion is the majority of the body (רובו). It explains why the Mishnah used 'head' instead of 'majority' — because the latter clause mentions 'its head' when dead, so the first clause also uses 'head' for consistency.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על שמואל ממשנתנו האומרת ש'ראשו' של נפל פוטר את הבא אחריו, ומתרצת ש'ראשו' האמור במשנה פירושו רובו, ולא הראש בלבד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'its head' regarding a live birth after a nefel, and questions whether 'head' really means the majority of the body (רובו).
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah should have said 'majority' but used 'head' for consistency with the latter clause which mentions 'its head' when dead.

items.text: בירור הצורך בשתי משניות: אדם ובהמה
items.text_en: Gemara challenges Shmuel from a baraita and distinguishes animal vs. human
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah teaches that once the head emerges it is considered a birth, citing a baraita that says even if the head was retracted it is considered born. It then considers that the baraita might refer to an animal, and that humans are different because they lack a 'prozdor' (vestibule). Conversely, animals cannot learn from humans because of the significance of the human face.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת מדוע יש צורך ללמד דין יציאת ראש הן באדם והן בבהמה, ומסבירה שאין ללמוד זה מזה משום שבבהמה אין פרוזדור ובאדם חשיבות פרצוף הפנים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah teaches that once the head emerges it is considered a birth, and cites a baraita that says even if the head was retracted it is considered born.
The Gemara suggests that the baraita might refer to an animal, and that humans are different because they lack a 'prozdor' (vestibule).
The Gemara objects that animals cannot learn from humans because of the significance of the human face.

items.text: תיובתא דשמואל ממשנת נדה
items.text_en: Refutation of Shmuel from a baraita about the forehead
items.desc_en: A baraita states that when a child emerges normally, it is considered born once the majority of its head emerges, defined as the forehead (פדחת). This directly contradicts Shmuel's position, and the Gemara declares it a refutation.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ממשנה במסכת נדה שיציאת רוב הראש נחשבת ללידה, ומכאן תיובתא לשמואל הסובר שראש נפל אינו פוטר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that when a child emerges normally, it is considered born once the majority of its head emerges, defined as the forehead (פדחת).
The Gemara declares this baraita a conclusive refutation (תיוּבְתָּא) of Shmuel's position.

items.text: מחלוקת ריש לקיש ורבי יוחנן: פדחת פוטרת בכל מקום חוץ מנחלה
items.text_en: Dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on the forehead's effect
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish says the forehead exempts in all contexts except inheritance, citing the verse 'יַכִּיר'. Rabbi Yochanan says even for inheritance it exempts. The Gemara explains that 'all contexts' includes the case of a convert who gave birth while still a gentile but whose fetus's forehead emerged before conversion — she does not observe days of impurity or bring a birth offering.
items.desc: ריש לקיש אומר שפדחת פוטרת בכל מקום חוץ מנחלה, משום דרשת 'יכיר', ורבי יוחנן חולק ואומר שאף לנחלה פוטרת. הגמרא מביאה דוגמה לגיורת שיצאה פדחת ולדה בגיותה.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that the forehead (פדחת) exempts in all contexts except inheritance, citing the verse 'יַכִּיר' (he shall recognize).
Rabbi Yochanan argues that the forehead exempts even for inheritance.
The Gemara explains that 'all contexts' includes the case of a convert whose fetus's forehead emerged while she was still a gentile — she does not observe days of impurity or bring a birth offering.

items.text: Challenge from the law of identifying a corpse for a wife's testimony
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of identifying a corpse for a wife's testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites sources that for identification of a corpse (to permit a wife to remarry), one must recognize the face with the nose, not just the forehead. Abaye or Rav Kahana explain that this is different because the Sages were stringent in the case of a wife's testimony. The Gemara questions this stringency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that for identification of a corpse, one must recognize the face with the nose, not just the forehead.
Another baraita is cited: testimony requires both forehead and face with the nose.
Abaye or Rav Kahana explain that the case of a wife's testimony is different because the Sages were stringent there.
The Gemara objects: but we learned that they were lenient in accepting testimony from a witness who heard from another witness, or from a woman, slave, or maidservant.
The Gemara resolves: the Sages were lenient only at the end of the process (after the husband is presumed dead), but at the beginning (identifying the corpse) they were not lenient.
The Gemara introduces an alternative answer (but the text is cut off).

items.text: Gemara objects to the stringency claim
items.text_en: Gemara objects to the stringency claim
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Sages were lenient in allowing testimony from a witness who heard from another witness, a woman, a slave, or a maidservant. It answers that the leniency applies only at the final stage (to permit remarriage), but at the initial stage (to identify the corpse) they were not lenient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Sages were lenient in allowing testimony from a witness who heard from another witness, a woman, a slave, or a maidservant.
The Gemara answers that the leniency applies only at the final stage (to permit remarriage), but at the initial stage (to identify the corpse) they were not lenient.

items.text: תירוץ חלופי לרבי יוחנן
items.text_en: Alternative resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution (ואיבעית אימא) to the challenge, though the text breaks off without completing the argument.
items.desc: הגמרא מציעה תירוץ נוסף לדעת רבי יוחנן, אם תרצה אמור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative resolution (ואיבעית אימא) to the challenge, but the text breaks off without completing the argument.

items.text: Opening distinction between 'yakhir' and 'hakkrat panim'
items.text_en: Opening distinction between 'yakhir' and 'hakkrat panim'
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by distinguishing between the terms 'yakhir' and 'hakkrat panim', setting up the context for the dispute about converts and firstborn status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between the terms 'יַכִּיר' (recognize) and 'הַכָּרַת פָּנִים' (recognition of face), setting up the context for the dispute about converts and firstborn status.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish on a convert's firstborn
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish on a convert's firstborn
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish argue whether a convert who had children before conversion has a firstborn for inheritance. The Gemara explains their reasoning and notes that both disputes are necessary to avoid assuming they would agree in the other case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says a convert who had children before conversion has no firstborn for inheritance, while Resh Lakish says he does.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: the child was already the father's first strength (ראשית אונו) before conversion.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Resh Lakish's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Resh Lakish's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Resh Lakish's reasoning: a convert is like a newborn, so his previous children are not considered his for inheritance.

sub.text: Gemara's connection to a parallel dispute
sub.text_en: Gemara's connection to a parallel dispute
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the same amoraim hold parallel positions on whether a convert fulfilled the mitzvah of פרייה ורביה (procreation).

The Gemara explains that both disputes are necessary, because each case has a unique factor that could lead one to think the other amora would agree, so both rulings are needed to clarify their positions.

items.text: Mishnah analysis: woman who already gave birth
items.text_en: Mishnah analysis: woman who already gave birth
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes a Mishnah about a man who married a woman who had already given birth, and questions whether the child is a firstborn for inheritance. It concludes that the case involves a convert with children, and the ruling excludes Rabbi Yose HaGelili's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man who had no children and married a woman who had already given birth (whether as a freed slave or convert) produces a child that is a firstborn for inheritance but not for the priest.
The Gemara asks: from whom did she give birth? If from a Jewish man without children, why specify a convert or slave? Even a native Jewish woman would be the same.
The Gemara answers: it must be from a convert who had children before conversion, and the Mishnah teaches that the child is a firstborn for inheritance.
The Gemara rejects this: it is always from a Jewish man without children, and the Mishnah only needed to teach that the child is not a firstborn for the priest.

The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah excludes Rabbi Yose HaGelili's opinion, who would say the child is a firstborn for both inheritance and the priest, by teaching that it is not a firstborn for the priest.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yose HaGelili's view
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yose HaGelili's view
items.desc_en: Ravina or Rav Acha identifies a supporting baraita as following Rabbi Yose HaGelili's opinion that 'petter rechem' requires the womb to be opened by an Israelite.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if a man had children while a gentile and then converted, he has a firstborn for inheritance — supporting Reish Lakish.

Ravina (or Rav Acha) explains that this baraita follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who derives from 'פֶּטֶר רֶחֶם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל' that the child must be born from an Israelite mother, and the baraita applies that logic to the convert's case.

items.text: דין לויה שילדה בכור פטור מחמש סלעים
items.text_en: Exemption of a Levite woman's son from five sela'im
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava states that a Levite woman's son is exempt from the five-sela redemption. The Gemara discusses the father's identity, with Rav Papa suggesting a non-Jew, and Mar bar Rav Yosef citing Rava that the exemption is based on 'petter rechem' regardless of the father.
items.desc: רב אדא בר אהבה אומר שלויה שילדה בכור, בנה פטור מחמש סלעים. הגמרא דנה ממי נתעברה: אם מישראל, קשה דהא בתר אב אזלינן; רב פפא מתרץ שנתעברה מגוי, ואף לדעת המזהמים הוולד נקרא לוי פסול. מר בריה דרב יוסף מתרץ בשם רבא שנתעברה מישראל, ושאני הכא דכתיב 'פטר רחם'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava states that a Levite woman's son is exempt from the five-sela redemption.
The Gemara asks: If the Levite woman conceived from a Kohen or Levite, why specify a Levite? Even an Israelite woman would be exempt.
Rav Papa answers that the Levite woman conceived from a non-Jew, and even according to the view that a non-Jew renders the offspring unfit, a Levite is still called 'unfit' and exempt.

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Yosef citing Rava
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef citing Rava
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef says in the name of Rava that the Levite woman conceived from an Israelite, and the exemption is based on the verse 'פטר רחם' (the opening of the womb), which depends on the mother's status.

items.text: קושיה על רב פפא ממשנה בכהנת ולויה
items.text_en: Mishnah on priestly and Levite women and the father's identity
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes a Mishnah about a woman who married within three months and gave birth, noting that priestly and Levite women are exempt. It questions the father's identity, leading to a dispute between Rav Papa and Mar bar Rav Yosef, concluding that the Mishnah refers to a priest's daughter married to an Israelite.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על שיטת רב פפא ממשנה העוסקת בכהנת ולויה שילדו, ומשמע שהן פטורות. הגמרא דנה ממי נתעברו: אם מכהן או לוי, קשה; אם מגוי, קשה לכהנת כיון שנפסלה. מר בריה דרב יוסף מיישב שהמשנה עוסקת בכהנת שנתעברה מישראל, ורב פפא מיישב שהמשנה עוסקת בישראלית שנתעברה מכהן.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, stating that a woman who married within three months and gave birth, including a priestess or Levite, produces a child who is a firstborn for the priest but not for inheritance.

The Gemara infers that priestesses and Levites are exempt from the redemption payment, and questions the father's identity, arguing that if the father were a priest or Levite, even an Israelite woman would be exempt.
Rav Papa suggests the father is a gentile, but then questions why a priestess would be exempt, citing a previous discussion with Rabbah about a priestess impregnated by a gentile.

Rabbah objects that a Levite woman retains her sanctity even after forbidden relations, citing a baraita that she may eat tithes, but a priestess who has relations with a gentile becomes a חללה (profaned woman) and loses her sanctity.
The Gemara notes that Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava resolves the difficulty by positing the father is an Israelite, but questions how Rav Papa would explain the Mishnah.
The Gemara concludes that the father is a priest, and the woman is actually an Israelite, but the Mishnah calls her 'priestess' because her son is a priest.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Ḥisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Ḥisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Rav Ḥisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna argue whether a ḥalal son must redeem himself if his father died within thirty days of his birth. Rav Ḥisda says he must, because the father did not acquire his redemption; Rabbah bar Rav Huna says he is exempt, because the son can claim he comes from the power of a man with whom one cannot litigate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Ḥisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna regarding a ḥalal son whose priest father died; it first states the agreed-upon case: if the father died after thirty days, the son is not obligated to redeem himself because the father already acquired the redemption.
Rav Ḥisda argues that when the father died within thirty days, the son must redeem himself because the father did not yet acquire the redemption money.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna argues that the son is exempt because he can claim he comes from the power of a man (his father) with whom the priest cannot litigate.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah of a convert who gave birth
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah of a convert who gave birth
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbah bar Rav Huna's reasoning from a mishnah where a pregnant convert gives birth and the child is a firstborn to the priest. The Gemara asks why the son cannot claim he comes from the power of a gentile with whom one cannot litigate. The answer is that a gentile has no lineage (ḥayis), so the claim does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbah bar Rav Huna's reasoning by citing a mishnah where a pregnant convert gives birth and the child is a firstborn to the priest, asking why the son cannot claim he comes from the power of a gentile with whom one cannot litigate.
The Gemara answers that the case of a gentile is different because he has no lineage (חַיִיס), so the claim does not apply.

items.text: Ruling of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
items.text_en: Ruling of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish rules that if a priest died within thirty days and left a ḥalal son, the son must redeem himself because the father did not acquire his redemption. If the father died after thirty days, the son is exempt because the father had already acquired his redemption.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish rules that if a priest died within thirty days of the birth of his ḥalal son, the son must redeem himself because the father did not acquire his redemption.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish adds that if the father died after thirty days, the son is exempt because the father had already acquired his redemption.

items.text: Mishnah of a woman who did not wait three months
items.text_en: Mishnah of a woman who did not wait three months
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a mishnah about a woman who did not wait three months after her husband's death and gave birth. The child is a firstborn to the priest but not for inheritance. The Gemara questions why the child does not take a portion as a simple son, and Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the mishnah refers to the child born after him, who is not a firstborn for inheritance.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah is cited: a woman who did not wait three months after her husband's death and then married gives birth to a child who is a firstborn to the priest but not for inheritance.
The Gemara questions why the child of uncertain paternity takes a share as a simple son, since each potential father's son could reject him.

Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the mishnah's ruling that the child is not a firstborn for inheritance is needed only for the son born after him, to teach that the later son is not a firstborn for inheritance.

items.text: Discussion of authorization (harsha'ah) between heirs
items.text_en: Discussion of authorization (harsha'ah) between heirs
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the two children cannot write authorization to each other to collect inheritance. It suggests the mishnah is without authorization, but then supports Rabbi Yannai's distinction: if the children were recognized and later mixed, they can write authorization; if they were never recognized, they cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the two children cannot write authorization (הרשאה) to each other to collect the inheritance together, and notes that the mishnah is interpreted as dealing with a case where authorization was given.
The Gemara supports Rabbi Yannai's distinction: if the children were initially recognized and later mixed, they can write authorization; if they were never recognized, they cannot.

items.text: Mishnah: Defining a firstborn for inheritance and priesthood
items.text_en: Mishnah: Defining a firstborn for inheritance and priesthood
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists cases where a woman miscarries various forms, and the subsequent child is a firstborn for both inheritance and priesthood. It also discusses a child born by caesarean section and the one after him, with Rabbi Shimon ruling that the first is a firstborn for inheritance and the second for the five selas.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by asking which child is a firstborn for both inheritance and priesthood, and lists cases of miscarriages after which the subsequent child qualifies.
The mishnah states that a child born by caesarean section and the one after him are not firstborn for either inheritance or priesthood.
Rabbi Shimon rules that the first child born by caesarean section is a firstborn for inheritance, and the second child is a firstborn for the five-sela redemption.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the mishnah's rulings
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the mishnah's rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasoning behind the Tanna Kamma's and Rabbi Shimon's positions. The Tanna Kamma requires both 'and they bore him' and 'opened the womb' for inheritance and priesthood respectively. Rabbi Shimon follows his own view that 'she gave birth' includes a caesarean section, and he holds that a firstborn for one matter is considered a firstborn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first son born by caesarean section is not a firstborn for inheritance because the verse 'וְיָלְדוּ לוֹ' (and they bore him) is required, and for redemption because the verse 'פָּטַר רֶחֶם' (opened the womb) is required.

The Gemara explains that the second son is not a firstborn for inheritance because the verse 'רֵאשִׁית אוֹנוֹ' (first of his strength) is required, and for redemption because the Tanna Kamma holds that a firstborn for one matter is not considered a firstborn.
Rabbi Shimon rules that the first son is a firstborn for inheritance, following his own reasoning that the verse 'תֵּלֵד' (she bears) includes a caesarean section.
Rabbi Shimon rules that the second son is a firstborn for redemption, because he holds that a firstborn for one matter is considered a firstborn.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: תאומים זכרים ותשלום פדיון הבכור
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a woman who gave birth to twin boys without having previously redeemed a firstborn: the father gives five sela to a priest. If one twin dies within thirty days, the father is exempt. If the father dies and the sons survive, Rabbi Meir says if they gave before dividing the inheritance they gave, otherwise they are exempt; Rabbi Yehuda says the property is obligated. If there was a male and female, the priest gets nothing.
items.desc: המשנה פותחת במקרה של אשה שלא ביכרה וילדה שני זכרים, והאב חייב לתת חמש סלעים לכהן. אם אחד מת בתוך שלושים יום – האב פטור. במקרה שהאב מת והבנים חיים, נחלקו רבי מאיר ורבי יהודה: רבי מאיר פוטר אם חלקו, ורבי יהודה מחייב את הנכסים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a woman who gave birth to twin boys without having previously redeemed a firstborn: the father gives five sela to a priest, and if one twin dies within thirty days, the father is exempt.
The Mishnah presents the case where the father dies and the sons survive: Rabbi Meir rules that if they gave before dividing the inheritance they gave, otherwise they are exempt.
Rabbi Yehuda states that the property is obligated, implying the sons must pay even after dividing.
The Mishnah concludes that if there was a male and a female, the priest gets nothing.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא: מתי מת האב?
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the timing of the father's death
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: when did the father die? If after thirty days, why would Rabbi Meir say they are exempt after dividing? The property was already obligated. Rather, if he died within thirty days, what difference does dividing make? In either case, each son can push the priest off to the other.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם האב מת לאחר שלושים יום, מדוע רבי מאיר פוטר כשחלקנו? הרי הנכסים משועבדים. ואם מת בתוך שלושים יום, הקושיה היא שגם כשלא חלקנו יכול הכהן לפנות לכל אחד ולהידחות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: when did the father die? If after thirty days, why would Rabbi Meir exempt them after dividing? The property was already obligated.
The Gemara asks: if the father died within thirty days, what difference does dividing make? In either case, each son can push the priest off to the other.

items.text: תירוץ רבי ירמיה: שותפות וגבייה
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's answer: two partners and a creditor
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya says this teaches that if two people named Yosef ben Shimon in the same city bought a field as partners, a creditor can collect from them, because the creditor can say: whichever of you I am claiming from, I am taking your share.
items.desc: רבי ירמיה מסיק מהמשנה שבמקרה של שני שותפים ששמם זהה, בעל חוב יכול לגבות מהשדה המשותפת, שכן הוא יכול לטעון שלכל אחד מהם יש חלק. כך גם כאן, כשהבנים לא חלקנו, הכהן גובה מהנכסים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya answers the gemara's objection by asserting that the case teaches a rule about two people named Yosef ben Shimon who bought a field as partners: a creditor can collect from either, claiming whichever share is owed.

items.text: דחיית רבא: אין לגבות מהשותף לפני הדיון עם הלווה
items.text_en: Rava's objection: the guarantor principle
items.desc_en: Rava objects: since a person's assets are guarantors for him, can it be that one cannot claim from the debtor himself but can claim from the guarantor? And we have a mishnah that a lender cannot collect from the guarantor first.
items.desc: רבא דוחה את דברי רבי ירמיה: אין זה הגיוני לגבות מהשותף (הערב) לפני שנתבע מהלווה עצמו, כפי שנלמד ממשנה שאין לגבות מהערב תחילה.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects: since a person's property is a guarantor for him, can one sue the guarantor before the debtor? The Mishnah teaches that a creditor cannot collect from a guarantor first.

items.text: תירוץ רבא: האב מת לאחר שלושים יום ויש רק חמש סלעים
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: father died after thirty days with limited assets
items.desc_en: Rava explains: actually the father died after thirty days, and if there were many assets the priest would collect. Here we deal with only five sela. And everyone agrees with Rav Asi's principle that brothers who divided are half heirs and half purchasers, and a Torah-written loan (like the redemption obligation) is not subject to the usual rules.
items.desc: רבא מסביר שהמשנה עוסקת במקרה שהאב מת לאחר שלושים יום, אך הירושה היא רק חמש סלעים. לכן, אם חלקנו, כל אחד מחזיק בחצי, והכהן לא יכול לגבות מאף אחד מהם כי כל אחד דוחה אותו. לעומת זאת, אם לא חלקנו, הכהן גובה מהנכסים המשותפים. רבא מוסיף שכולם מקבלים את דברי רב אסי שאחים שחלקו נחשבים כחצי יורשים וחצי לקוחות, ושהלוואה הכתובה בתורה גוברת.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves: the father died after thirty days, and the case is where there are only five sela in the estate, so the sons cannot both pay.

The Gemara invokes Rav Asi's principle that brothers who divide an inheritance are considered half heirs and half purchasers, and everyone agrees that a loan written in the Torah (like pidyon haben) is treated as a written debt.

items.text: Resolving the dispute: five and not half-five
items.text_en: Resolving the dispute: five and not half-five
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda is not about Rav Papa's principle, but about whether the obligation requires exactly five selas or even half of five. Rabbi Meir holds 'five and not half-five', while Rabbi Yehuda holds 'five and even half-five'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute is not about Rav Papa's principle, which is universally accepted, that an oral loan is collected from heirs but not from purchasers.
The Gemara explains that the dispute is about the interpretation of 'five selas': Rabbi Meir holds 'five and not half-five', while Rabbi Yehuda holds 'five and even half-five'.

items.text: Objection from the baraita about ten zuz
items.text_en: Objection from the baraita about ten zuz
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Yehuda holds 'five and even half-five', then the baraita's requirement of ten zuz each is unnecessary; even less would suffice. It concludes that the baraita must refer to ten zuz of inheritance, proving Rabbi Yehuda holds 'five and not half-five'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Yehuda holds 'five and even half-five', then his ruling about 'the property became obligated' should require the man to be obligated, not the property.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda requires ten zuz each for brothers to be liable, implying a minimum threshold.
The Gemara questions the meaning of 'ten zuz for this and ten zuz for that', and argues that if Rabbi Yehuda holds 'five and even half-five', the baraita should not specify ten zuz.
The Gemara objects that even less than ten zuz would suffice if Rabbi Yehuda holds 'five and even half-five'.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita refers to ten zuz of inheritance, proving that Rabbi Yehuda holds 'five and not half-five'.

items.text: הסברת המחלוקת בדברי רב אסי ורב פפא
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: dispute over Rav Asi and Rav Papa
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: all agree on 'five and not half-five', and the dispute is about the principles of Rav Asi and Rav Papa regarding debt collection from heirs versus purchasers.
items.desc: הגמרא מסבירה שכולם מודים שפודים רק חמש שלמות, והמחלוקת היא לגבי שיעור הנכסים הזמינים: רבי מאיר סובר כדברי רב אסי ורב פפא שרק מחצית מהנכסים משועבדת, ורבי יהודה חולק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative resolution: all agree on the principle of 'five and not half-five', and the dispute is actually about the principles of Rav Asi and Rav Papa regarding debt collection from heirs versus purchasers.

items.text: קושיה על רבי יהודה ממות האב בתוך שלושים
items.text_en: Objection from the seifa: timing of the father's death
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the father died after thirty days, the property is already liened, so why would Rabbi Meir exempt? If within thirty days, why would Rabbi Yehuda obligate, since the sons can push each other off?
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם האב מת בתוך שלושים יום, מדוע רבי יהודה מחייב את הבנים? הרי הבן יכול לדחות את הכהן בטענה שאינו בכור. הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שבה רבי יהודה מחייב גם כשחלקו, ומקשה על כך.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the father died after thirty days, the property is already liened, so why would Rabbi Meir exempt? If within thirty days, why would Rabbi Yehuda obligate, since the sons can push each other off?

items.text: דברי רבי ירמיה ורבא על שני יוסף בן שמעון
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the case involves two Yosef ben Shimon, where the creditor can collect from the buyer because he can claim he is collecting from his own debtor's share. Rava rejects this, stating that all property is surety for the debt, reverting to the first explanation.
items.desc: רבי ירמיה מביא דין: אם שני אנשים בשם יוסף בן שמעון בעיר אחת, ואחד קנה שדה מחבירו, בעל חוב גובה ממנו. רבא דוחה ואומר שנכסי אדם הם ערבים לו, והכל חוזר ללשון הראשונה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya resolves the difficulty by positing two Yosef ben Shimon in one city, where the creditor can collect from the buyer by claiming he is taking his own debtor's share or the other's share that was already encumbered.
Rava rejects Rabbi Yirmeya's explanation, asserting that all property is surety for the debt, so the case reverts to the first explanation.

items.text: משנת ערבוב ולדות ופדיון בכור
items.text_en: Mishnah: cases of two women who did not redeem their firstborn
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents various scenarios of two women who gave birth to sons, detailing when the father must give five selas to the priest, and the rules if one child dies within thirty days. It also covers cases of mixed genders and one mother who had previously redeemed.
items.desc: המשנה מפרטת דינים שונים בערבוב ולדות של נשים שילדו, וקובעת כמה סלעים חייב האב לתת לכהן, ובאילו מקרים פטור. דוגמאות: שתי נשים שלא ביכרו וילדו שני זכרים – נותן עשר סלעים; זכר ונקבה – חמש סלעים; שתי נקבות וזכר – פטור.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of two women who had not previously given birth, each bearing a male, and the father must give ten sela coins to the priest; if one son dies within thirty days, the priest returns five sela if given to one priest, but cannot be reclaimed if given to two priests.

The Mishnah rules that when the births include a male and a female, or two males and a female, the father gives five sela coins; but if there are two females and a male, or two males and two females, the priest receives nothing.

The Mishnah states that if one mother had previously given birth and the other had not, and they bore two males, the father gives five sela coins; if one son dies within thirty days, the father is exempt.

The Mishnah presents the dispute: if the father dies and the sons live, רבי מאיר (Rabbi Meir) says they are exempt if they divided the property before giving, while רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) says the obligation already took effect on the property; in a case of a male and a female, the priest receives nothing.

The Mishnah rules that when two women from different husbands each bear a male, each father gives five sela coins; if one son dies within thirty days and they gave to one priest, he returns five sela, but if to two priests, they cannot reclaim.

The Mishnah states that if the births are a male and a female, the fathers are exempt but the son must redeem himself; if two females and a male, or two females and two males, the priest receives nothing.

The Mishnah concludes: if one woman had previously given birth and the other had not, and they are from different husbands, the husband of the woman who had not previously given birth gives five sela coins; if the births are a male and a female, the priest receives nothing.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על דין שני כהנים
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Shmuel's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between one priest and two priests regarding the ability to recover payment, since even with one priest the payer could be pushed off. Shmuel answers.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע כשנתנו לשני כהנים אינם יכולים להוציא מידם, ואילו כהן אחד יכול לדחותם? הרי גם כהן אחד יכול לדחות כל אב. שמואל עונה על כך.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between two priests and one priest regarding the inability to recover payment, since even with one priest the payer could be pushed off.
Shmuel begins his answer to the Gemara's question.

items.text: דין הרשאה במקרקעין ובמטלטלין
items.text_en: Clarification on writing a court order for movables
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses the Nehardeans' practice of not writing a court order for movables, explaining that this applies only when the debtor denies the debt, but if he does not deny, they do write it.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בשאלה האם ניתן לכתוב הרשאה (אדרכתא) על מטלטלין, ומבחינה בין מקרה שבו הנתבע מכחיש את הטענה לבין מקרה שבו אינו מכחיש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the practice of writing a court order for movables, citing the Nehardeans' rule that they do not write such an order for movables.
sub.desc: פותחת בדין הרשאה במקרה של פדיון בכור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case where the debtor denies the debt (no order is written) and where he does not deny (an order is written).
