items.text: קל וחומר לאיסור עישור ממין למין
items.text_en: Kal vachomer for grain and grain
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have a source that wine and oil cannot be tithed from each other; from a kal vachomer, grain and grain (which are kilayim) should also not be tithed from each other.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמד שאין מפרישים תרומה מיין על דגן או מדגן על דגן, ועונה בקל וחומר: ומה יין ושמן שאינם כלאיים זה בזה ואין מתעשרים מזה על זה, יין ודגן או דגן ודגן שהם כלאיים זה בזה – אינו דין שלא יתעשרו?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have a source that wine and oil cannot be tithed from each other; from a kal vachomer (קל וחומר), grain and grain (which are kilayim) should also not be tithed from each other.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמד שאין מפרישים תרומה מיין על דגן או מדגן על דגן, ועונה בקל וחומר מין ושמן.

items.text: קושיית רבי יאשיה ותשובת הגמרא
items.text_en: Rabbi Yoshiya's alternative derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yoshiya, who defines kilayim differently, would need a different kal vachomer. It presents his version: wine and oil, which are not kilayim even through another substance, cannot be tithed from each other; grain and grain, which are kilayim through another substance, certainly cannot.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על הקל וחומר הקודם לפי שיטת רבי יאשיה, הסובר שאיסור כלאיים חל רק בזריעה ביד אחת. הגמרא מתרצת שההיקש הוא על דרך 'על ידי דבר אחר': ומה יין ושמן שאינם כלאיים אפילו על ידי דבר אחר ואין מתעשרים, יין ודגן שהם כלאיים על ידי דבר אחר – אינו דין שלא יתעשרו?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yoshiya, who defines kilayim differently, would derive the law that different grain types cannot be tithed from each other.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על הקל וחומר הקודם לפי שיטת רבי יאשיה, הסובר שאיסור כלאיים חל רק בזריעה ביד אחת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents Rabbi Yoshiya's alternative kal vachomer: wine and oil, which are not kilayim even through another substance, cannot be tithed from each other; grain and grain, which are kilayim through another substance, certainly cannot.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שההיקש הוא על דרך 'על ידי דבר אחר': ומה יין ושמן שאינם כלאיים אפילו על ידי דבר אחר ואין מתעשרים, יין ודגן שהם כלאיים על ידי דבר אחר – אינו דין שלא יתעשרו?

items.text: דין שני מינים בעלמא מדרבנן
items.text_en: Source for two species rabbinically
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that two species (even not kilayim) cannot be tithed from each other? It answers: these are rabbinic laws, and the rabbis modeled them after Torah law—just as Torah law prohibits tithing two species from each other, so too rabbinic law.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמד איסור עישור משני מינים שאינם דגן (כגון עדשים ופולים). התשובה: תקנת חכמים היא, וכל תקנת חכמים היא כעין דאורייתא – מה דאורייתא שני מינים אינם מתעשרים מזה על זה, אף דרבנן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that two species (even not kilayim) cannot be tithed from each other?
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמד איסור עישור משני מינים שאינם דגן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: these are rabbinic laws, and the rabbis modeled them after Torah law—just as Torah law prohibits tithing two species from each other, so too rabbinic law.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמד איסור עישור משני מינים שאינם דגן.

items.text: קושיית רבא בר רב חנן על מעשר בהמה
items.text_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan's objection from animal tithe
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan objects to Abaye: if so, regarding animal tithe, where the verse does not write 'and all tithe of cattle and tithe of flock'...
items.desc: רבא בר רב חנן מקשה לאביי: אם כן, לגבי מעשר בהמה, שלא נכתב בתורה 'וכל מעשר בקר ומעשר צאן' אלא 'וכל מעשר בקר וצאן', מה הדין?

sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan's objection to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan objects to Abaye: if so, regarding animal tithe, where the verse does not write 'and all tithe of cattle and tithe of flock'...
sub.desc: רבא בר רב חנן מקשה לאביי: אם הכלל שלפיו שני מינים אינם מתעשרים זה מזה נלמד מכפל המילים בתורה, הרי במעשר בהמה לא נכתב כפל לשון, ומה הדין?

items.text: Gemara's question on tithing different grains
items.text_en: Gemara's question on tithing different grains
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether different types of grain can be tithed from one onto another, similar to the case of sheep and goats. Abaye and Rabbi Ila answer with the verse 'רֵאשִׁיתָם' to exclude this possibility.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether different types of grain can be tithed from one onto another, similar to the case of sheep and goats, and notes that the verse 'וָצֹאן' (and the flock) implies all flock is one.

Abaye and Rabbi Ila answer that the verse 'רֵאשִׁיתָם' (the first part of them) teaches that one must give the first part for each type of produce separately, preventing tithing different grains together.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation for grains
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation for grains
items.desc_en: Rava argues that even without 'רֵאשִׁיתָם', the verse 'דָּגָן' itself implies all grain is one category, unlike the case of sheep and goats where 'וָצֹאן' includes both. He explains that 'בָּקָר וָצֹאן' excludes inter-tithing, but 'דָּגָן' excludes other species.

sub.desc_en: Rava argues that even without the term 'רֵאשִׁיתָם', the word 'דָּגָן' itself implies all grain is one category.
Rava explains that if the verse had written 'all animal tithe', one might think it includes undomesticated animals, but a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from sacrificial animals excludes them.
Rava concludes that the verse 'בָּקָר וָצֹאן' teaches that cattle and sheep may not be tithed together, but sheep and goats may be tithed together.
Rava resolves that the term 'דָּגָן' is necessary to exclude other types of food from the obligation of tithes.

items.text: המשך הדיון על צירוף מינים
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding cattle and sheep
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Nachman challenges whether cattle and sheep can be tithed together. Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman answers with the verse 'הָעֲשִׂירִי'. A second version has Rava using a comparison to grain tithes, but he retracts that view, and some attribute it to Rav Pappa.
items.desc: רבא ורב הונא דנים באפשרות לערב בקר וצאן, ומר זוטרא מבהיר שרבא מקבל את דעת אביי. מובאת דעה נוספת בשם רבא על היקש מעשר בהמה למעשר דגן, והגמרא מבהירה שרבא חזר בו מדעתו הקודמת.

sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Nachman's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Nachman objects to Rava's derivation, suggesting that the verse might teach to intermingle cattle and sheep for tithing.
sub.desc: רב הונא מקשה על רבא: אפשר לפרש שהפסוק בא לערבב בקר וצאן יחד.

sub.text_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman's answer
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman answers that Rava also accepts the verse 'הָעֲשִׂירִי' (the tenth) as teaching separate tithing, so the derivation is unnecessary.
sub.desc: רב הונא מקשה על רבא: אפשר לפרש שהפסוק בא לערבב בקר וצאן יחד.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version has Rava saying that even without 'עֲשִׂירִי', animal tithe is juxtaposed to grain tithe, so one species cannot be tithed for another.
sub.desc: יש אומרים שרבא סובר שאפילו בלי הפסוק 'העשירי' אי אפשר לערב, כי הוקש מעשר בהמה למעשר דגן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rava himself previously said the juxtaposition applies only to the year, not to other matters.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי רבא עצמו אמר שההיקש הוא רק לעניין שנה ולא לדבר אחר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rava retracted that earlier opinion, or alternatively, one of the opinions was said by Rav Pappa.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי רבא עצמו אמר שההיקש הוא רק לעניין שנה ולא לדבר אחר.

items.text: Mishnah: Combining animal tithes over distance
items.text_en: Mishnah: Combining animal tithes over distance
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that animal tithes combine within a shepherd's visual range (16 mil). If animals are 32 mil apart, they do not combine. If the owner has animals in between, he can tithe them in the middle. Rabbi Meir adds that the Jordan River interrupts for animal tithe.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that animal tithes combine within the distance a grazing animal can walk (16 mil).
The Mishnah adds that if the distance between the animals is 32 mil, they do not combine.
The Mishnah states that if the owner has animals in the middle, he brings them all and tithes them in the middle.
Rabbi Meir adds that the Jordan River interrupts for animal tithe.

items.text: Gemara: Source for 16 mil
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for 16 mil
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the 16-mil distance. Rabbah bar Sheila cites the verse 'עוֹד תַּעֲבֹרְנָה הַצֹּאן עַל יְדֵי מוֹנֶה', and the Sages determined that a shepherd's eye can see that far.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source of the 16-mil distance for joining flocks.
Rabbah bar Sheila cites the verse 'עוֹד תַּעֲבֹרְנָה הַצֹּאן עַל יְדֵי מוֹנֶה' and explains that the Sages determined a shepherd's eye can see up to 16 mil.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the 32-mil case and intermediate animals
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the 32-mil case and intermediate animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 32 mil as not combining, implying less does combine, but earlier it said 16 mil is the limit. It explains the Mishnah's phrasing is to introduce the case of intermediate animals. Rav says five from each side and five in the middle combine, while Shmuel says even five from each side and one in the middle suffices, as the shepherd can see it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 32 mil as not combining, implying less does combine, when earlier it said 16 mil is the limit.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah mentions 32 mil only to introduce the case of intermediate animals.
The Gemara asks how many animals must be in the middle to combine the flocks.
Rav says five from each side and five in the middle combine, as the middle five are fit for both sides.
Shmuel says even five from each side and one in the middle suffices, as the shepherd can see it and count it.

items.text: Challenge to Rav's ruling
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav's ruling
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that challenges Rav's position: if one has five animals in Kfar Hananya and five in Kfar Otni, they do not combine unless he also has one in Tzippori. This is presented as a refutation of Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a baraita as an objection to Rav: if one has five animals in Kfar Hananya and five in Kfar Otni, they do not combine unless he also has one in Tzippori, which is presented as a refutation of Rav.

items.text: Shmuel's resolution of the challenge
items.text_en: Shmuel's resolution of the challenge
items.desc_en: Shmuel explains the baraita according to Rav's view: it refers to a case where there are nine animals on each side and one in the middle, which can join either side.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel resolves the challenge to Rav by explaining that the baraita refers to nine animals on each side with one in the middle, which can join either side.

items.text: Rav Pappa's extension of Shmuel's principle
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's extension of Shmuel's principle
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that according to Shmuel, even a shepherd can combine the animals, and even the shepherd's dog can combine them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that according to Shmuel, even a shepherd or his implements can combine the flocks.

items.text: Rav Ashi's inquiry about the shepherd's dog
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's inquiry about the shepherd's dog
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether the shepherd's dog combines the animals, since it comes when called, or perhaps sometimes it does not come and the shepherd must go fetch it. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether the shepherd's dog combines the animals, since it comes when called, or perhaps sometimes it does not come and the shepherd must go fetch it. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Rabbi Meir's ruling on the Jordan River
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's ruling on the Jordan River
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir says the Jordan River interrupts for ma'aser behemah. Rabbi Ammi qualifies this: only if there is no bridge, but if there is a bridge, it combines them.

sub.desc_en: רבי מאיר (Rabbi Meir) rules that the Jordan River interrupts the combination of flocks for מעשר בהמה (animal tithe).
רבי אמי (Rabbi Ammi) qualifies that the river only divides when there is no bridge; a bridge combines the flocks.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Ammi from a baraita
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Ammi from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rabbi Ammi's statement that the issue is proximity. A baraita is brought: animals on opposite sides of the Jordan or two valleys do not combine, and certainly not outside the land. This challenges Rabbi Ammi, as outside the land is like a place with a bridge, yet it says they do not combine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rabbi Ammi's statement that the Jordan River's partition is due to lack of proximity.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: animals on opposite sides of the Jordan or in two valleys do not combine, and certainly not outside the land.
The Gemara challenges: outside the land is like a place with a bridge, yet the baraita says they do not combine, contradicting Rabbi Ammi.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative explanation for Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative explanation for Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Meir's reasoning: the verse 'the Jordan shall border it on the east' indicates that Scripture made it a separate boundary.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan provides an alternative explanation for Rabbi Meir's ruling: the verse 'והירדן יגבל אותו' (the Jordan shall border it) shows that Scripture made the Jordan a separate boundary, not merely a physical obstacle.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the boundary concept
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the boundary concept
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that other boundaries are also described with similar language, but distinguishes: regarding the land, all of Eretz Yisrael is one boundary, but the Jordan is not considered land, as the verse says 'land' and not 'Jordan'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Jordan is a separate boundary, then other boundary descriptions like 'the border was drawn' should also create separate boundaries, which is absurd.

The Gemara answers that the case of tribal boundaries is different because the verse 'this shall be your land according to its borders round about' teaches that all of Eretz Yisrael is one single boundary.
The Gemara objects that if all of Eretz Yisrael is one boundary, then the Jordan should also be included, but the verse says 'land' and not 'Jordan', excluding the river.

items.text: Difficulty with Rabbi Ammi's position
items.text_en: Difficulty with Rabbi Ammi's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's explanation, it makes sense that the Mishnah specifically mentions the Jordan, but according to Rabbi Ammi, why not teach all rivers? This remains a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: according to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's explanation, it makes sense that the Mishnah specifically mentions the Jordan, but according to Rabbi Ammi, why not teach all rivers? This remains a difficulty.

items.text: מחלוקת תנאים: האם הירדן חלק מארץ כנען
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about the Jordan's status
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute may be between Tannaim: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira holds that the Jordan is not part of Eretz Canaan, while Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai holds that it is, based on verses.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שבה נחלקו רבי יהודה בן בתירה ורבי שמעון בן יוחאי בשאלה אם הירדן נחשב חלק מארץ כנען. רבי יהודה סובר שהירדן אינו ארץ כנען, ואילו רבי שמעון למד מיריחו שגם הירדן בכלל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute about the Jordan's status may be between Tannaim, citing Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira who holds that the Jordan is not part of Eretz Canaan based on the verse 'אַרְצָה' (into the land).
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא הפותחת בדברי רבי יהודה בן בתירה, הדורש את הפסוק 'כי אתם עוברים את הירדן ארצה כנען' ומוכיח שהירדן אינו חלק מארץ כנען.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai argues that the Jordan is part of Eretz Canaan, using a verbal analogy from Jericho to the Jordan based on the verse 'מֵעֵבֶר לְיַרְדֵּן יְרֵחוֹ' (beyond the Jordan at Jericho).
sub.desc: רבי שמעון בן יוחאי חולק ומביא ראיה מפסוק אחר, 'מעבר לירדן יריחו קדמה מזרחה', ומקיש: כשם שיריחו ארץ כנען, כך גם הירדן.

items.text: Definition of the Jordan for ma'aser behemah
items.text_en: Definition of the Jordan for ma'aser behemah
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that 'Jordan' only refers to the area from Beit Yericho downward. The Gemara clarifies that this applies to ma'aser behemah, not to vows, where one follows common language.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana (Rabba bar bar Chana) in the name of רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) states that the name 'Jordan' applies only from Beit Yericho downward.
The Gemara asks: For what halakhic matter is this statement relevant?
The Gemara considers: If it were for a vow, one follows common language, so anywhere called 'Jordan' would be forbidden.
The Gemara resolves: Rather, the statement applies to מעשר בהמה (animal tithe).

items.text: Supporting baraita on the Jordan's course
items.text_en: Supporting baraita on the Jordan's course
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that describes the Jordan's course from the Cave of Pamyas through various seas, and confirms that 'Jordan' only refers to the area from Beit Yericho downward.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that describes the Jordan's course from the Cave of Pamyas through various seas, and confirms that 'Jordan' only refers to the area from Beit Yericho downward.

items.text: Etymology of the name 'Jordan'
items.text_en: Etymology of the name 'Jordan'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Jordan is named because it descends from Dan. Rabbi Abba tells Rav Ashi that they learn this from a verse about Leshem being called Dan, and Rabbi Yitzchak identifies Leshem as Pamyas, from which the Jordan emerges.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan asks why the river is called ירדן (Jordan) and answers that it descends from דן (Dan).
Rabbi Abba tells Rav Ashi that they derive the connection from the verse where Leshem is renamed Dan.
Rabbi Yitzchak identifies Leshem as Pamyas, and a baraita confirms that the Jordan emerges from the Cave of Pamyas.

items.text: Rav Kahana's ruling on vows regarding the Jordan
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's ruling on vows regarding the Jordan
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana states that the 'remembrance' of the Jordan is from the Cave of Pamyas: if one vows not to drink from the Cave of Pamyas, he is forbidden from all the Jordan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana rules that the 'remembrance' of the Jordan is from the Cave of Pamyas, so a vow not to drink from the Cave of Pamyas forbids all Jordan water.

items.text: Remembrance of blood and liver
items.text_en: Remembrance of blood and liver
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the 'remembrance' of blood is the liver, as per Rabbi Yitzchak: a liver that has dissolved conveys impurity in a quarter-log.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the 'remembrance' of blood is the liver, citing Rabbi Yitzchak's ruling that a liver that has dissolved conveys impurity in a quarter-log.

items.text: Remembrance of water and the Euphrates
items.text_en: Remembrance of water and the Euphrates
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the 'remembrance' of water is the Euphrates, as per Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: one who vows from the waters of the Euphrates is forbidden from all waters of the world. The Gemara clarifies that this applies when one says 'from waters that come from the Euphrates', since all rivers are below three rivers, and those three are below the Euphrates.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana states that the 'remembrance' of water is the Euphrates, citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav that one who vows from the waters of the Euphrates is forbidden from all waters of the world.
The Gemara asks what the circumstances are, and clarifies that if one says 'I will not drink from the water of the Euphrates', only the Euphrates is forbidden, not other rivers.

The Gemara explains that the vow applies when one says 'from waters that come from the Euphrates', citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav that all rivers are below three rivers, and those three are below the Euphrates.

items.text: דיון על מקור מי הפרת ומעיינות הסמוכים לו
items.text_en: Identifying the Euphrates' source
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya identifies the 'eyes that are raised' as the sluices of the Euphrates. The Gemara objects that the Euphrates is listed among the four rivers of Eden, implying it is a single river. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak or Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that the Euphrates mentioned in Genesis is the original river, distinct from its later branches.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על דברי רב משרשיא, הטוען שמעיינות גבוהים נובעים ממי הפרת, מהפסוק בספר בראשית המונה את הפרת כאחרון הנהרות. רב נחמן בר יצחק (או רב אחא בר יעקב) מתרץ שהכוונה לפרת המקורי שממנו התפצלו שאר הנהרות.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya identifies the 'eyes that are raised' as the sluices of the Euphrates.
sub.desc: רב משרשיא טוען שמעיינות גבוהים נובעים ממי הפרת דרך סולמות תת-קרקעיים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Euphrates is listed as the fourth river of Eden, implying it is a single river, not the source of others.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מהפסוק המונה את הפרת כאחרון הנהרות, מה שמראה שאינו המקור.

sub.text: רב נחמן בר יצחק (או רב אחא בר יעקב)
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak / Rav Acha bar Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak or Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that the Euphrates mentioned in Genesis is the original river, distinct from its later branches.
sub.desc: רב נחמן בר יצחק (או רב אחא בר יעקב) מתרץ שהכוונה לפרת המקורי שממנו התפצלו שאר הנהרות.

items.text: ברייתא על שם הפרת ומחלוקת אמוראים על מקור מימיו
items.text_en: The name 'Perat' and its blessing
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Meir explaining that the river was originally called 'Yubal' but is called 'Perat' because its waters are fruitful and multiply. This supports Shmuel's view that a river is blessed from its source, and contradicts Rav's view that rain in the west is a great witness for the Euphrates.
items.desc: ברייתא בשם רבי מאיר מבארת ששמו של הפרת הוא 'יובל' על שם הפסוק בירמיהו, ושמו 'פרת' משום שמימיו פרים ורבים. הגמרא מציינת שדברי רבי מאיר מסייעים לשמואל הסובר שהנהר מתברך ממימיו עצמו, וחולקים על רב הסובר שגשמים במערב הם העדות הגדולה לפרת.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Meir explaining that the river was originally called 'Yubal' but is called 'Perat' because its waters are fruitful and multiply.
sub.desc: ברייתא בשם רבי מאיר מבארת ששמו של הפרת הוא 'יובל' על שם הפסוק בירמיהו, ושמו 'פרת' משום שמימיו פרים ורבים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Meir's statement supports Shmuel's view that a river is blessed from its source, and contradicts Rav's view that rain in the west is a great witness for the Euphrates.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציינת שדברי רבי מאיר מסייעים לשמואל הסובר שהנהר מתברך ממימיו עצמו, וחולקים על רב הסובר שגשמים במערב הם העדות הגדולה לפרת.

items.text: מעשה אביו של שמואל וסתירה בדברי שמואל
items.text_en: Shmuel's father's practice and Shmuel's own ruling
items.desc_en: Shmuel's father would make mikvaot for his daughters in Nisan and open them in Tishrei. In Nisan he followed Rav's concern that rainwater might become the majority over flowing water, invalidating the mikveh. In Tishrei he opened them, but this contradicts Shmuel's own statement that water is only purified by flowing water in the Euphrates during Tishrei.
items.desc: הגמרא מספרת שאביו של שמואל עשה לבנותיו מקווה בניסן (מחשש שמי גשמים יהיו הרוב) והציב מפצים בתשרי (לצניעות). הגמרא מעירה שדברי שמואל על כך שהנהר מתברך ממימיו סותרים את דבריו במקום אחר, שם הוא אומר שמים מטהרים בזוחלין רק בפרת בתשרי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Shmuel's father would make a ritual bath for his daughters in Nisan, following Rav's concern that rainwater might become the majority over flowing water.
sub.desc: הגמרא מספרת שאביו של שמואל עשה לבנותיו מקווה בניסן, מחשש שמי גשמים יהיו הרוב על מי הנהר הזורם, ולכן לא הסתפק בטבילה בנהר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds that Shmuel's father would open the mats in Tishrei, allowing immersion in the river itself.
sub.desc: הגמרא מוסיפה שאביו של שמואל הציב מפצים בתשרי, לצניעות בנותיו בעת טבילתן בנהר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Shmuel's own ruling — that water is only purified by flowing water in the Euphrates during Tishrei — contradicts his father's practice of making a mikveh in Nisan.
sub.desc: הגמרא מעירה שדברי שמואל על כך שהנהר מתברך ממימיו סותרים את דבריו במקום אחר, שם הוא אומר שמים מטהרים בזוחלין רק בפרת בתשרי.

items.text: משנת הלוקח או ניתן במתנה פטור ממעשר בהמה
items.text_en: Mishnah: Exemption of purchased or gifted animals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an animal acquired through purchase or gift is exempt from the tithe of cattle. The Gemara asks for the source of this law, and Rav Kahana cites a verse: 'The firstborn of your sons you shall give to Me; so shall you do with your ox and your sheep,' implying only animals born in one's possession are subject to the tithe.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שהלוקח או מי שניתן לו במתנה פטור ממעשר בהמה. הגמרא דורשת את הפסוק 'בכור בניך תתן לי כן תעשה לשורך לצאנך' כדי ללמוד שהחיוב חל רק על הנולדים ברשותו, לא על קנויים או מתנה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an animal acquired through purchase or gift is exempt from the tithe of cattle.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת וקובעת שהלוקח או מי שניתן לו במתנה פטור ממעשר בהמה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of this law.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה המקור לדין זה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana cites the verse 'The firstborn of your sons you shall give to Me; so shall you do with your ox and your sheep,' implying only animals born in one's possession are subject to the tithe.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה המקור לדין זה.

items.text: Opening derivation from the verse
items.text_en: Opening derivation from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by deriving that purchased or gifted animals are exempt from tithe, based on a comparison to one's children.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by deriving that purchased or gifted animals are exempt from tithe, based on a comparison to one's children.

items.text: Applying the verse to tithe
items.text_en: Applying the verse to tithe
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the verse applies to tithe, since it is written about firstborn. It answers that the phrase "כֵּן תַּעֲשֶׂה" teaches that the law of purchase exemption applies to animal tithe as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the verse applies to tithe, since it is written about firstborn.
The Gemara answers that the phrase "כֵּן תַּעֲשֶׂה" teaches that the law of purchase exemption applies to animal tithe as well.

items.text: Rejecting alternative applications
items.text_en: Rejecting alternative applications
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers and rejects applying the verse to sin-offerings, peace-offerings, or the festival burnt-offering, based on analogies to one's son.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests applying the verse to sin-offerings and guilt-offerings, arguing that like a son, they are not brought for a sin.
The Gemara suggests applying the verse to burnt-offerings and peace-offerings, arguing that like a son, they are not brought by vow or gift.
The Gemara suggests applying the verse to the festival burnt-offering, arguing that like a son, it has no fixed time.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Asi's statement
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Asi's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the blanket exemption of purchased animals, citing Rabbi Asi's ruling that ten fetuses purchased in utero are subject to tithe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the blanket exemption of purchased animals from tithe, citing Rabbi Asi's ruling that ten fetuses purchased in utero are subject to tithe.

items.text: Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by interpreting the verse "תַּעֲשֶׂה" to mean that the exemption applies only at the time of tithing, not to animals purchased before birth.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by interpreting the verse 'תַּעֲשֶׂה' (you shall do) to mean that the exemption for purchased animals applies only at the time of tithing, not to animals purchased before birth.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's support and challenge
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's support and challenge
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar supports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling with the same verse, but Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim challenges him with a mishnah that purchase applies to a מחוסר זמן (an animal not yet of age).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that ten purchased fetuses enter the pen for tithing.
The Gemara objects that the mishna explicitly exempts purchased animals from tithe.
Rabbi Elazar supports Rabbi Yochanan by citing the verse 'תעשה' (you shall do), explaining that the exclusion of purchased animals applies only at the time of doing.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim challenges Rabbi Elazar with a baraita that the exemption of a purchased animal applies even to a מחוסר זמן (an animal not yet of age).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar dismisses the challenge, suggesting the mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda who holds that a מחוסר זמן is considered like a firstborn and can enter the pen for tithe.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar dismisses the challenge, suggesting the mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda who holds that a מחוסר זמן is considered like a firstborn and can enter the pen for tithe.

items.text: ברייתא על אתנן זונה והתירוץ על סמך דברי רבי יוחנן
items.text_en: Final objection and resolution
items.desc_en: A Tanna cites a case of a harlot's hire that enters the pen, but the Gemara notes the purchase exemption applies. The Gemara concludes by reaffirming Rabbi Asi's ruling about fetuses.
items.desc: תנא שונה ברייתא לפני רב: איזהו אתנן שנכנס לדיר להתעשר? כל שנתנו לה וחזר ולקחו הימנה. הקושיה: הרי נפסל בלקוח! הגמרא מתרצת שדברי רבי אסי בשם רבי יוחנן על עוברים שנרכשו נשמטו ממנו, כלומר הברייתא עוסקת במקרה שהחזיר ולקח בעודו במעי אימו.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches before Rav that the hire of a harlot which enters the pen for tithing is any animal given to her and then bought back from her.
sub.desc: תנא שונה ברייתא לפני רב המגדירה אתנן זונה שנכנס לדיר להתעשר כזה שנתנו לה וחזר ולקחו ממנה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the animal should be disqualified as a purchase, exempt from tithe.
sub.desc: תנא שונה ברייתא לפני רב המגדירה אתנן זונה שנכנס לדיר להתעשר כזה שנתנו לה וחזר ולקחו ממנה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Tanna overlooked the ruling of Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan that purchased fetuses enter the pen, so the baraita refers to a fetus bought back from the harlot.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שדברי רבי אסי בשם רבי יוחנן על עוברים שנרכשו נשמטו מהתנא, כלומר הברייתא עוסקת במקרה שהחזיר ולקח בעודו במעי אימו.

items.text: דין אתנן זונה: גויה לעומת ישראלית
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of etnan for a Jewish vs. gentile harlot
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies a gentile harlot, suggesting it could have taught a Jewish harlot. It cites Abaye's distinction: a gentile harlot's hire is forbidden, but a priest who cohabits with her is not flogged for 'lo yechallel zar'o'; a Jewish harlot's hire is permitted, but the priest is flogged. The Gemara derives the prohibition from a gezerah shavah of 'to'evah' from forbidden relations, limiting it to cases where kiddushin cannot take effect.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת מדוע יש צורך לקנות את הבהמה בחזרה מהזונה כדי שתהיה חייבת במעשר, ומסבירה שהברייתא עוסקת בזונה גויה. לאחר מכן מובאת מחלוקת אבאי: בזונה גויה האתנן אסור, ובזונה ישראלית מותר, תוך דיון בטעם האיסור ובחיוב המלקות לכהן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita must refer to a gentile harlot; let the harlot tithe the animal herself.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע יש צורך לקנות את הבהמה בחזרה מהזונה, והלא היא עצמה יכולה לעשרה, ומתרצת שהברייתא עוסקת בזונה גויה שאינה בת חיוב מעשר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: let the baraita establish the case with a Jewish harlot, and it teaches that a Jewish harlot's hire is not considered etnan.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אפשר היה להעמיד את הברייתא בזונה ישראלית, והיא עצמה תעשר את הבהמה, ומתרצת שהברייתא מלמדת שאתנן זונה ישראלית אינו אסור.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states the distinction: a gentile harlot's hire is forbidden, but a priest who cohabits with her is not flogged; a Jewish harlot's hire is permitted, but the priest is flogged.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה את שיטת אביי המבחין בין זונה גויה שאתננה אסור וכהן הבא עליה פטור ממלקות, לבין זונה ישראלית שאתננה מותר וכהן הבא עליה לוקה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives the prohibition of a gentile harlot's hire via a gezerah shavah of 'to'evah' from forbidden relations, limiting it to cases where kiddushin cannot take effect.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבארת את טעם האיסור באתנן זונה גויה: גזירה שווה מתיבת 'תועבה' האמורה בעריות, ללמד שדין אתנן נוהג רק במי שאין קידושין תופסין בה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a priest who cohabits with a gentile harlot is not flogged because the offspring are not considered his seed.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבארת מדוע כהן הבא על זונה גויה פטור ממלקות משום 'לא יחלל זרעו': הוולד אינו נחשב לזרעו של הכהן כי הוא גוי.

items.text: משנת האחין והשותפין
items.text_en: Mishnah: Brothers and partners regarding kalbon and animal tithe
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that brothers and partners who are liable for the half-shekel (kalbon) are exempt from animal tithe, and vice versa. If they acquired animals from the joint estate, they are liable; otherwise, they are exempt. If they divided and then repartnered, they are liable for kalbon but exempt from animal tithe.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שאחים ושותפים חייבים בקלבון ופטורים ממעשר בהמה, ולהיפך. היא מפרטת שאם קנו מתפיסת הבית חייבים במעשר, ואם חלקו וחזרו ונשתתפו חייבים בקלבון ופטורים ממעשר.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: brothers and partners liable for the half-shekel (קלבון) are exempt from animal tithe, and vice versa.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בכלל: אחים ושותפים חייבים בקלבון ופטורים ממעשר בהמה, ולהיפך.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah clarifies that animals acquired from the joint estate obligate tithe; if divided and repartnered, they are liable for the premium and exempt from animal tithe.
sub.desc: המשנה מפרטת: קנו מתפיסת הבית חייבים במעשר; חלקו וחזרו ונשתתפו חייבים בקלבון ופטורים ממעשר.

items.text: דרשת הפסוקים: מעשר בהמה בשותפות
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of exemption for partners from animal tithe
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from 'yihyeh lecha' that animal tithe does not apply to partnership animals. It questions that this verse is written about the firstborn, but answers that since the firstborn already applies to partnerships, the verse is applied to animal tithe instead.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא הדורשת את הפסוק 'יהיה לך' להוציא שותפות ממעשר בהמה, אך כוללת קניין מתפיסת הבית. נשאלת קושיה שהפסוק עוסק בבכור, והתשובה היא שאם אינו ענין לבכור, תנהו ענין למעשר בהמה.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verse 'יִהְיֶה לְךָ' (it shall be yours) that animal tithe applies only to individually owned animals, not partnership animals, and includes those acquired through inheritance from the father's house.
sub.desc: הברייתא דורשת את הפסוק 'יהיה לך' להוציא שותפות ממעשר בהמה, אך כוללת קניין מתפיסת הבית.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse 'יִהְיֶה לְךָ' is written regarding firstborn animals, not animal tithe.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שהפסוק הנדון עוסק בבכור, לא במעשר בהמה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that since the firstborn obligation already applies to partnerships (as per the verse 'וּבְכוֹרוֹת בְּקַרְכֶם וְצֹאנְכֶם'), the verse is applied instead to animal tithe, teaching that it does not apply to partnership animals.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שהפסוק הנדון עוסק בבכור, לא במעשר בהמה.

items.text: פירוט רבי ירמיה: ארבעה מצבים
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah's four cases and the Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah enumerates four scenarios: liable for both (divided money but not animals), exempt from both (divided animals but not money), liable for kalbon but exempt from tithe (divided both), and liable for tithe but exempt from kalbon (divided neither). The Gemara questions the obviousness of the second case, explaining that it was necessary to teach that dividing animals does not imply intent to divide the entire partnership, so they remain exempt from kalbon.
items.desc: רבי ירמיה מפרט ארבעה מצבים של שותפים: חייבים בשניהם (חלקו בכספים ולא בבהמה), פטורים משניהם (חלקו בבהמה ולא בכספים), חייבים בקלבון ופטורים ממעשר (חלקו בשניהם), וחייבים במעשר ופטורים מקלבון (לא חלקו כלל). הגמרא מסבירה שהחידוש הוא במקרה שחלקו בבהמה ולא בכספים.

sub.desc_en: רבי ירמיה (Rabbi Yirmeyah) introduces four possible scenarios regarding liability for the premium (קלבון) and animal tithe (מעשר בהמה).
sub.desc: רבי ירמיה פותח ואומר שיש ארבעה מצבים אפשריים לגבי חיוב שותפים בקלבון ובמעשר בהמה.

sub.desc_en: רבי ירמיה (Rabbi Yirmeyah) explains the first two cases: liable for both when they divided money but not animals, exempt from both when they divided animals but not money.
sub.desc: רבי ירמיה מבאר את המצב הראשון: חייבים בשניהם כשחלקו בכספים ולא בבהמה; ואת המצב השני: פטורים משניהם כשחלקו בבהמה ולא בכספים.

sub.desc_en: רבי ירמיה (Rabbi Yirmeyah) explains the third case: liable for the premium and exempt from tithe when they divided both money and animals.
sub.desc: רבי ירמיה מבאר את המצב השלישי: חייבים בקלבון ופטורים ממעשר כשחלקו גם בכספים וגם בבהמה.

sub.desc_en: רבי ירמיה (Rabbi Yirmeyah) explains the fourth case: liable for tithe and exempt from the premium when they divided neither money nor animals.
sub.desc: רבי ירמיה מבאר את המצב הרביעי: חייבים במעשר ופטורים מקלבון כשלא חלקו כלל לא בכספים ולא בבהמה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the obviousness of the second case, suggesting that dividing animals might indicate intent to divide the entire estate, thus obligating them in the premium.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: פשיטא? ומסבירה שהחידוש הוא במקרה שחלקו בבהמה ולא בכספים, שהיה מקום לחשוב שכיוון שחלקו בבהמה גילו דעתם לחלוק ויתחייבו בקלבון, וקא משמע לן שאינו כן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case was necessary to teach that dividing animals does not imply intent to divide the entire partnership, so they remain exempt from the premium.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: פשיטא? ומסבירה שהחידוש הוא במקרה שחלקו בבהמה ולא בכספים, שהיה מקום לחשוב שכיוון שחלקו בבהמה גילו דעתם לחלוק ויתחייבו בקלבון, וקא משמע לן שאינו כן.

items.text: מחלוקת אמוראים: מתי חלוקה נחשבת כשותפות
items.text_en: Dispute among Rav Anan, Rav Nachman, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rav Anan limits the Mishnah's ruling that dividing animals exempts from kalbon to cases where they divided dissimilar animals (e.g., kids vs. rams), but if they divided like for like, each can claim his original share, so they are liable. Rav Nachman disagrees, holding that even with like for like, they cannot claim original shares. Rabbi Elazar limits the exemption to unequal divisions (e.g., nine vs. ten), but equal divisions allow claiming original shares. Rabbi Yochanan holds that even equal divisions do not allow claiming original shares.
items.desc: רב ענן ורב נחמן נחלקים לגבי חלוקה שווה (גדיים כנגד גדיים): רב ענן סובר שאז אין נחשבים כשותפים, ורב נחמן סובר שגם אז נחשבים. רבי אלעזר ורבי יוחנן נחלקים באופן דומה לגבי חלוקה במספרים שווים (תשעה כנגד תשעה).

sub.desc_en: Rav Anan limits the Mishnah's exemption from kalbon to cases where they divided dissimilar animals (kids vs. rams), but if they divided like for like, each can claim his original share, so they are liable.
sub.desc: רב ענן מבחין בין חלוקה במינים שונים, הנחשבת כשותפות, לבין חלוקה שווה באותו מין, הנחשבת כחלוקה רגילה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman disagrees, holding that even with like-for-like division, they cannot claim original shares, so they are exempt from kalbon.
sub.desc: רב נחמן חולק וסובר שגם בחלוקה שווה באותו מין אין אומרים שזה חלקו הראשון, והם נחשבים כשותפים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar limits the exemption to unequal divisions (e.g., nine vs. ten), but equal divisions allow claiming original shares, so they are liable.
sub.desc: רבי אלעזר מביא מחלוקת מקבילה לגבי מספרים לא שווים: חלוקה במספרים שונים נחשבת כשותפות, אך במספרים שווים – לא.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan holds that even equal divisions do not allow claiming original shares, so they are exempt from kalbon.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן חולק וסובר שגם בחלוקה שווה במספרים אין אומרים שזה חלקו הראשון, והם נחשבים כשותפים.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle and its necessity
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's principle and its necessity
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan's statement about brothers being purchasers aligns with his view that they return property in the Jubilee. It then justifies why both the case of animals and the case of land are needed to teach this principle.

items.text: Objection from partners dividing and Rav Ashi's answer
items.text_en: Objection from partners dividing and Rav Ashi's answer
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita about partners dividing animals, where one takes ten and the other nine with a dog, and the animals opposite the dog are forbidden. If there is retroactive clarification, one could clarify which animal is with the dog. Rav Ashi answers that the case is where the animals are not all equal, and the dog is worth slightly more than one animal, so the extra value spreads across all.

items.text: Mishnah: Animals excluded from the pen for tithing
items.text_en: Mishnah: Animals excluded from the pen for tithing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists animals that do not enter the pen for tithing: kil'ayim, tereifah, yotzei dofen, mechusar zeman, and a yatom. It defines a yatom as one whose mother was slaughtered and then gave birth. Rabbi Yehoshua adds that even if the mother was slaughtered and the placenta remains, it is not a yatom.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of the exceptions from verses
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of the exceptions from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the exceptions from the verse: 'shor o khesev' excludes kil'ayim, 'o ez' excludes a nidmeh, 'ki yivaled' excludes yotzei dofen, 'vehayah shiv'at yamim' excludes mechusar zeman, 'tachat imo' excludes a yatom. Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka uses a gezeirah shavah of 'tachat' from the consecrated animals to include tereifah.

items.text: Inclusion of other animals and the dispute about tumtum and androginos
items.text_en: Inclusion of other animals and the dispute about tumtum and androginos
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'hakol' includes, and answers it includes the animals listed in a baraita: rove'a, nirba, muktzah, ne'evad, etnan, mechir, tumtum, and androginos. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Shimon that tumtum and androginos do not enter. The Gemara explains the derivation: a gezeirah shavah from consecrated animals, but the Torah explicitly includes these via the verse 'ki mashchatam bahem mum bam', and the principle that wherever 'hashchata' is stated it refers to arayot or avodah zarah. Since ma'aser is not invalidated by a mum, arayot and avodah zarah do not invalidate it. Rove'a and nirba are arayot, muktzah and ne'evad are avodah zarah, etnan is arayot, mechir is linked to etnan. Tumtum and androginos are a safek, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda holds that the Torah excluded safek from consecrated animals, and ma'aser learns from them via gezeirah shavah.

items.text: Another baraita and the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Another baraita and the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: A baraita is taught: all enter the pen except kil'ayim and tereifah, according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabbi Akiva says he heard from him also yotzei dofen, mechusar zeman, and yatom. The Gemara questions the first tanna: if he learns via gezeirah shavah, he should exclude all; if not, how does he know kil'ayim? It answers that he does learn the gezeirah shavah, and regarding yotzei dofen...

items.text: Aggadic digression: unusual cases and natural wonders
items.text_en: Aggadic digression: unusual cases and natural wonders
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts several unusual cases: a pig with sixty ribs, a massive cedar log, and a giant egg of the Bar Yochani bird. It concludes with Rav Ashi's explanation that the egg was a 'muzarta' (a non-viable egg).

items.text: Mishnah: Three gathering points for ma'aser behemah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three gathering points for ma'aser behemah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the three annual times for tithing animals: on the eve of Pesach, Shavuot, and Sukkot, according to Rabbi Akiva. Ben Azzai and Rabbi Elazar/Rabbi Shimon offer alternative dates. The Mishnah explains why the third date is not on Rosh Hashanah but on 29 Elul, and discusses the rules of joining animals from different periods.

items.text: Gemara: Reason for three gathering points and their timing
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason for three gathering points and their timing
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why there are three gathering points, and Rabba bar Sheila answers: corresponding to the three seasons (winter, spring, summer). It then asks why these specific times, and Rabbi Tanchum bar Chiyya begins to answer.

items.text: Opening explanation of the Mishnah's rationale
items.text_en: Opening explanation of the Mishnah's rationale
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's rule allowing sale and slaughter before the 'goren' (threshing floor) is because one prefers that a mitzvah be done with his money, and then he can buy and eat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's rule allowing sale and slaughter before the goren is so that animals are available for pilgrims, and one prefers that a mitzvah be done with his money, then he can buy and eat.

items.text: Definition of 'goren' and 'paras'
items.text_en: Definition of 'goren' and 'paras'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the term 'goren' is used, answering that the untithed produce is like a threshing floor. It then defines 'paras' as at least fifteen days, based on Rabbi Yossi bar Yehuda, and Rabbi Abahu explains 'paras' means half, specifically half of the thirty-day period before Passover when laws are studied.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the term 'goren' (threshing floor) is used for the period when tithes are forbidden.
The Gemara answers that the untithed produce is like a threshing floor, hence the term.
The Gemara asks how long the 'paras' period is.
Rabbi Yossi bar Yehuda defines 'paras' as at least fifteen days.
The Gemara asks what the scriptural or logical source is for this definition.
Rabbi Abahu explains that 'paras' means half, specifically half of the thirty-day period before Passover when laws are studied, citing a baraita.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel provides an alternative opinion that the period is two weeks (fourteen days).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Ben Azzai on Adar dates
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Ben Azzai on Adar dates
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Ben Azzai regarding the date for tithing: Rabbi Akiva holds that Adar near Nisan can be full or deficient, so no fixed date; Ben Azzai holds it is always deficient, so a fixed date on the 29th of Adar.

sub.desc_en: Ben Azzai states the dates for tithing: on the 29th of Adar and the 1st of Sivan.
The Gemara asks what is the point of dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Ben Azzai.
The Gemara explains: Rabbi Akiva holds that Adar near Nisan can be full or deficient, so no fixed date; Ben Azzai holds it is always deficient, so a fixed date on the 29th of Adar.

items.text: Explanation of Ben Azzai's dates for Elul and Av
items.text_en: Explanation of Ben Azzai's dates for Elul and Av
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Ben Azzai sets the date for Elul-born animals on the 29th of Elul: because Elul animals are tithed separately, and the 30th is avoided due to the possibility of Av being deficient, requiring a distinction between new and old.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the date of the first of Sivan is chosen because Elul-born animals are few, and if one were to tithe earlier, the animals would not be fully grown by the festival.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Ben Azzai's principle
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Ben Azzai's principle
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Ben Azzai's date for Elul-born animals on the 29th of Av follows his own view that Elul-born animals are tithed separately.
The Gemara asks why the tithing is not done on the 30th of Av, and answers that Av may be deficient, requiring a distinction between new and old animals.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's opinion and reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's opinion and reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon set dates on the 1st of Nisan (like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel), 1st of Sivan, and 29th of Elul (because they hold Rosh Hashanah for animal tithe is 1st of Tishrei). They give two reasons for not tithing on 1st Tishrei: to distinguish new and old, and because it is a Yom Tov when tithing is impossible due to counting (sekarta).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's opinion that the dates for animal tithe are the 1st of Nisan, 1st of Sivan, and 29th of Elul.
The Gemara explains that the 1st of Nisan follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view (two weeks before Pesach), and the 1st of Sivan follows the earlier reasoning.
The Gemara explains that the 29th of Elul follows Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's own view that Rosh Hashanah for animal tithe is the 1st of Tishrei.
The Gemara asks why they set the date on the 29th of Elul rather than the 1st of Tishrei, and suggests it is to distinguish new and old animals.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon gave two reasons: to distinguish new and old, and because the 1st of Tishrei is a Yom Tov when tithing is impossible due to counting (סקרתא).

items.text: Ben Azzai's ruling and its source
items.text_en: Ben Azzai's ruling and its source
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir sets the new year for animal tithe on 1st Elul, while Ben Azzai says Elul animals are tithed separately. A baraita quotes Ben Azzai saying that since the sages disagree, Elul animals are tithed alone. The Gemara questions why he doesn't decide which opinion is more reasonable, and notes his humility. Rabbi Yochanan says this ruling is a tradition from the prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Meir's ruling that the new year for animal tithe is 1st Elul, and Ben Azzai's dissenting view.
A baraita quotes Ben Azzai explaining that because the sages disagree, Elul animals are tithed separately.
The Gemara questions why Ben Azzai does not decide which opinion is more reasonable, and anticipates the objection that he might not understand their reasoning.
The Gemara rejects that objection by citing a baraita where Ben Azzai claims all sages are like garlic peel to him, showing his confidence in understanding their reasoning.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves that Ben Azzai's ruling is a tradition received from the prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, not his own reasoning.

items.text: Practical application of Ben Azzai's principle and Rava's ruling
items.text_en: Practical application of Ben Azzai's principle and Rava's ruling
items.desc_en: A baraita explains Ben Azzai's principle: animals born in Av and Elul do not combine, nor do Elul and Tishrei, but Av and Tishrei do combine. The Gemara clarifies this is not obvious, as it teaches that years separate but threshing floors do not. Rava rules that according to Ben Azzai, if one has five born in Av, five in Elul, and five in Tishrei, he gathers them all into the corral to be tithed together.

sub.desc_en: A baraita explains Ben Azzai's principle: animals born in Av and Elul do not combine, nor do Elul and Tishrei, but Av and Tishrei do combine.
The Gemara questions why the baraita is necessary, since the rule seems obvious.
The Gemara answers that one might have thought that just as years separate, threshing floors also separate, so the baraita teaches that they do not.
Rava rules that according to Ben Azzai, if one has five animals born in Av, five in Elul, and five in Tishrei, he gathers them all into the corral to be tithed together.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's first case
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's first case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that if one takes one animal from the Elul group and the rest are exempt, analyzing whether Rosh Hashanah for animal tithe is Elul or Tishrei. It concludes that the Mishnah's case is necessary to prevent a potential error.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling by analyzing the two possible dates for Rosh Hashanah of animal tithe (Elul or Tishrei) and showing that in either case the animals from different months should combine.
The Gemara answers that the animals cannot combine for a different granary because the Torah requires a definite tenth, not a doubtful one.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling is necessary to prevent a decree that one might mistakenly take from the exempted animals.

items.text: Mishnah: Method of tithing animals
items.text_en: Mishnah: Method of tithing animals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the proper procedure for tithing animals: gathering them into a pen with a small opening, counting them one by one, marking the tenth with red paint, and declaring it tithe. It also discusses cases where the procedure is not followed and the dispute between Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages about taking ten from a hundred or one from ten.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking the proper method for tithing animals and describes the procedure: gathering them into a pen with a small opening, counting them, and marking the tenth with red paint.
The Mishnah rules that even if the marking or counting was not done properly, the animals are still tithed.

The Mishnah presents the case of taking ten from a hundred or one from ten, and records the dispute between the Sages (who say it is not tithe) and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda (who says it is tithe).
The Mishnah concludes with the case where a counted animal jumps back into the pen, ruling that the animals are exempt or must graze until blemished and then be eaten by the owners.

items.text: Gemara: The method of counting and the reason for the small opening
items.text_en: Gemara: The method of counting and the reason for the small opening
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the Mishnah's procedure, explaining that the mothers are outside and the lambs inside, so they bleat and the lambs run out to their mothers. It addresses why the lambs cannot be led out, citing the verse 'ya'avor' (it shall pass), and why they cannot be enticed with greens, due to a decree against purchased or orphaned animals.

sub.desc_en: The baraita elaborates on the Mishnah's procedure: the mothers are outside and the lambs inside, so the lambs bleat and run out to their mothers.
The Gemara asks why the lambs cannot simply be led out by hand.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'יַעֲבוֹר' (it shall pass) implies the animal passes on its own, not that it is led.
The Gemara asks why greens cannot be thrown to entice the lambs out.
Rav Huna answers that it is a decree (גזירה) due to purchased or orphaned animals that might be improperly enticed.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of laws from verses and the dispute of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of laws from verses and the dispute of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from verses that a tereifah is exempt from tithe, that counting with a staff is a mitzvah but not essential, and that even without naming it 'tithe' it is sanctified. It then discusses the dispute between Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding taking ten from a hundred or one from ten, explaining that Rabbi Yosei follows Abba Elazar ben Gomel's teaching about two terumot.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites verses to derive that a tereifah is exempt from tithe, that counting with a staff is a mitzvah but not essential, and that even without naming it 'tithe' it is sanctified.

The baraita continues, deriving that even without naming it 'tithe' it is sanctified, and then presents the dispute: the Sages say that taking ten from a hundred or one from ten is not valid tithe, while Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says it is valid.
The Gemara asks: What is the reasoning of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda?

The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda follows Abba Elazar ben Gomel's teaching that the verse 'ונחשב לכם תרומתכם' (and it shall be considered your terumah) refers to two terumot, and just as the great terumah (תרומה גדולה) is taken by estimation and intention, so too the tithe can be taken in a non-standard manner.

items.text: Opening argument: ma'aser behemah taken by estimation and thought
items.text_en: Opening argument: ma'aser behemah taken by estimation and thought
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that just as terumat ma'aser is taken by estimation and thought, so too ma'aser behemah, because the Torah calls ma'aser a 'terumah' and links animal tithe to grain tithe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that just as terumat ma'aser is taken by estimation and thought, so too ma'aser behemah, because the Torah calls ma'aser a 'terumah' and links animal tithe to grain tithe.

items.text: Rava's statement: the tenth is sanctified by itself
items.text_en: Rava's statement: the tenth is sanctified by itself
items.desc_en: Rava asserts that the tenth animal is sanctified automatically. The Gemara asks for the source, citing a baraita that even if one does not call it 'tenth', the verse 'the tenth shall be holy' implies it is holy regardless.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara quotes Rava's statement that the tenth animal is inherently sanctified, and asks: from where does Rava derive this?
The Gemara proposes that Rava's source is a baraita which derives from the verse 'עֲשִׂירִי יִהְיֶה קֹדֶשׁ' that the tenth animal is holy even if not explicitly designated.
The Gemara suggests a baraita: the verse 'the tenth shall be holy' implies sanctity even without verbal designation.

items.text: First objection: perhaps 'holy' was called, not 'tenth'
items.text_en: First objection: perhaps 'holy' was called, not 'tenth'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita might mean he called it 'holy' but not 'tenth', so it does not prove automatic sanctity. It then offers a different baraita: if one called the ninth 'tenth' and the tenth emerged silent, the ninth is eaten with a blemish and the tenth is tithe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita might only require calling it 'holy', not 'tenth', and then proposes a different baraita as Rava's source: if one called the ninth 'tenth' and the tenth emerged without speaking, the ninth is eaten with a blemish and the tenth is tithe.
The Gemara offers a different baraita: if one called the ninth 'tenth' and the tenth emerged silent, the ninth is eaten with a blemish and the tenth is tithe.

items.text: Second objection: perhaps the tenth was identified
items.text_en: Second objection: perhaps the tenth was identified
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita might be different because the tenth was already identified, or because he gestured toward it, not proving automatic sanctity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita might be different because the tenth was clarified or because the owner gestured toward it.

items.text: Third attempt: baraita with a dead tenth
items.text_en: Third attempt: baraita with a dead tenth
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where one called the ninth 'tenth' and the tenth died in the pen: the ninth is eaten with a blemish and all are exempt. The Gemara asks: why are all exempt? Is it not because the tenth was sanctified?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a different baraita as Rava's source: if one called the ninth 'tenth' and the tenth died in the pen, the ninth is eaten with a blemish and all are exempt, implying the tenth was inherently sanctified.
The Gemara asks: why are all exempt? Is it not because the tenth was sanctified?

items.text: Fourth objection: perhaps exempted by proper counting
items.text_en: Fourth objection: perhaps exempted by proper counting
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that perhaps they were exempted because of proper counting, as Rava himself said that proper counting exempts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the exemption might be due to the principle of 'proper counting' (מנין הראוי) which Rava himself holds exempts.

items.text: Fifth attempt: baraita with a surviving tenth and a contradiction
items.text_en: Fifth attempt: baraita with a surviving tenth and a contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where one called the ninth 'tenth' and the tenth remained in the pen: the ninth is eaten with a blemish and the tenth is tithe. But another baraita says the ninth is non-sacred, creating a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes yet another baraita as Rava's source: if one called the ninth 'tenth' and the tenth remained in the pen, the ninth is eaten with a blemish and the tenth is tithe, but another baraita states the ninth is unconsecrated, creating a contradiction.

The Gemara raises a contradiction: another baraita states that the ninth is non-sacred (חולין), conflicting with the first baraita's ruling that the ninth is eaten with a blemish (implying it has some sanctity).

items.text: Resolution: attributed to Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda
items.text_en: Resolution: attributed to Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda
items.desc_en: A tanna recited before Rav Sheshet that the baraita is Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda's opinion in the name of Rabbi Shimon, resolving the contradiction.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna recited before Rav Sheshet that the baraita is attributed to Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon, resolving the contradiction.

items.text: The ninth animal's sanctity and the logical argument
items.text_en: The ninth animal's sanctity and the logical argument
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the Mishnah's statement that the ninth animal is not sanctified unless the name 'tenth' is removed from it. A logical argument is proposed comparing the ninth to the eleventh, but the Gemara rejects this comparison, noting that the eleventh, for which a tenth has been designated, is different from the ninth, for which no tenth has yet been designated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the Mishnah's rule that the ninth animal is not sanctified unless the name 'tenth' is removed from it, and introduces a logical argument.

The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if the eleventh animal, which can sanctify another to be sacrificed, requires removal of the name 'tenth' to be sanctified, then the ninth, which cannot sanctify another, certainly requires it.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of the kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of the kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the kal vachomer: the eleventh is more stringent because it can sanctify another to be sacrificed, so it requires removal of the name 'tenth'; the ninth, which cannot sanctify another, does not require removal.
The Gemara offers an alternative distinction: the eleventh has a designated tenth, so it requires removal of the name 'tenth'; the ninth has no designated tenth yet, so it does not require removal.

items.text: Rava's principle: a valid count exempts
items.text_en: Rava's principle: a valid count exempts
items.desc_en: Rava states that a valid count (מנין הראוי) exempts animals from tithing. The Gemara seeks the source for this principle, initially suggesting a Mishnah where one of the counted animals jumps in, but rejects this due to possible alternative interpretations. Rava then derives it from the verse 'ya'avor' (shall pass), implying that animals that have already passed are exempt, referring to those exempted by a valid count.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that a valid count (מנין הראוי) exempts animals from tithing, and the Gemara asks for the source of this principle.

The Gemara suggests that Rava's principle might be derived from a Mishnah where one of the counted animals jumps in, exempting all, implying the counted animals themselves were exempted by a valid count.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the Mishnah refers to a case where the animals were tithed upon them (i.e., the counted animals were already tithed), not that they were exempted by a valid count.
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that the Mishnah explicitly says 'from the tithed ones' (מן המעושרין), indicating they were already tithed, not that they were exempted by a valid count.
The Gemara further objects that 'מעושרין' might mean 'tithe' specifically, and the Mishnah's ruling that they 'shall graze' (ירעו) supports this interpretation.

Rava resolves the issue by deriving the principle from the verse 'יַעֲבוֹר' (shall pass), implying that animals which have already passed (i.e., exempted by a valid count) are not subject to tithing, and the Gemara concludes that this is indeed the source.

items.text: Supporting baraita for Rava
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rava
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rava's principle: if one had ten lambs, counted five, and one of them died, the ruling depends on whether the dead animal was from the counted or the uncounted group, demonstrating that a valid count exempts.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rava's principle: if one had ten lambs, counted five, and one of them died, the ruling depends on whether the dead animal was from the counted or the uncounted group, demonstrating that a valid count exempts.

items.text: Rava's cases of animals exiting through multiple openings
items.text_en: Rava's cases of animals exiting through multiple openings
items.desc_en: Rava presents several cases involving fourteen lambs exiting through different openings, illustrating the application of 'a valid count exempts' even in situations of uncertainty. The Gemara questions why Rava repeats this teaching, and explains that he is teaching that even a doubtful valid count (ספק מנין הראוי) also exempts.

sub.desc_en: Rava presents the first case: fourteen lambs, six exit one opening, four another, four remain; if the remaining four exited with the six, one is taken and the rest join another threshing floor.
Rava gives the alternative: if not, the six are exempt and the four and four join another threshing floor.

Rava presents the second case: four exit one opening, six another, four remain; if the four exited with the six, one is taken and the rest are exempt; otherwise the four and six are exempt and the four join another threshing floor.

Rava presents the third case: four exit one opening, four another, six remain; if the six exited through one opening, one is taken and the rest are exempt; otherwise the four are exempt and the six join another threshing floor.
The Gemara asks why Rava repeats this teaching, since he already stated the principle of מנין הראוי (a valid count) once.
The Gemara explains that Rava teaches that even a doubtful valid count (ספק מנין הראוי) also exempts, not just a certain one.

items.text: Rava's ruling on fifteen lambs
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on fifteen lambs
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if one has fifteen lambs, he may not select ten and then tithe them, leaving the rest exempt. Rather, he must bring all into the pen, take out ten, and tithe one, with the remainder joining another batch. A baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that with fifteen lambs, one must bring all into the pen, take out ten, and tithe one, with the remainder joining another batch, rather than selecting ten outside the pen.
A baraita is cited in support of Rava's ruling, repeating the same case and conclusion.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Method of tithing
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Method of tithing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not select ten animals and take one, leaving the rest exempt; rather, one must gather all animals into a pen and count them out one by one, with the tenth becoming tithe.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the proper method of animal tithing: one must gather all animals into a pen and count them out one by one, not select ten and take one from them.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution of a contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution of a contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: a baraita says that with nineteen lambs, after taking one from ten, the remaining nine are exempt, not joined to another batch. Rav Huna bar Sehora explains that the baraita deals with a pen with two openings, where nine exit through each, and the one that could go either way is considered. The Gemara considers alternative explanations but concludes that Rav Huna's interpretation is correct, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak praises him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that with nineteen lambs, after taking one from ten, the remaining nine are exempt and do not join another batch.
Rav Huna bar Sehora explains before Rava that the baraita deals with a pen having two openings, where nine exit through each opening and the one remaining lamb is eligible for either.
The Gemara objects: why not explain the baraita as a case where one counted nine and called the tenth 'one' from the start, since the tenth is sanctified automatically?
The Gemara offers another alternative: explain the baraita as dealing with a threshing floor where animals are counted in pairs, since the tenth is sanctified by the count of animals.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak praises Rav Huna bar Sehora's mother for raising a son who explained the tradition at the festival in accordance with its true meaning.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of confusion in counting
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of confusion in counting
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses cases where two animals exit together, or where the count is confused (e.g., calling the ninth 'tenth', etc.). Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda debate whether the eleventh animal is sanctified and can be offered as a peace-offering and effect substitution.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of two animals exiting together, stating that the ninth and tenth are confused.

Rabbi Meir rules that if one miscalls the ninth 'tenth', the tenth 'ninth', and the eleventh 'tenth', all three are sanctified: the ninth is eaten with a blemish, the tenth is ma'aser, and the eleventh is offered as a peace-offering and effects substitution.
Rabbi Yehuda objects: can a substitute animal itself effect substitution? The response from Rabbi Meir's school is that if it were a substitute, it would not be offered.

Rabbi Yehuda concludes: if one calls the ninth 'tenth', the tenth 'tenth', and the eleventh 'tenth', the eleventh is not sanctified, establishing the rule that the eleventh is sanctified only when the name 'tenth' is removed from the actual tenth.

items.text: Gemara: Debate on the principle of counting
items.text_en: Gemara: Debate on the principle of counting
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that when counting in pairs, the tenth animal is sanctified according to its count. Rav Mari and Rav Kahana debate whether this means the tenth in the owner's count or the tenth animal by number. The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah's case of confusion, concluding that Rabbi Yochanan's statement applies only when one intends to count in pairs, not when it happens accidentally. Rava adds that the Persian custom of calling ten 'one' explains a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that when one counts animals in pairs (זוגות) or in groups (קינטרין), the tenth animal is sanctified according to its count.
The Gemara asks what the phrase 'according to its count' (למניינו) means.
Rav Mari explains that the tenth animal is sanctified according to the owner's own count (i.e., the tenth in the sequence of pairs).
Rav Kahana explains that the tenth animal is sanctified according to the actual count of animals (i.e., the tenth animal by number).
The Gemara cites the Mishnah's case where two animals exit together, causing confusion in the count.

The Gemara objects that according to Rav Kahana's view (that the tenth animal by number is sanctified), the Mishnah's confusion should not arise, since the ninth and tenth animals would be correctly identified.
Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that his statement applies only when one intentionally counts in pairs, not when the pairing happens accidentally.
The Gemara brings a baraita about counting backwards, which challenges Rav Mari's view by implying that the tenth animal is called 'one' in the count.
Rava resolves the difficulty by noting that the Persian custom of calling ten 'one' explains why the tenth animal is referred to as 'one' in the count.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one calls the ninth animal 'tenth', the tenth 'ninth', and the eleventh 'tenth', all three are sanctified.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one calls the ninth animal 'tenth', the tenth 'ninth', and the eleventh 'tenth', all three are sanctified.

items.text: Gemara's derivation and objection
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation and objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a verse that only the ninth, tenth, and eleventh are sanctified, not the eighth or twelfth. It then raises a contradiction from a baraita that says the error must be 'designated' like the tenth itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse to derive that only the ninth, tenth, and eleventh are sanctified, and raises the possibility of including the eighth and twelfth.
The Gemara answers that just as the tenth is sanctified only when adjacent to the count, so too its mistaken designation is sanctified only when adjacent.
The Gemara objects with a baraita that requires the error to be 'designated' like the tenth itself, contradicting the previous answer.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by attributing the baraita to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who holds that the eleventh is only sanctified if the owner remained silent about the ninth and then called the tenth 'ninth' and the eleventh 'tenth'. This view aligns with Rabbi Yehuda that tithe error is like a substitute, and with his father that one cannot substitute again.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by attributing the baraita to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who holds that the eleventh is only sanctified if the owner remained silent about the ninth and then called the tenth 'ninth' and the eleventh 'tenth', aligning with Rabbi Yehuda that tithe error is like a substitute (תמורה) and with his father that one cannot substitute again.

items.text: Rava's cases of two animals emerging together
items.text_en: Rava's cases of two animals emerging together
items.desc_en: Rava discusses cases where two animals emerge together in the ninth or tenth count. If two emerge in the ninth and are called 'ninth', the tenth and unconsecrated animals are mixed; if called 'tenth', the tenth and ninth are mixed. Similarly for two in the tenth. The Gemara explains that this teaches that when they emerge simultaneously, both are sanctified even though the name 'tenth' is not removed from the tenth.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens with the first case: two animals emerge in the ninth count; if he calls them 'ninth', the tenth and unconsecrated animals are mixed, because the tenth is sanctified on its own and he is calling the ninth 'ninth'.
Rava adds the second sub-case: if he calls both 'tenth', the tenth and ninth are mixed because he is calling both 'tenth'.
Rava gives the third case: two emerge in the tenth; if called 'tenth', the tenth and eleventh are mixed; if called 'eleventh', the tenth and unconsecrated are mixed.
The Gemara explains that Rava's cases teach that when two emerge simultaneously (בבת אחת), both are sanctified even though the name 'tenth' is not removed from the tenth.

items.text: Rav Ashi's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges Rava's statement from a Mishnah that if the name 'tenth' is not removed, the eleventh is not sanctified. The Gemara answers that this rule applies only when animals emerge one after another, but when they emerge simultaneously, both are sanctified. The 'this is the rule' phrase comes to include a case where the tenth emerged and the owner did not speak.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges Rava's statement by citing the Mishnah's rule that if the name 'tenth' is not removed, the eleventh is not sanctified.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's rule applies only when animals emerge one after another, but when they emerge simultaneously, both are sanctified.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah already explicitly teaches the case of one after another, so what does the phrase 'this is the rule' come to include — perhaps simultaneous emergence?
The Gemara resolves that the phrase 'this is the rule' comes to include a case where the tenth emerged and the owner did not speak, so the name 'tenth' was not removed.

items.text: Support from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Support from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where two animals emerged in the tenth and were called 'tenth', yet the tenth and eleventh are mixed, seemingly contradicting the rule. It resolves that the case is where one animal emerged first and was called 'eleventh', then they became mixed and emerged together, so the name 'tenth' was removed from the tenth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: a baraita states that two animals emerged in the tenth and were called 'tenth', yet the tenth and eleventh are mixed, even though the name 'tenth' was not removed from the tenth.

The Gemara initially suggests that the baraita supports the rule that when two emerge simultaneously, both become sanctified, but then rejects this and resolves that the case is where one animal emerged first and was called 'eleventh', then they became mixed and emerged together, so the name 'tenth' was removed from the tenth.
