The Gemara objects that the baraita explicitly says 'did not precede', which seems to contradict the resolution that one emerged first, and then reinterprets 'did not precede' to mean they became mixed afterward.

items.text: Discussion of Rabbi's opinion
items.text_en: Discussion of Rabbi's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the baraita aligns with Rabbi, who holds that calling the tenth 'eleventh' does not remove the name 'tenth' if one has many animals. Rava explains that Rabbi's ruling applies only when one has many animals, but here there are not many, so the name is removed. A baraita is cited showing Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda dispute this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the baraita aligns with Rabbi, who holds that calling the tenth 'eleventh' does not remove the name 'tenth'.
The Gemara answers that even according to Rabbi, his ruling applies only when one has many animals, but here there are not many, so the name is removed.
A baraita is cited showing Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda dispute this, and Rava explains that Rabbi's principle applies only when one has many animals.

items.text: Three conflicting baraitot on two animals in the tenth
items.text_en: Three conflicting baraitot on two animals in the tenth
items.desc_en: Three baraitot present conflicting rulings for two animals that emerged in the tenth: one says they graze, another says they are offered, and a third says they die. The Gemara resolves that the one saying 'graze' follows the Rabbis, who hold that one does not bring sacred animals to a state of disqualification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents three conflicting baraitot regarding two animals that emerged in the tenth: one says they graze, another says they are offered, and a third says they die.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the baraita that says 'graze' follows the Rabbis, who hold that one does not bring sacred animals to a state of disqualification.

items.text: Attribution of the baraitot to Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Attribution of the baraitot to Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the baraita stating that animals should be offered refers to Rabbi Shimon's view that consecrated animals can be brought even if blemished, while the baraita stating that they should die reflects Rabbi Yehuda's view that a ma'aser error constitutes a temurah, and temurat ma'aser must die.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction between the two baraitot by attributing the one that says 'they shall be offered' to Rabbi Shimon, who permits bringing blemished consecrated animals, and the one that says 'they shall die' to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a ma'aser counting error creates a temurah, and temurat ma'aser must die.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yehuda's position from a mishnah and baraita
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yehuda's position from a mishnah and baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the claim that Rabbi Yehuda holds temurat ma'aser dies, citing a mishnah where Rabbi Meir implies that Rabbi Yehuda believes temurat ma'aser is offered. A baraita further shows that Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between the eleventh animal and a shelamin, but still allows the eleventh itself to be offered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehuda's position that temurat ma'aser (the substitute of a tithe animal) dies, citing a mishnah where Rabbi Meir implies that Rabbi Yehuda holds it is offered.

A baraita is cited showing that Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between the eleventh animal and a shelamin, but still allows the eleventh itself to be offered, contradicting the claim that temurat ma'aser dies.

items.text: Proof from a Sifra that the eleventh is offered
items.text_en: Proof from a Sifra that the eleventh is offered
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Sifra that derives from the verse 'If from the cattle' that the eleventh animal is included with shelamin, and notes that the anonymous Sifra follows Rabbi Yehuda, further supporting that he holds the eleventh is offered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Sifra that derives from the verse 'אם מן הבקר' (If from the cattle) that the eleventh animal is included with שלמים (peace offerings).
The Gemara asks whether one might include the ninth animal as well, and answers that consecration sanctifies only after the original, not before, so only the eleventh is included.

The Gemara notes that the unattributed Sifra follows Rabbi Yehuda, and it teaches that the eleventh animal is included with שלמים (peace offerings), further supporting that Rabbi Yehuda holds the eleventh is offered.

items.text: Resolution by Rabbi Shimon bar Abba: dealing with ma'aser in the present time
items.text_en: Resolution by Rabbi Shimon bar Abba: dealing with ma'aser in the present time
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba resolves the contradiction before Rabbi Yochanan by explaining that the baraita deals with ma'aser in the present era, where the concern is a stumbling block (eating unconsecrated meat). The Gemara clarifies that even one animal would be problematic, but the baraita mentions two to preempt the concern that one might delay them until they develop a blemish.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba before Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba before Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita deals with מעשר (tithe) in the present time, where the concern is a stumbling block (eating unconsecrated meat).
The Gemara asks why the baraita specifically mentions two animals, since even one would be problematic.

The Gemara clarifies that the baraita uses the style of 'it is not necessary' — even one animal would die, but two are mentioned to preempt the concern that one might delay them until they develop a blemish.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Papi and Rav Papa on a messenger's error in ma'aser
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Papi and Rav Papa on a messenger's error in ma'aser
items.desc_en: An amoraic dispute is presented: Rav Papi says in the name of Rava that if the messenger called the ninth 'tenth' it becomes consecrated, but calling the eleventh 'tenth' does not. Rav Papa argues that even calling the ninth 'tenth' does not consecrate it, because the owner sent him to correct, not to err.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute: Rav Papi in the name of Rava rules that if the messenger called the ninth animal 'tenth' it becomes consecrated, but calling the eleventh 'tenth' does not.
Rav Papa argues that even calling the ninth 'tenth' does not consecrate it, because the owner sent the messenger to correct, not to err.

items.text: Comparison to the laws of terumah and resolution
items.text_en: Comparison to the laws of terumah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Papa's view from a mishnah where a messenger who adds or subtracts ten percent in terumah still effects terumah. The answer distinguishes: in terumah, since there are varying standards (generous vs. stingy), the owner implicitly authorized the messenger's judgment, but in ma'aser, the error is a mistake, and the owner did not authorize that.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Papa's view by citing a mishnah where a messenger who adds or subtracts ten percent in תרומה (priestly portion) still effects valid תרומה.

The answer distinguishes: in תרומה, since there are varying standards (generous vs. stingy), the owner implicitly authorized the messenger's judgment, but in מעשר (tithe), the error is a mistake, and the owner did not authorize that.
